Every public multiplayer match is reported to the hub when it ends: the final standings, and every incident the simulation raised, in order, with where the players involved stood. The hub shows the history at /matches, one match at /matches/<id>, a player's matches at /players/<name>, and a linked account's on its profile (/users/<id>). Matchmaking and ranking will build on the same records later; for now the job is to collect everything.

host's game hub (mjolnircore.com) MJOLNIRHud Scripts/matchlog.lua POST /api/v1/matches records incidents + positions, POST /api/v1/matches/claims writes match_.json ─┐ GET /api/v1/matches[/{id}] MJOLNIRLobby Scripts/matches.lua │ match_outbox.txt GET /api/v1/players/{name}/stats sends the outbox to the hub <─┘ GET /api/v1/users/{id}/match-stats D1: matches, match_players, participant's game match_events, match_claims MJOLNIRHud asks the host for the match id, (migrations/0014_matches.sql) writes claim_.json MJOLNIRLobby sends it

The host's incident handler gets every player's incidents; a fireteam client's gets almost none (multiplayer_hud.md), so only the host records. MJOLNIRHud already hooks OnIncident_Event for the kill feed. While its match log is recording, the hook also reads K2_GetActorLocation() of the incident's CauseObjectActor and EffectObjectActor: for a kill, the killer's and the victim's bipeds, at the moment the incident arrives. Every incident is kept except the respawn countdown (respawn_tick, respawn_final_tick): kills, deaths, suicides, spawns (with the spawn point), medals and commendations, flags, joins and quits, the end. Positions are the map's Unreal world space, in centimetres, Z up. They are real biped positions (checked 2026-10-03 on Blood Gulch: a bot standing still died a few centimetres from where it spawned). The cause object can be a vehicle when the killer drove one. A match is public if MJOLNIRLobby listed it on the hub at any point while it ran: the Lobby writes the listing's id to MJOLNIRLobby\listing.txt while listed, and the HUD reads it every five seconds. A private match is recorded and thrown away at its end.

The record is MJOLNIRHud\match_<id>.json, already in the shape the hub's MatchReport takes. It is rewritten every 30 seconds as an abandoned match, so a crash leaves what happened up to then. match_current.txt names the match being recorded; found at the next start, it marks a match a crash cut short, whose checkpoint is then sent. At the end (round_over, game_over, or the host leaving the map: abandoned) the file is written a last time and its id is appended to match_outbox.txt. An abandoned match under a minute long with no kill is not kept. The id is 32 random hex digits, made by the host. The hub never shows it; it is what a participant cites to claim its seat.

MJOLNIRLobby's matches.lua reads match_outbox.txt every 15 seconds and sends one file at a time through the native hub call public games use (mjolnir_hub_call, the launcher's key). A file is deleted once the hub has it (200/201) or refuses it for good (400, 409, 413, 422). No connection or a 5xx retry in a minute, a 429 in five; 401/403 (an old launcher sign-in) and 404 (a hub without these routes) in ten. Lua has no directory listing, hence the outbox. The HUD only appends to it; the Lobby rewrites it to the entries whose files remain. Both run on the game thread, so they never interleave.

A seat is a player as the host's game named them. Names are not identities, so each participant's own game claims its seat with its own hub key: A client's HUD asks the host: ServerExecRPC("MJOLNIR matchid"), every ten seconds until answered. The host's HUD hook (self is the asker's controller) answers on that controller: ClientMessage("MJOLNIR match <id> <public> <index> <name>", "MJOLNIR"), with the seat as the host recorded it. The host ignores its own outgoing answers, which its hook also sees. If public, the client writes claim_<id>.json and queues it. A private answer is asked again every 30 seconds, since a game can go public. These are the RPCs MJOLNIRLobby's messages already ride (multiplayer_postgame.md); the Lobby and the level loader ignore the new verbs. No object scans on either side. The hub keeps claims apart from seats (match_claims) so either can arrive first; whichever lands second links the seat (match_players.user_id). A claim links only a seat of the same name, one account per seat and one seat per account per match; a newer claim replaces the account's own older one. The host's seat is linked by the report itself (host_index). Both writes take the lobbies:write scope every launcher key already has (migration 0013), so nobody signs in again.

hub/src/lib/api/matches.ts. The report is validated (16 seats, 20,000 events, six hours), stored in one D1 batch, seats and events each inserted by a single json_each statement (D1 counts statements against a request's budget). The hub works out each seat's place and outcome (win, loss, draw; none for an abandoned match) and the match's winner: the team with more points, or the top score alone (a shared top is a draw). The host's clock is trusted only to the last week and never ahead of the hub's. Reporting the same id twice from the same account is a no-op; from another, 409. A listing id that still exists must be the caller's. Chat: the host's game also sends each match's chat log (POST /matches/chat, migrations/0020); a reported public match shows it on /matches/<id>, naming a hub account only for a line from a seat linked to that account, while a private game's log is read only by moderators from the report queue. Pages: /matches (filters by game type and map, player search), /matches/<id> (scoreboard by team, the timeline, and the kill and death positions over the map, per player with ?p=<index>), /players/<name> (the combat record below), and the same record on /users/<id>.

players/_components/PlayerRecordView.tsx draws a career from the match tables (lib/api/player-record.ts), read on each view; no rollup table yet. The career signature (CareerRing.tsx): every match the player fought in as a spoke around a ring, oldest at the top and clockwise, kills reaching out and deaths reaching in, wins gold. Matches with no kill or death are left off it, and it keeps the newest 200. Form: career K/D match by match, and personal bests. Battlegrounds: where the player stood for each kill and died, over the map (?map=<CODE>, the newest 600 marks). It defaults to their busiest map. Arsenal: kills by weapon and class. The class with 40% of 15 or more kills names the player's style; otherwise "All-rounder". Rivals: who they traded the most kills with, one row a person, by account when the seat is linked and by name when it is not. Medal case: only the incidents in MEDAL_TYPES. A kill raises a run of sibling incidents (sniper_kill, precision_comm, ...), so a new medal has to be added to that list and to MEDALS in players/_components/record.ts. A medal the game sends together with one that stands for it (a headshot beside a sniper headshot, MEDAL_HIDDEN_BY) is counted once.

A match's page (/matches/<id>) shows the same medals for that match: a Medals column on the scoreboard and, under it, each player's medals by kind (matches/_components/medals.ts, from the match's own events, with the same list and the same hiding). Win rate counts finished matches only: an abandoned match has no outcome. A name page links a hub profile only when every linked seat under that name is the same account.

/leaderboards ranks hub accounts by kills, K/D, wins, win rate, headshots and best match, all time or over 30 or 7 days (lib/api/leaderboards.ts). Two rules decide what counts, both about trust: Only a linked seat places. Anyone can play under any name, so a name on a board would be a way to wear someone else's record. Only a match with two linked seats counts. A report is its host's word, and a host alone, or alone with AI bots, could otherwise fill a board. So a board can read lower than the career total on a profile, and the page says so. K/D needs 20 kills over 3 matches, and win rate 3 finished matches, to place. Banned accounts never show. Two colluding accounts can still report what they like: weighing host trust is what real ranking still has to add.
The hub › The map under the positions

A match on a map the hub has a preview model of draws its kills and deaths over the level with three.js (MatchMap.tsx, mapViewer.ts): a top-down minimap (orthographic, panned and zoomed) or the level in 3D to orbit. A cut slider takes off everything above a height, so a lower floor shows on Prisoner or Chill Out; the map's faces point into the play space, so an indoor map is seen through its roof either way. Hovering a dot shows the kill. Other maps, and a browser without WebGL, get the plain SVG plot. Under the map, a replay (MatchReplay.tsx): play the match at 10× to 120× (the default plays it in about a minute) or scrub it, and the map, either kind, shows only what had happened by then, the last moments larger and the rest faded. Ticks on the scrub bar mark when each kill (gold) and death (red) came. The timeline follows the replay, and a row jumps the replay to it. "Show all" goes back to the whole match. The models are hub/public/map-previews/<CODE>.glb, listed in hub/src/app/matches/_components/map-previews.json, made from a converted map's output folder (ce_map_conversion.md): python tools/level/export_map_preview.py out/bgl BGL hub/public/map-previews --manifest hub/src/app/matches/_components/map-previews.json
The hub › The map under the positions

It takes scene.gltf (the BSP with its scenery; no sky, no glass or water), quantized (KHR_mesh_quantization) to 100 KB to 1.2 MB a map, with a vertex colour for the textures: CE's texture pass with the base map shrunk to 16×16 and each detail map as its average colour, times the lightmap. The model is glTF metres, Y up, at CE coordinates; a recorded Unreal position is (x, z, y) / 100 in it. Checked 2026-10-05 against 12 prod matches on 12 maps: every recorded position falls inside its map's model. Re-export a map whenever it is re-converted.

A report is the host's word. The hub records who reported it, and seats link only to the accounts that claim them, but standings are not verified. Ranking built on this should weigh hosts (agreement between participants' own views, per-host history) before it trusts a report.

0014_matches.sql. Migration 0001 carried unused placeholder matches and match_players tables; 0014 renames them to legacy_* rather than dropping them unseen. Like every migration it must be applied to production by hand before the hub deploy that uses it (pnpm db:migrate:prod).

Hub: hub dev server with local D1 (pnpm db:migrate), a seeded user and key, then POST reports and claims. Claim before and after the report, a wrong name, a taken seat, a duplicate report, another account's id. Game, one PC (2026-10-03): host BGL Slayer with a CreatePlayer bot and a hand-written listing.txt; blam unit_kill (unit (list_get (players) 1)) for deaths; mjolnir_auto endgame. The record, posted to the local hub, rendered as written. Two PCs (2026-10-03, tools/remote/jip-test.mjs, PC 2 joining PC 1's public BGL match under way): PC 2 claimed seat 1 in the match PC 1 recorded. The host's record held two real kills (an assault rifle first blood; a Warthog splatter, WarthogDriver modifier 3, the cause position the vehicle's), with positions for both players. Posted to a local hub, claim first, both seats linked. The first run had claimed seat 0: a joiner reads index 0 on the host for a few seconds after it is seated, so the host now answers only with the asker's own recorded seat. A host's ban list kicks a banned joiner about a second in; an old ban of the test account looked like a failed join until it was cleared.

Heatmaps across matches per map, from match_events (indexed by type), over the same preview models. Periodic position samples (where players walk, not just where they die). Ranking: per-account ratings from linked seats in completed matches.

Everyone who plays online signs the MJOLNIR launcher in with Discord, so in game a player is shown by their hub account, its name and avatar, instead of their Steam or Xbox name. From the post-game screen a player can report another. Moderators review reports at /moderation, and can ban a player from matchmaking. Status as of 2026-10-10: the hub, the HUD and the Lobby work end to end on one PC against a local hub. The two-PC exchange (a joiner proving itself to a host) is still untested. Update 2026-10-21: shipped in mods-v0.22.0 (PR #172), and the hub side reached main with that merge. No two-PC test of the exchange is recorded since.

A name is the host's to trust or not: anyone can call themselves anything, and the scoreboard, the kill feed and above all a report must not name the wrong account. So each player proves its account to the host with a ticket from the hub: joiner's game hub host's game POST /identity/tickets ───────────▶ ticket for (joiner, {platform_name, audience=host} audience host, in-game name), 15 minutes iam ─────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ (ServerExecRPC) POST /identity/tickets/resolve ◀─ {tickets} ──▶ {platform_name, player, reports, matchmaking_ban} checks platform_name == the sender's in-game name ids ◀──────────────────────────────────── (ClientMessage) The audience. Only the host the ticket names can trade it. A host that took a joiner's ticket and passed it to another host would get nothing for it. The joiner learns the host's account from the host's own ids broadcast. The in-game name. The hub returns the name the ticket was issued for. The host keeps the answer only if it is the name of the controller that sent the ticket. Even with a valid audience, a ticket stolen in transit names nobody else. The host itself asks POST /identity/tickets with no audience. That makes no ticket and just answers who it is and whether it is banned.

The roster is keyed by in-game name, as everything else between the host and its fireteam already is (ballots, bans, seats). Each entry is the account id, its name (display name, else the Discord username) and its public report count. ids goes out when the roster changes, every 30 s while anyone else is connected, and when a client asks (whois, sent by a client that has not heard one). Every machine writes what it knows to MJOLNIRLobby\identities.txt, one line per player: <in-game name>\t<account id>\t<hub name>\t<reports>. MJOLNIRHud reads that file; it never touches the hub itself.
Who is who › Where the hub name shows

Tab scoreboard (MJOLNIRHud): the name, plus the avatar in a new Avatar<i> image per row. Kill feed and winner line: the name. A joiner's "joined the game" line waits up to 8 s for its account (its ticket lands a few seconds after the join), then falls back to the in-game name. Since MJOLNIRHud 0.7.0 (PR #189, mods-v0.25.0) each feed row also shows both players' avatars. Match chat (PR #200, mods-v0.27.0): the sender's hub name and avatar. The game's FIRETEAM panel (top right of the main menu): each row's NameText. The game's view model rewrites its names every few seconds, and each row writes its text again in OnBackingDataChanged, so squadpanel.lua hooks that (and OnListItemObjectSet) and sets the hub name after it. Renaming the view model's DisplayName does not stick. Our lobby's player list (WBP_MJOLNIRLobby): the name. Name tags over teammates: the hub name is written into the game's PlayerNameValue when a tag is shown. This one is untested; the game may write its own name back. Post-game screen (MJOLNIRLobby): the name and avatar per row. p.name stays the in-game name everywhere it is a key: match seats and claims, host bans, ballots. Only what is drawn changes.

The game's hub call reaches nothing but the hub (mjolnir_lobby.c refuses another host, and must not carry the launcher key to one). So the hub proxies avatars: GET /api/v1/users/{id}/avatar returns the Discord avatar at 64 px, or Discord's default one for an account without one. It is a PNG, cached at Cloudflare for a day and in browsers for an hour. The Lobby fetches each account's avatar once a session with the hub call's FILE mode, into MJOLNIRMaps\_covers\av_<id>.png. Lobby and HUD read the file into a texture with ImportFileAsTexture2D, the way map covers are read. No native change was needed.

On the post-game screen every row is now a button (RowButton<i>). A row is enabled when its player has a hub account and is not you; clicking it opens the report panel: who: avatar, hub name, the in-game name if different, and the public report count; WHY: one of CHEATING, BETRAYING, HARASSMENT, GRIEFING / AFK, QUITTING, NAME OR AVATAR, OTHER; WHAT HAPPENED: an optional note of up to 1000 characters, in a MultiLineEditableTextBox (typing works on the menu stack); SEND REPORT / CANCEL. The report is POST /api/v1/players/reports with: the account the host resolved for that seat; the reason and the note; the in-game name the reporter saw; the match's id: the host's own record, or the id the host told the client. MJOLNIRHud now writes it into last_match.txt (field 8 of the match line). Each player line in last_match.txt gained three fields: the account id, the hub name and the report count. One report per reporter, player and match: a second one gets 409, and the panel says it was already sent. The vote lasts 20 s, which is not enough to write a report. While anyone has the panel open, the host holds the countdown: opening or closing the panel sends reporting 1 or reporting 0; the hold lasts at most 90 s per vote, and a player's hold lapses after 120 s; the vote message gained a ninth field, held, so every screen says VOTING PAUSED / A PLAYER IS FILING A REPORT.
Reporting a player › What is public

Only the number. A profile's Multiplayer section (/users/<id>) shows Reports: the reports against the account that a moderator has not dismissed. The same figure is stats.player_reports on GET /api/v1/users/{id}, and appears in the report panel and in the roster. Who reported, and why, is for moderators only.

At /moderation, moderators and admins get Player reports, grouped by the player reported (most reports first), with tabs for Open, Upheld and Dismissed. Each player shows: every report against them, with its reason and note; who filed it and when; the name it was filed under; a link to the match when the host reported it, or a flag when either player is not linked to a seat in it. Update 2026-10-21: since PR #200 (mods-v0.27.0) a report from a match whose host sent its chat log opens that log (GET /moderation/match-chat/{host_match_id}, hub/src/lib/api/matches.ts, migration 0020), with the reported player's lines marked. Since PR #201 this desk is the Players tab of /moderation. The decisions: Uphold: the report stands and stays in the public count. Dismiss: unfounded; it leaves the public count. Ban from matchmaking: a reason (the player sees it) and 1, 3, 7 or 30 days, or permanent. It replaces a ban in force, upholds the player's open reports, and takes down a game they have listed. Only an admin can ban a moderator or an admin. Lift ban. Matchmaking bans lists the bans in force. Every decision is written to audit_log.
Moderation › What a matchmaking ban does

Where Effect POST /lobbies 403 matchmaking_banned, with the reason and end; the game's status line shows it GET /lobbies/{id}/join the same 403: no connection string GET /lobbies a banned host's games are not listed Ban issued the banned player's listing is deleted; their heartbeat then 404s and the game stops listing A public game's host resolves a banned joiner's ticket, sends them back to their menu (kick) It is not a hub ban (users.banned_at): the account still signs in, downloads and comments. A banned player can still join a friend's game by invite: that never touches the hub. Their identity is still resolved there, and they are kicked only if that game is public.

hub/src/lib/api/players.ts, migrations/0018_player_identity_reports.sql: identity_tickets: the hash of each ticket, never the ticket. Rows expire after 15 minutes and are swept when new ones are issued. player_reports: its own table, because reports.reason is a CHECK enum about mods that SQLite cannot widen. A unique index on (reporter, subject, match). matchmaking_bans: kept after they end or are lifted. The ban in force is one that is not lifted and has not expired. Route Who POST /identity/tickets lobbies:write (every launcher key) POST /identity/tickets/resolve lobbies:write, the ticket's audience GET /users/{id}/avatar anyone POST /players/reports lobbies:write, 30 an hour GET /moderation/player-reports, POST /moderation/player-reports/{id} moderators GET/POST /moderation/matchmaking-bans, DELETE /moderation/matchmaking-bans/{user_id} moderators GET /moderation/match-chat/{host_match_id} (matches.ts, since PR #200) moderators Like every migration, 0018 must be applied to production by hand before the hub deploy that uses it (pnpm db:migrate:prod).

build_mjolnir_ui.py adds three things, so chunk 984 must be rebuilt and cooked: Avatar<i> images to the scoreboard and post-game rows; RowButton<i> around each post-game row; the Report panel. An older container still works: the Lua checks each new widget and draws text only, with no click.

One PC, 2026-10-10: Setup. The game was pointed at a local hub (MJOLNIR_HUB_URL). The launcher's account was seeded there with only its key's hash. The rebuilt chunk 984 replaced pakchunk900-MJOLNIRHUB-mjolnir-ce-runtime-0_P (the UI container as the runtime ships it). Identity. The Lobby resolved the account, wrote identities.txt and cached the avatar. The Tab scoreboard showed the hub name and avatar in place of the in-game name. Post-game. A hand-written last_match.txt showed the post-game rows with avatars, and a row without an account had none. Clicking a row opened the panel and held the vote. Typing reached the text box. SEND REPORT filed the report with its reason, note, in-game name and match id, then the panel closed and the vote resumed. Fireteam and lobby. The FIRETEAM panel and our lobby's player list showed the hub name, and it survived the view model's refreshes. The delayed "joined" line is covered by the Lua tests only: it needs a second player. Hub API. Tickets, the audience check, reports and their duplicates, bans refusing POST /lobbies and joins, lifting, and the avatar proxy. The moderation page and the profile count were checked in a browser.

Two PCs. A joiner's ticket reaching the host, the roster reaching the joiner, and a banned joiner kicked from a public game. Name tags. Whether the game keeps our hub name in a tag. Unverified players. A public game could refuse players with no resolved account (an old launcher, or no sign-in) after a grace period. Not done, because it would send away anyone on a stale sign-in. Reporting from the website. A participant could report from /matches/<id> too, for when the post-game screen is gone. Linking seats from tickets. The host could cite resolved accounts in its match report, so seats link without each client's claim.

AI players that fill a multiplayer match (issue #247): the simulation's own AI, given a seat and a name on MJOLNIR's scoreboard. They run on the host; a fireteam client sees them through the simulation's own replication. Proven on Blood Gulch on 2026-10-25, host and one joiner on two PCs: the bots walk the map, fight the players and each other, die and respawn, and both machines' feeds and boards name them and count the same kills. In team games they play for red and blue (PC 1, 2026-10-31): the two sides fight each other, a bot leaves the players of its own side alone, and its kills score for its team.

Where What level bake, blam.bots (level_format.md) bot squads, a zone of firing positions, an objective, AI pathfinding for the map's BSP; <CODE>.bots.json, where the squads stand crates/blam-sbsp/src/pathfinding.rs the pathfinding tables, from a structure BSP's collision shell MJOLNIRLobby's DLL, mjolnir_bots_enable lets ai_place place squads in a Megalo game, and makes elites short enough for low doorways there MJOLNIRLobby's DLL, mjolnir_bots_teams in a team game, gives AI units the multiplayer team of their side MJOLNIRLobby settings.lua BOTS, BOT TYPE and BOT DIFFICULTY on the PLAYERS page of the host's game settings: bots=N;bot_type=K;bot_level=L in the settings line tools/level/build_bot_characters.sh the bots' characters: the Spartan, and every kind at each difficulty MJOLNIRHud Scripts/bots.lua places, names, respawns and directs the bots on the host MJOLNIRHud main.lua, relay.lua bot seats on the board and in the feed, on the host and its clients MJOLNIRHud commands.lua /bots <0-15> [kind] [level]: the host changes this match's bots

ai_place refuses multiplayer games. Its core returns unless the game mode is campaign or Firefight; a Megalo match is neither. MJOLNIRLobby's DLL patches that one test (found by its bytes, so an update that moves it is left alone). Nothing else gates AI: once placed they think, path and fight (re/ai_in_multiplayer.md). Converted maps have no navigation. Their BSP replaces B40's geometry, but the scenario still carries B40's pathfinding for it. The bake builds the pathfinding from the map's own collision: every walkable shell surface (normal within about 49 degrees of up, not breakable) is a sector, every collision edge touching one is a link, oriented so its walkable side is on the left (CE's winged edges are already the rings the sim walks), and the shell gets one 2D reference per surface naming its sector. Blood Gulch: 2947 sectors, 4930 links, one connected area of 2828 sectors. Two things cut a converted map's ground that the edges alone miss, and the bake handles both the way B40's own data does (re/ai_in_multiplayer.md):

Steps. A riser under 0.1 wu (where the AI globals' hoist step begins) between two floors becomes a step sector, walkable, linked to both. Short bands of a taller riser, or a slab's side face hanging below its floor, do not. Cracks. Maps built of separate slabs meet floor to floor without sharing an edge: edge to edge, overlapping a hair, or across a crack. Two floor edges that both drop away, face each other within 0.1 wu and lie less than a step apart in height join through an intersection link, a hint on each floor's edge naming a link that joins the two. Neither is a jump, a hoist, a ladder or a teleporter: ground those reach stays apart. On Night Lockout (PC 1, 2026-10-30) bots walked back and forth across its slab seams (two bots, 14 crossings in two minutes) and one crossed the lower level to kill the idle player.

AI stand still without orders. They hold firing positions in their task's areas until they see someone, and AI far from every player go idle. Each bot is forced active when placed (ai_force_active), the bake gives the objective the tasks area_0 .. area_15 (a map with fewer areas repeats them, one with more shares them out, so every task the HUD names is there) and makes hunt follow the players (radius 3 wu, every player slot), and the host's HUD orders each bot every 8-16 s, waking its body first (see "Bots frozen in place" below): three times in four after an enemy, otherwise (ai_set_task <squad> mjolnir_bots area_<r>) to a random area. An enemy human is hunted: the hunt task and (ai_magically_see_object <squad> (player_get n)), where n counts the players there are (player_get returns the nth player in the players table, not a seat), so the HUD passes the target's rank among the humans in seat order. In a team game an enemy is anyone on the other side, a bot too: a bot is no player, so it gets an area walk and (ai_magically_see <squad> <enemy squad>). A human whose side the HUD has not read yet is no one's target in a team game.

Where bots spawn. On the map's own player starts. The bake stands each bot squad on one of the starts on the ground the bots walk (bots_finish), so a bot appears where a player would. Squad k of every kind takes the k-th start farthest first: the first start, then each time the one farthest from those already taken. A level lists its starts a base at a time, so taken in the level's order (as before 2026-10-31) the first eight bots on Blood Gulch all stood at one base and fought there. A map with more starts than squads (15 per kind) never uses the rest. The bake also writes where each squad stands, <CODE>.bots.json (Unreal cm, by squad index; with each area's extent and the areas each area_<k> task covers), which the map's pack carries beside its level file (map/bots.json, installed to ue4ss/MJOLNIRMaps/<CODE>/; a test install's goes to MJOLNIRLevelLoader's levels/). With it, the host's HUD picks a bot's squad each time it places the bot, so the bot comes in where its side is. A side has no base of its own: a converted map's player spawns are all neutral, and on Blood Gulch Team Slayer the red host's first spawn landed at the south base in one match and the north in another. So the HUD does what the game's respawns do for players, in order:

a free squad of the bot's kind (none another bot out holds); never within 2 wu of anyone; with an enemy about, a start no enemy is within 25 wu of, or failing that the starts farthest from the enemies (within 10 wu of the farthest); with its side about and the enemies clear, the starts nearest one of its side (within 8 wu of the nearest); with no one about, its own squad k (the farthest-first order); otherwise one of what is left at random. In Free for All everyone is an enemy, so a bot comes in away from all of them. The first bots wait up to 5 s for the humans' first spawn. A bot starts each life with what a player starts with: the hub's bots.json gives every Spartan squad the assault rifle (the default multiplayer loadout), elites the plasma rifle and grunts and jackals the plasma pistol. Anything better it picks up off the ground, as a player would. (Until 2026-11 a Spartan's squad carried one of a mixed list, so bots came in with snipers and rockets.) On Blood Gulch Team Slayer (PC 1, 2026-10-31) the red host spawned at the north base: the three red bots came in beside him and the five blue bots at the south base. A map without the file (every map published before it) keeps squad k for bot k, as before.

Why bots stand still. Seen on Night Lockout and Blood Gulch: a bot sent to hunt a player it cannot reach (on ground the pathfinding does not join) waits at the nearest point; the HUD picked area_<r> from 0-15 while most maps baked fewer areas, so those orders went nowhere (every map bakes all sixteen tasks since 2026-10-31); and on narrow ground hunt's 3 wu radius found no firing position to stand on until the bake narrowed the grid there. An AI with no target holds its task's positions: the simulation's own search follows a target it lost, it does not roam. Bots frozen in place. Three things kept bots still for minutes on Blood Gulch (PC 1, 2026-10-31, re/ai_in_multiplayer.md):

A sleeping body. A bot's body falls asleep in the physics when it stands still, as anyone's does, and sometimes its AI does not wake it again: the AI goes on thinking and its squad takes every order, but the body neither moves nor turns, not even when shot. A Spartan stood so on open ground for five and a half minutes. ai_force_active does not wake a body; (object_wake_physics (ai_get_unit <squad>)) does, and the Spartan walked off within a second of it. So every order the HUD gives a bot starts with that line, and a bot whose body stays asleep waits for its next order (8-16 s), not for minutes. The flag rooms. A bot on the lower floor under a base's deck, by the flag, stayed there: ordered anywhere, it walked about the room, a little way up an exit ramp and back, and stopped; a jackal stayed over half an hour, a grunt over 20 minutes. A converted map's collision is there twice, as the map's own shell and as a copy of it placed as instanced geometry, at one height to within f32 rounding, and the rounding decides which one the simulation meets under a bot: on the flag-room floors the copy nearly every time, elsewhere a third to two thirds of the time.

On the copy a bot is on no sector (the bake gives the copy no pathfinding of its own, and giving it the shell's crashed the game): it keeps the last place it stood on the shell and walks a path it already has, but cannot plan a new one, and wanders until it steps back onto the shell, which in a flag room means an exit ramp. Bots stood so beside the bases too; path followers had no plan in 29 to 48% of samples. Since 2026-10-31 the bake lowers the copy 0.001 wu under the shell: in two 10-minute matches the followers had no plan in 0.35% and 0.38% of samples, and no bot stayed in a flag room longer than 53 s. A map published before then keeps the trap until it is rebaked. Elites in the side doorways. The ramp from a base's deck down to each side door passes under the door's lintel, 0.82 wu above the ramp at its inner edge. An upright elite (0.8 wu tall, radius 0.18) does not fit on that slope: one walking down jams its head on the lintel's corner, facing the door, twitching, and stays until it turns back (one stood five minutes; sent down on purpose, it jammed every time it took the ramp), and one climbing stops 0.1 short of the corner and backs down, so no elite walks onto a deck. Spartans, grunts, jackals and a crouching elite fit. Flagging the ramps crouchable in the pathfinding changes nothing: an AI crouches for danger, cover or a script, never for its path.

Leaving the ramps out of the pathfinding is no answer either: they are the only way to walk onto a deck. An elite whose standing capsule is 0.70 tall passes both ways, and 0.72 still jams (tested live by writing the capsule, which the game builds from the tag's heights at load). Since 2026-10-31 the lobby DLL makes every elite 0.70 tall in a Megalo game once the host's HUD has started bots. It acts in Megalo games only, and a match's tags unload when it ends, so campaign elites should keep their height (by construction; not measured in a mission). On PC 1, an elite sent down from the south deck took the ramp three times out of five and walked out of the door each time (the other two times it dropped off the deck); HUD elites walked down two of the ramps, and one walked up onto the deck.

Stuck bots are placed again. A bot that stays within 6 wu for 40 s is woken and sent to an area that does not hold it (an area_<k> order, with no other order for 15 s); a bot that waited at a firing position or fought in one place walks off, and one that has neither left nor reached that area is erased and placed again on a start, as a respawn without a death (the HUD logs stayed ... placing it again). With the lowered copy it catches bots idle under their orders, jammed or blocked: on Blood Gulch with eight bots, 12 in 10 minutes, half of them stuck by the simulation's own reading and the rest bots whose actors had stopped following them. It judges only a bot whose actor it has seen move since placing it: a placement sometimes takes an actor that stays where the bot came in while the bot walks off, and placing that bot again only takes another. A bot that wanders wider than 6 wu is not caught. The areas come from the map's bots.json, so a map baked before 2026-10-31 (no areas there) gets no such help.

Who bots fight (measured in Team Slayer on Blood Gulch, 2026-10-30; re/ai_in_multiplayer.md). Every unit carries a campaign team and a multiplayer team. A player's unit is on red or blue with no campaign team; the simulation puts a bot's on its squad's campaign team (covenant) with no multiplayer team, every tick. In a Megalo game a unit with no multiplayer team is everyone's enemy, and bot against bot is decided by campaign teams: bots of one team never fight each other (covenant, flood, sentinel and heretic bots do fight one another). That is how bots play Free for All: every one covenant, attacking every player and leaving the other bots alone. No script function gives an AI unit a multiplayer team (mp_ai_allegiance is compiled out, ai_allegiance gated to campaign).

Red and blue bots. In a team game each bot plays for a side. MJOLNIRLobby's DLL (mjolnir_bots_teams) turns the unit update's or dx, 0xff00 (multiplayer team -1) into a call to a few bytes of its own that look the multiplayer team up by campaign team, in a table the HUD writes (native\bot_teams.txt: covenant 3 plays for red 0, flood 8 for blue 1). A bot's squad is put on its side's team (ai_set_team: covenant for red, flood for blue) before its ai_place, and the new actor takes it. Moved after placing, a blue bot was red for a tick, and a blue Spartan could keep the red armour MJOLNIRLevelLoader tinted it as it appeared (seen on PC 1). Red and blue bots fight on sight and bots of one side leave each other alone, and the game's damage code knows the sides: a red bot's hit on a red player is flagged friendly (bDamagedByFriendly), and a player's kill of a bot on their side raises kill_betrayal.

Players get their side's campaign team too. An AI picks its enemies by campaign teams alone: when it notices a unit it marks it an enemy if either campaign team is -1 or the allegiance matrix says so, and never asks the Megalo team rule (re/ai_in_multiplayer.md). A player's unit has campaign team -1 in a Megalo game, so before this every bot took every player for an enemy: in an isolated run a red bot killed the red host who walked up to it, as covenant, as sentinel and as human. A player's unit copies its pair from the player every tick, so while the table is in, the DLL gives each player on red the covenant campaign team and each player on blue flood. A red bot then sees a red player as one of its own and a blue player as an enemy. Tested isolated on Blood Gulch (2026-10-31, PC 1, nobody at the keyboard): a red covenant grunt beside the red host held fire for 35 s; with the table turned around (flood red, covenant blue) a grunt moved to flood before its placement held fire beside the host, now flood, and a covenant elite placed beside them took the host's shields in seconds.

The DLL changes the code on the simulation thread between ticks, puts it back when the HUD clears the table (the match ends), and on its own once the game is not a Megalo one; Free for All leaves it alone. A bot's side is chosen when it is first placed, for the side with fewer players (humans and bots); on a tie the side with fewer humans, as a human plays better than a bot; then blue. It keeps that side for the match, and the board files it there (its biped reports the side too, so kills of it read right). Slayer's score ignores bots. Its kill trigger counts kills of players, so the round never ended on bot kills. With bots playing, the host's HUD ends the match itself when anyone (bot or player) reaches the score to win, the way the game's own round_over does: final standings, then the post-game screen. A fireteam client gets no round_over; it follows the host's travel. AI are not players. Their incidents carry player index -1 and the AI biped's actor: a player who kills a bot raises Kill (no death), or kill_betrayal and no Kill when the bot is on their side; a bot that kills a player raises the player's death (no Kill). The HUD gives bot k the seat 100 + k (the match log records only seats 0-15, so bots never reach the hub) and translates -1 to the seat by actor, then counts both ways (a kill_betrayal of a bot as a kill: -1 in Team Slayer).

A bot killed by a bot raises nothing: no Kill, no death, only kill medals such as first_blood with no seats. Its body stays an actor where it fell, so the HUD would have counted it alive and never placed it again. The HUD reads each bot's unit on its actor instead (BlamObjectDamage:IsDead(), every 0.25 s), and the actor's blueprint keeps each hit's aftermath (Blam Aftermath Result: the damage owner's actor, the damage type and modifier the incidents carry, and bBodyDepleted on the killing blow). When the owner is another bot, the HUD queues the Kill the game would have raised: the feed, the board, the team score and the fireteam's clients all have it. A bot that dies with no player's Kill naming it within 2 s (a fall, its own grenade) waits out the respawn time with no line.

A map offers kinds (blam.bots.types), each with count squads of its own: spartan_<k>, elite_<k>, grunt_<k>, jackal_<k> on Blood Gulch. The host's BOT TYPE picks one (SPARTANS, ELITES, GRUNTS, JACKALS) or MIXED, which takes them in turn; /bots 6 elites changes it mid-match. A map baked before kinds has bot_<k> squads only, which every kind falls back to. Every kind plays a character of MJOLNIR's own at each difficulty level (tools/level/build_bot_characters.sh): mjolnir_bot_<kind>_<level> for spartan, elite, grunt and jackal, and normal, heroic and legendary, each with mjolnir_bot_generic_<level> as its parent. A map bakes a squad set per kind and level (spartan_legendary_<k>; 180 squads on Blood Gulch) and the host's BOT DIFFICULTY (default LEGENDARY) or /bots 6 elites heroic picks one. A map baked before levels has <kind>_<k> squads, which a bot falls back to.

Accuracy. AI aim from per-weapon accuracy bounds and times for normal, heroic and legendary. A Megalo match always plays at Normal: the simulation reads the difficulty (game options +0x1e4) in about fifteen places, through two helpers and inline copies, all gated to campaign and Firefight, and some of them also scale the players. So the bot characters carry their level's values in their Normal slots instead: mjolnir_bot_generic_<level> is ai\generic so tuned, and each bot character tunes its own weapon entries the same way (normal keeps the shipped values). There is no Easy: the characters have no easy accuracy. Spartans. No Spartan AI character ships, so mjolnir_bot_spartan is the Marine's (trooper: human weapons, grenades, cover) in the players' own body, objects\characters\spartans\spartans. Their squads are on the Covenant team, since a Marine's own team is the players'. Shields and health. An AI unit's vitality comes from its character's vitality block, not its body's model, and the Marine's has no shield (0) and a body that heals itself. So build_bot_characters.sh reads the players' model (objects\characters\spartans\spartans, new damage info) and writes it into the Spartan bot characters: body 45, shield 70, the shield back after 6 s over its recharge time (3 s), no body regeneration, at every level. A Spartan bot takes the hits a player takes.

Checked in game 2026-11-21 (Blood Gulch, values poked into the running game): bots had read 105 body and no shield; with these they read 45 and 70, and a bot and the player hit by the same damage_object for 40 lost the same 57% and refilled frame for frame. The player's shield starts back a second before the model's stun time (7 s) says, so the bots' delay is the stun time less a second; at 7 a bot recharged a second late. The host's Shields setting is a player trait and does not reach bots. Every machine in the match needs the characters' containers, pakchunk995-MJOLNIRBOT-<kind>-<level>_P (15). They ship in the CE runtime pack from 1.16.0, which every map with bots requires.
Identity: which actor is which bot

Bot actors come from a pool (BP_EliteBipedActor_C and friends; a pooled one waits at the origin), and an erased AI leaves its actor where it stood for the next placement to reuse. So bots are placed one at a time, and the bot just placed is the actor that came out of the pool, or jumped more than 4 m, since its ai_place (a jump between two scans, 0.25 s apart, which only a teleport makes). An actor is that bot's until the Kill that names it. A Spartan bot's actor is the players' class, BP_SpartansBipedActor_C, so an actor a player spawned in (their player_spawn names it) is never taken for a bot. The actors come from Scripts/bipeds.lua, one NotifyOnNewObject on the bipeds' native ancestor armed when the HUD loads, before any map. It sees every biped actor as it is made, the pools a map makes as it loads included, so a match never walks the object array for them. FindAllOf costs about 23 ms a class in a match:
Identity: which actor is which bot

Scanning six classes every tick held the game thread 135 ms three times a second. Scanning the seven classes once when bots started (until MJOLNIRHud 0.19.1) made a 108–129 ms Hud tick 3 s into hosted matches, and again on up to three rescans. A watch on a Blueprint class's own path needs the class loaded, and a Blueprint class can be unloaded and loaded again between maps at a new address. Spartans have no pool waiting, so a match starting before the first spawn (Forge on Yoyorast) once saw none of its Spartan bots. Each placement looked like a squad the map lacks, so each bot was placed four times and given up on: thirty-two AI with no seat on the board. A native class is never unloaded. A scan (every 0.25 s) reads only the actors out of the pool at the last read: the bots, their bodies left standing, and the players. Every pooled actor of a class is read only from the moment a bot of that class is due to be placed until it is seen, plus a full read every 5 s. The step uses only actors out of the pool, and a placement must see its actor leave the pool. Reading all of Blood Gulch's 271 pooled bipeds every scan was about 2,200 calls a second: with 8 bots, the Hud tick went from 11.6 to 5.0 ms/s (MJOLNIRHud 0.19.1, tools/tests/test_bots_scan.lua).
Identity: which actor is which bot

As a backstop, if the watch could not be armed, bots start with one scan of each class, and a placement that times out scans its own kind's class once before placing again (three a match at most). A try that gives up erases its squad.

A client hears bot seats in the host's relayed incidents (multiplayer_hud.md) and needs their names. When it meets a seat it cannot name it asks (ServerExecRPC "MJOLNIR bots?"), holding those lines up to 3 s; the host answers that player alone with MJOLNIR bots 100=Nadia (bot);101=..., and tells every player once when its bots change. In a team game each seat carries its side's letter (R100=Nadia (bot);B101=...), which a client from before sides skips: a relayed line has no biped to read the side from. Once it has the roster, a client drops its own copies of AI kills and deaths (they name the AI -1) and counts the host's.

The map needs bot squads and pathfinding in its scenario, so it is baked with blam.bots. Blood Gulch, from the hub install's own files and examples/levels/bloodgulch_bots.bake.level.json (the hub level.json with the loader-only keys left out, plus the bots block the PC 1 tests used): # the installed BSP, as the bake's --bsp payload mjolnir extract --out tags --filter "solo/bgl/" mjolnir level bake examples/levels/bloodgulch_bots.bake.level.json --standalone BGL \ --bsp 8=tags/Levels/Halo1/Solo/BGL/Generated/BSP_01_1_Start.scenario_structure_bsp \ --world-object /Game/Levels/Halo1/Solo/BGL/BGL.BGL --out-dir out Every machine in the match needs the same scenario. The test install put the result beside the hub's as pakchunk997-MJOLNIRBOTS-BGL_9_P, whose _9_P outranked the hub release's containers at the time. On launcher 0.24.0 and newer every hub container sorts above a hand-named one, so install a local build with mjolnir dev install <container> --name <name>, which loads above the hub release (chunk_numbering.md).
Making a map with bots › Giving a published map bots

Bots cannot be added at run time: the simulation reads the squads, zone, objective and pathfinding from the scenario when the map loads. But nothing except the scenario changes, so a published map pack is all it takes: HCE_PAKS=".../Meteorite/Content/Paks" python tools/level/add_bots.py ce-blood-gulch-2.1.0.mjolnir --runtime ^1.16.0 --sign For each pack, tools/level/add_bots.py takes the map container's BSP and world out of the pack, bakes the shipped level file (less the keys only the loader reads) with defs/level/bots.json as blam.bots, and packs the next minor version with the new map container in place of the old, and the bake's <CODE>.bots.json as map/bots.json. The bots stand on the map's own player starts. It stops unless every other container, and every package of the map container but the scenario, comes out byte-identical. Rebaking also brings the map's Forge palettes up to the current bake's (the only other difference from a 2.1.0 scenario). --bake-only rebakes and checks without packing. A weapon in bots.json that a map's palette lacks is left out of that map's turn. A map whose level file already has blam.bots is refused, and so is a container with more than one BSP or world.

Spartan bots all wear the default armour colour. Slayer's own script counts player kills only. The HUD's board counts bot kills, and the host's HUD ends the match when a bot or a bot's team reaches the score. Team games: a bot keeps its side when players join or leave (the teams can end uneven). A fireteam client's view of the sides (the roster's letters, its own copy of the units' teams) was tested on two PCs on 2026-11-07 (Team Slayer, 4 bots): both boards agree. Players' campaign teams: in a team game with bots a player's unit is covenant (red) or flood (blue) instead of no campaign team. Nothing else seen reads it in a Megalo game (player against player follows the multiplayer teams), but only Blood Gulch Team Slayer has been played so. Not yet seen in a whole match with the fix: what a side's bots do after a player of that side shoots one (the AI turns on a betrayer in campaign, which until now no one could see, since every bot shot every player anyway); whether bots now follow players of their side as allies do in campaign; and why, in one isolated run, a flood grunt and a covenant elite of the two sides stood 4 wu apart without fighting while the elite killed the host. Free for All: every bot is covenant, so bots never fight each other. A bot that falls or kills itself gets no suicide on the board. Maps with more starts than squads (15) leave the rest unused.

A map published before 2026-10-31 has no map/bots.json, so each bot comes back on the start it first used, whichever side is there. A map published before 2026-10-31 keeps the copy of its collision at the shell's height, where bots lose their place (Blood Gulch's flag-room floors above all), and has no areas for the HUD to send a stuck bot to: a rebake brings both. Only Blood Gulch is measured. A placement sometimes takes an actor that stays where the bot came in while the bot walks off. The HUD reads the bot's deaths from that actor, so it would neither see that bot die nor bring it back. Elites are 0.70 tall on the host only (the lobby DLL, "Bots frozen in place" above). A fireteam client's elites keep 0.8; whether its view of one stutters at a low doorway is not tested on two PCs. The model is drawn at full height, so an elite's head may show through a lintel it passes under (not looked at). Other maps are not checked for low doorways. Why a bot's AI sometimes leaves its sleeping body asleep is not known. The HUD sends bots to hunt players they cannot reach. A map published before 2026-10-31 still has as many area tasks as it baked areas, so some of the HUD's roaming orders go nowhere until it is rebaked. No jump, hoist or ladder links, so bots do not use teleporters, lifts or man cannons, and ground reached only that way stays apart.

Night Lockout's two levels meet only by drops and jumps: its bots play the lower one (16 of its 33 starts; the upper level holds 14). Some converted shells keep a copy of the vertices along each seam between pieces (13 of the 48 hub maps). Those seams are cracks of width 0 now and join like any other.

/sounds (or /mixer) in match chat, or mjolnir_sounds in the console, opens a panel over the match with a slider for each sound the map plays. Each player sets their own levels. They are kept for that map on that PC and read again whenever the map loads.

One row for each sound tag the Level Loader plays (the level file's source, the Halo 2 or CE tag path): Kind shown What it is From BACKGROUND a map-wide loop (Halo 2's follow the BSP zone you are in) environment.sounds.background N PLACES a sound scenery loop placed N times environment.sounds.emitters NOW AND THEN, a-b S Halo 2 detail one-shots, a random variant every a to b seconds environment.sounds.details MACHINE a turning machine's one-shots gears[].motion.events DOOR a moving machine's open, opened and button sounds doors[].sounds ALL SOUNDS at the top scales every row together. A dot marks the sounds heard from where the player stands: a background in the current zone, or a placed sound within its falloff. Levels run from -24 dB to +12 dB in 1 dB steps. Sliding to the far left mutes the sound. RESET ALL puts every row back at 0 dB. DONE closes the panel and saves the file.

mods/MJOLNIRLevelLoader/Scripts/mixer.lua holds the levels. factor(key) returns the sound's level times ALL SOUNDS as a linear gain. syncVolumes multiplies each loop's volume by that factor beside the game's volume sliders. details.lua, gears.lua and doors.lua multiply each one-shot by it when it plays. The panel is WBP_MJOLNIRSoundMixer, cooked into chunk 984 by build_mjolnir_ui.py. It is generic: 12 rows that Lua names, fills and collapses, with pages for longer lists. Its sliders send no events Lua can take, so the loader reads them 10 times a second, only while the panel is open. While open, input goes to the UI, so the player stands still. DONE, or /sounds again, hands input back. Levels are saved to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Meteorite\Saved\MJOLNIR_SoundMix_<map>.json, keyed by tag path, so a rebuilt map keeps them: { "version": 1, "map": "ZAN", "levels": { "*": -3, "sound\ambience\zanzibar\zanzibar_ocean_loop\zanzibar_ocean_loop": 4 } } Without the cooked panel (an older pakchunk984-MJOLNIRUI), the command logs that the panel is not installed. Sounds then play at their built levels. A level file built before door and gear sounds carried their tag (gen_ce_level.py writes source now) keys those rows by the wave's path, and names door rows by the door's tag and event.

The hill uses a dedicated energy-field material so its boundary stays readable while players can see through it. Restrained moving plasma, a visible translucent veil and glowing rails define the field; a layered beacon 1.1 metres in diameter and a ground anchor mark the centre. The hill's state colours remain gold when empty, cyan for you, orange-red for another player, violet when contested, and the owning team's colour in team modes. The runtime is mods/MJOLNIRHud/Scripts/hill.lua. These are client-side visual actors: changing their rendering does not change the simulation's scoring boundary. The existing player/height approximation and multiplayer limitations are described in game_modes.md.

Shader chunk 966 is reserved for KOTH and the CTF flag's cloth. Its shared shader library must keep the Meteorite_Chunk966 identity when packaging and installing. The cloth master (/Game/MJOLNIR/Cloth/M_CE_FlagCloth, Scripts/build_flag_cloth.py) shares the chunk rather than taking a number of its own: the launcher numbers other hub containers 900 + their load order, so a new 9NN number would collide with some player's map container. A 966 built by build_koth.ps1 alone lacks the cloth master; MJOLNIRLevelLoader then moves the cloth's strips from Lua. Asset Purpose /Game/MJOLNIR/KOTH/M_KOTH_Field Translucent perimeter field and glowing rails /Game/MJOLNIR/KOTH/M_KOTH_Beacon Central vertical beacon pakchunk966-MJOLNIRKOTH-Windows.{pak,utoc,ucas} Dedicated KOTH materials and shader library unreal/MJOLNIRMaterials/Scripts/build_koth_materials.py creates the materials and their chunk label. The classic M_CE_Plasma masters are unchanged. If the dedicated KOTH assets are unavailable, the runtime falls back to the existing CE plasma material; if neither is available, the direction line remains.

The container ships in the CE runtime pack from 1.19.0 (tools/level/build_ce_runtime.sh). The launcher names it pakchunk966-MJOLNIRHUB-mjolnir-ce-runtime-<j>_P: hub::shader_chunk keeps the 966 because the container carries a shader library. The helper below is for trying a new build of the materials on one PC; take its container out of Paks again afterwards, or it hides whatever the hub is missing.

Use UE 5.5 and this branch's Meteorite cook project. The fork-layout plugins, shader settings and property retargeting are required; see the project setup. On a fresh checkout, build the two target receipts first from the repository root: $build = 'C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.5\Engine\Build\BatchFiles\Build.bat' $project = "$PWD\unreal\MJOLNIRMaterials\Meteorite.uproject" & $build MeteoriteEditor Win64 Development "-Project=$project" -WaitMutex -MaxParallelActions=4 & $build Meteorite Win64 Shipping "-Project=$project" -WaitMutex -MaxParallelActions=4 cargo build -p blam-cli Build a reviewable package: powershell -NoProfile -File tools/ue/build_koth.ps1 The helper runs the material builder through editor_cmd.ps1, then cook.ps1. It rejects compiler errors, stale logs, failed fork-layout validation, and a missing successful retarget of the two KOTH materials. Each run creates a new directory under ignored .dream-loop/koth-package/ containing content/, editor/cook logs, an input snapshot and a SHA-256 receipt.json. Inputs must remain unchanged through packaging. -OutputDir selects another package root. Nothing is installed by default.

The default CPU mask is 0x0F (four logical CPUs), following the cook script's documented all-core power issue. -Mask selects a different nonzero affinity; the helper temporarily overrides MJ_CPU_MASK and re-applies affinity to its own editor and shader-worker descendants when the editor resets it. It restores the environment afterward. Build and cook share the project's named mutex, so another conversion cannot replace staging before the package is copied.

Close the game, then explicitly request a build and install: powershell -NoProfile -File tools/ue/build_koth.ps1 -Install # Or select an install explicitly (Xbox: the directory named Content): powershell -NoProfile -File tools/ue/build_koth.ps1 -Install -GameDir 'C:\Games\Halo Campaign Evolved' Steam libraries are discovered automatically; MJOLNIR_GAME_DIR is also supported. Installation refuses while HaloCampaignEvolved is running. It copies only the three named chunk966 files into Meteorite/Content/Paks, saves previous versions under the run's previous-install/, checks installed hashes, and writes installed.json. Copy or hash failures trigger rollback of those files while the game remains stopped; a failure record preserves recovery details. It does not deploy HUD Lua or other containers. Deploy the branch's HUD scripts separately using the normal local mod workflow. To undo an installed update, close the game and restore those three previous files. For a first install with no previous files, remove only the three KOTH files; the HUD will use its fallback. Keep the package and backups until the visual check is complete. This helper does not publish a release.

For live checks, follow game automation: launch, finish stock sign-in, verify mjolnir_auto state reports signed_in=1, then host a private match with mjolnir_auto host PRS koth private or use BGL. Confirm the loaded mode: released maps without KOTH in their mode list can fall back to Slayer. A bridge-loaded visual preview in that case checks rendering only. Capture the 3D world with foreground:true; the default window capture can show a black world. Compare the hill from outside, inside, and across a roof edge, and check empty, owned and contested states. A stand-in player list is useful for colour inspection but does not prove live multiplayer state replication.

The branch-local Editor Development and Shipping targets built successfully. lua tools/tests/test_hill_marker.lua passes, including mocked material selection, actor reuse, parameter updates, material recreation, fallback, retry and visibility checks. The build helper passed six temporary-filesystem simulations covering installation, rollback and input-change detection. The final material cook compiled both materials, passed fork-layout validation, retargeted both packages and installed the three chunk966 files with matching hashes. The local evidence is under .dream-loop/koth-package/20261105-025531-639818/ (ignored build output). Live bridge previews loaded the workspace's hill module in private PRS and BGL matches; the final wider beacon and stronger field were inspected on BGL. Gold and cyan were visually sampled; other state transitions are covered by the Lua tests. The installed released HUD differs from this branch, so these previews do not establish deployed HUD integration or end-to-end KOTH scoring. Two-PC replication and a controlled final-effect GPU performance comparison have not been performed. Generated concept images remain design references; the screenshots capture the running game. No release was published.

PWR uses the existing Blam simulation and native Megalo interpreter. Unreal renders the authored map, objective fields and cosmetic parachute. Lua stages the mode, handles a Space key event and presents a bounded native snapshot; it does not implement movement, captures, respawns, scoring or match timers.

The v5 world has a 2 × 2 km playable terrain with three Forerunner sites, connected vehicle roads, four crossings, a descending river and a lake. Its surrounding 8 km mountain field is a render-only backdrop. The gameplay area has not expanded to 8 km. Gaea supplies eroded terrain; Unreal Landscape, Nanite scenery and baked PCG instances render it. Blam retains authoritative collision, vehicles and the native Warfare rules. The current visual build uses levels/warfare/pwr/upgrade-v5-visual5.json and the isolated world-v5-visual5 conversion. Its forest contains 4,470 trees, 804 rocks and 279,388 grass instances. Water uses native Fluid Flux surfaces and saved flow/depth/foam states; this is baked playback, not a map-wide real-time fluid simulation. See water integration, surface materials, mature pine and terrain preservation for their build contracts. The original basin commands and acceptance history below describe the first prototype. Do not apply its prepare_runtime.py step to the expansion: the expansion uses refresh_native_probes.py with vehicle-spawn-policy-v1.json to preserve verified vehicle spawn heights and bind probes to the newly compiled collision. Local installation receipts and fresh native acceptance evidence live under out/pwr/world-v5.

Select map PWR / Pelican Warfare and mode PELICAN WARFARE in the MJOLNIR lobby, then start a private match. The installed preview starts with one player after a five-second warmup. Press Space to leave the Pelican and again to deploy the parachute; automatic exit and deployment are fallbacks. Stand on A, B or C on foot for eight seconds to capture a neutral site. Owned uncontested sites score once per second. After a death you respawn at your base and board your team's waiting Pelican, which leaves with everyone aboard on the next minute of combat; the target is 500 control points.

mjolnir megalo write --mode warfare --vehicle-label-pool --out warfare.mglo builds the variant. Install it in MJOLNIRLevelLoader/variants/warfare.mglo. The bundled mode_descriptors.lua registers the mode only for PWR and shares its lobby, loader and scoreboard metadata. The installed variant controls the score threshold; persisted settings from another mode cannot change it. Warfare opts into a same-mode postgame rotation on its supported maps. With only PWR installed, no ballots replay PWR Warfare; LOBBY returns to manual map/mode selection. Other modes retain the existing mixed-map, mixed-mode vote.

Defaults are two connected players, 30 seconds of warmup, 60 seconds of insertion, first to 500 control points, or 20 minutes of combat. The three neutral koth_hill markers use spawn sequences 0, 1 and 2, matching the three koth_hills entries in level.json. Living players on foot capture; vehicle occupants do not. One side alone takes a neutral site in eight seconds; changing an enemy site takes eight seconds to neutralize and eight more to capture. Extra teammates do not accelerate capture. Opposing presence stops capture and scoring. An owned empty site continues to earn one point per second. Kills do not score. Each death respawns the player at their permanent Red or Blue home after five seconds, with unlimited lives and no suicide/betrayal delay; the native adapter then puts them aboard the next reinforcement wave (see waves and reinforcements). A wave leaves every reinforcement.interval_seconds (60) of combat and flies flight_seconds (30) of the insertion route, both from layout.json. CLI flags allow explicit development variants: --minimum-players, --warmup-seconds, --insertion-seconds, --capture-seconds, --warfare-minutes and --score. The lobby's fixed settings describe the shipped defaults; development timing variants are not editable lobby rules.

Run these commands from the repository root in PowerShell 7. They require the project's existing Rust/MSVC, Python, Blender, HEK and Unreal 5.5 toolchains. The commands use the Steam install and the PWR conversion/work directories in levels/warfare/pwr/upgrade.json; change those explicit paths for another installation. See the PWR source README for the isolated HEK build and initial CE conversion that produce pwr.level.json. Build the CLI, the map/canopy helper executables and both native DLLs: cargo build --release -p blam-cli cargo build --release -p ue-asset --examples cargo build --release -p blam-pack --examples cargo build --release -p ue-iostore --example extract_file pwsh -NoProfile -File native/lobby/build.ps1 pwsh -NoProfile -File native/map_registry/build.ps1 $env:MJOLNIR = (Resolve-Path target/release/mjolnir.exe).Path $env:EXAMPLES = (Resolve-Path target/release/examples).Path The ue-asset examples include mesh_rewrite and retarget_package; the blam-pack examples include package_add and native_material_clone. extract_file belongs to ue-iostore. Keep both environment variables set in the PowerShell session used below: the bake stage otherwise defaults to an older server-list worktree CLI and C:/haloce/target/debug/examples, which can silently mix tools from different checkouts. Reapply these assignments when resuming a stage in a fresh terminal.

The map-registry build also rebuilds and links mjolnir-mglo-cabi. It must match the variant grammar in this checkout. Replacing only the Lobby DLL leaves the installed map-registry staging validator at its old version. Build the Pelican and original canopy into staging directories, then patch, cook and assemble the map's private visual upgrade: $pwrGame = 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Halo Campaign Evolved' $pwrPaks = Join-Path $pwrGame 'Meteorite\Content\Paks' pwsh -NoProfile -File tools/level/build_warfare_pelican.ps1 -Paks $pwrPaks -OutDir out/pwr/pelican python levels/warfare/pwr/canopy/build.py --paks $pwrPaks --preview python levels/warfare/pwr/prepare_runtime.py --level C:/haloce/ce_conversions/warfare/PWR/converted/pwr.level.json python levels/warfare/pwr/upgrade.py --stages land,foliage,swap,collision python levels/warfare/pwr/upgrade.py --stages editor,cook,bake,assemble Current private container assignments are canopy 964, landscape 965 and Pelican 971. The runtime installer takes the generated container names; it does not hard-code a stale chunk number. Preserve the map's capture markers, permanent team spawns and named flags when rebaking.

Close the game before installing. The map install is local and creates no hub listing. The runtime installer copies the complete Loader, Lobby and HUD Scripts trees, both native DLLs, the variant plus its layout and the staged Pelican/canopy containers. This is a single compatible runtime: copying only the new Warfare scripts onto an older release can leave missing helper APIs. python levels/warfare/pwr/upgrade.py --stages install --local-install pwsh -NoProfile -File levels/warfare/pwr/install_runtime.ps1 -Game $pwrGame -SoloPreview -SoloPreview builds a one-player, five-second warmup variant for the private test. Omit that flag to restore the normal two-player, 30-second warmup. The user's current local installation uses -SoloPreview with the default 500-point target, recorded in out/pwr/runtime-20261108-224928/install-receipt.json. The five-point variants below were acceptance-test artifacts, not the final installed score limit. The installer writes out/pwr/runtime-<timestamp>/install-receipt.json and backs up each replaced runtime file before copying it. Standalone variant generation and validation, without installation, are:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force out/pwr/variants Out-Null target/release/mjolnir.exe megalo write --mode warfare --vehicle-label-pool --out out/pwr/variants/warfare.mglo target/release/mjolnir.exe megalo validate out/pwr/variants/warfare.mglo target/release/mjolnir.exe megalo read out/pwr/variants/warfare.mglo Launch and sign in at the frontend, then explicitly host a private PWR test: node tools/mcp/game/cli.mjs launch node native/lobby/smoke-warfare.mjs --host --jump --respawn --capture-a --seconds=90 The probe waits for frontend sign-in and requests host PWR warfare private. Its explicit flags request jump/deployment, kill the landed test player once to verify respawn, and teleport that player to capture A. It writes JSONL evidence under out/pwr/. To observe an already running match without those actions, use node native/lobby/smoke-warfare.mjs --seconds=50.

After insertion, node native/lobby/smoke-warfare-vehicles.mjs --drive --screenshots checks a private active layout-2 match with exactly one local player, then boards the home fleet's Warthog, Scorpion and Banshee through the installed probe volumes. It verifies each actual salted vehicle parent before four bounded one-second W inputs and records body displacement and player/vehicle health. --team=blue selects the other fleet; --seconds=3..5 adjusts total input time. --banshee-ascend additionally holds Space and requires upward displacement; that input binding still needs a live check. The harness leaves the final Banshee occupied, does not end the match, and makes no game calls without --drive. JSONL evidence and optional screenshots go to out/pwr/.

The loader requires level metadata warfare: {protocol: 20569, layout_revision: 3} and opens MJOLNIRLobby/native/mjolnir_lobby.dll with a configuration containing warfare-config 2, map PWR, layout 3 and protocol 20569. That number is the map's layout protocol; the Megalo rules publish their own revision in slot 2 (20570), so a rules change needs no new map. Its four exported Lua entrypoints are mjolnir_warfare_open, close, action and pump (all with the mjolnir_warfare_ prefix). Space sends only a jump/deploy request. The native adapter validates the simulation build, scenario, engine, instance, Megalo protocol and the four baked flight endpoint positions before acting. The endpoint check rejects an old PWR scenario even if its JSON was updated. Movement remains on the owning simulation peer; the host controls the named transports. Late joins and later respawns board the next reinforcement wave from the home base.

Global number slots are phase 0, phase age in ticks 1, rules magic 20570 at 2, the clock 3, connected count 4, scratch 5–6, Red/Blue score 7–8 and A/B/C site states 9–11. Phases are warmup 0, insertion 1, combat 2 and complete 3. A site state packs owner + 4 × (red present + 2 × blue present) 16 × (progress + 17): owner neutral 0, Red 1, Blue 2 in the low two bits, and capture progress in sixteenths toward Red (+16) or Blue (−16), counted against thresholds fixed when the variant is built (SiteState in warfare.rs). Steps, not ticks, keep the replicated value from changing every tick. A value under 16 is an owner alone (older variants, or before combat). Slot 3, the clock, counts the warmup down in whole seconds in phase 0 (-1 while fewer than the minimum players are connected), publishes the configured insertion duration in phase 1, then resets to zero and counts combat seconds in phase 2; the reinforcement schedule is derived from it. Phase, age, magic, clock, scores and owners have high replication priority, connected count low priority, and scratch remains local. Native code reads this state; Megalo owns it. An absent team's native score operand is -1 in the supported build; the published score mirror clamps that sentinel to zero without creating or changing the absent team's engine score.

levels/warfare/pwr/layout.json generates native/lobby/warfare_layout.h. The native build regenerates it; the portable test runner rejects stale output. Layout 2 uses a 2 km scenario, a ±950 m play area and 240 m flight altitude. The host projects desired world velocity into the verified full 3D vehicle axes, corrects bounded route/altitude error and caps speed at 30 m/s. Default automatic exit occurs at 54 of 60 seconds; explicit development durations scale the exit time without exceeding that speed cap. Descent has a 90-second timeout and accepts settled landings at any height inside the play volume. Slopes keep the canopy state until vertical movement settles. These expansion changes require live validation independently of the smaller prototype's successful insertion tests recorded below.

The loader publishes MJOLNIRLobby/native/warfare_state.txt every 500 ms; the HUD reads at the same interval. The warfare-state 3 format includes the reinforcement timing, layout revision and configured insertion duration. The HUD checks the complete format, ready/status flags, mirrored globals, exact uint64 instance text and current PWR world. Two advancing tick/time samples are required before accepting a file or a new instance. Live samples expire after two seconds without advancing; a verified final snapshot remains usable during stopped postgame and the engine's brief same-instance round reset before lobby travel. Malformed or stale files cannot change score. Team CONTROL totals and the winner come from accepted native scores, never summed player incidents. Individual control cells show a dash; kills and deaths remain visible. Final standings allow 1.5 seconds for the final publication to arrive.

The status line gives the warmup countdown, boarding, Space-to-jump, exiting, Space-to-deploy, canopy, landing/active and failed-deployment information, and for a waiting reinforcement rider the time to departure and whom they watch. The last ten seconds of warmup also count down large in the middle of the screen (warfare_countdown.lua). During combat it gives way to three zone tiles under the score (WBP_MJOLNIRWarfareZones, chunk 958 beside the tactical map, filled by warfare_zones.lua): owner colour, NEUTRAL / RED / BLUE / CAPTURING / NEUTRALIZING / CONTESTED, the capture bar, a pip for each team standing in the zone and a gold rim on the zone the local player stands in. A site changing hands puts "Red team captured zone B" (or "… neutralized zone B") in the kill feed on every client from its own snapshot. Three fixed holographic fields and A/B/C waypoints still mark the sites in the world. Contest and progress come from Megalo's published site state, never from rendered positions.

warfare_canopy.lua uses the original /Game/MJOLNIR/Maps/PWR/SM_PWR_Parachute.SM_PWR_Parachute mesh, a 274.4 cm relative Z offset and uniform scale 4.1166 from the canopy build metadata. It disables collision and shadows and attaches once to an existing validated cached biped. Unreal follows the attachment without a Lua movement loop. Only native stage 4 displays it; landing, death, missing/stale state and map exit hide it. Native drop stages currently exist for owning local players, so remote canopy visibility needs a verified replicated stage channel before it can be claimed. The cosmetic asset is optional for gameplay.

cargo test -p blam-megalo --lib --test warfare_behavior validates typed and independent grammar roundtrips plus deterministic warmup, capture, contested scoring, on-foot eligibility and victory behavior. Lua tests test_warfare_bootstrap.lua, test_warfare_hud.lua and test_warfare_canopy.lua cover bootstrap, freshness, score authority, persisted settings, presentation and canopy attachment lifecycle. test_lobby_postgame.lua covers the scoped Warfare rotation and the unchanged ordinary rotation.
