Design for the second round of Pelican Warfare (PWR) features, agreed 2026-11-22. It extends the prototype; read that first for the slot layout, the native adapter and the HUD bridge. Four features, in build order (1-3 are built; 4 is a design, see AI feasibility): Warmup countdown: a large centred countdown before insertion. Reinforcement waves: the dead wait, spectate their team, and fly back in together on a shared clock. Moving zones: each match picks where A, B and C are. Covenant waves: AI arrive on Spirit dropships, fight both teams and contest the zones. Decisions taken with the owner (2026-11-22): Covenant are hostile to both teams; Covenant inside a zone block capture and payout the way an enemy player does; reinforcements use one shared 60-second clock for both teams.

Global numbers are full. Megalo holds 12 global numbers and the variant uses all 12 (variant.rs refuses a 13th). New published values must be packed into existing slots or derived from them. Object numbers have room (5 of 8). Randomness exists. CU4 keeps Megalo action 25 Random Number and action 96 Get Random Object With Label, plus Delete Object (3). No engine respawn hold is needed. Instead of holding dead players in the engine's respawn queue (the respawn_sync_with_team bit is only inferred), the dead respawn after the normal short delay straight into a reinforcement Pelican parked at their team's flight start, which already exists for insertion. A spectator camera is available. SetViewTargetWithBlend already drives the view in MJOLNIRFlyCam and the HUD bench. A camera actor attached to a teammate's biped actor follows it with no Lua loop. The Spirit dropship exists as a vehicle. It is objects/Vehicles/covenant/tuning_fork/tuning_fork (its sounds are spirit_anim_door_*; Unreal has Vehicles/covenant/SpiritDropShip). It has 31 AI passenger seats (fork_p_*). It can be cloned the way tools/level/build_warfare_pelican.ps1 clones the Pelican. PWR has no AI data yet. No pathfinding, squads, zones or objectives. The blam.bots bake lane has never run on a 2 km heightfield shell. That, and the 16 Havok proxies the AI memory notes, are the open risks for feature 4.

The map's metadata keeps protocol 20569 and layout 3, so the published map does not change. The Megalo rules get their own magic in slot 2, 20570. The native DLL, HUD and variant ship together; each refuses the other's old revision. Slot 3 (the clock) changes meaning by phase: Phase Slot 3 0 warmup -1 while waiting for the minimum players, else whole seconds left 1 insertion the insertion duration in seconds (was also published in phase 0) 2 combat combat seconds elapsed (unchanged) Native reads the insertion duration only in phase 1. Slot 6 (scratch, never replicated) counts ticks inside the second in phases 0 and 2.

Megalo counts the warmup down in whole seconds in slot 3. The status line says "DEPLOYMENT IN 0:23" (or "WAITING FOR PLAYERS" while slot 3 is -1), and the last ten seconds count down large in the middle of the screen (MJOLNIRHud/Scripts/warfare_countdown.lua), gold for the last three, then "DEPLOY" for two seconds as insertion begins. The number is a Lua-made TextBlock in the game's own countdown face (Font_Oxanium Medium, from WBP_MatchStartCountdown) at 420 pt. A TextBlock's font can be set from Lua only before the widget first reaches the screen; SetFont afterwards changes nothing, and a hand-built font struct passed to SetFont crashed the game. Render scale works but blurs. Verified 2026-11-22 in a solo match at 4K, and the clock reached both joiners on three game copies.

Schedule. Wave k (k >= 1) leaves at combat second k x 60 and flies 30 seconds of its team's insertion route (reinforcement in layout.json, generated into warfare_layout.h and written to the state file for the HUD). It is derived from the replicated combat clock, so every machine agrees with no extra slot. The 30-second flight at the 30 m/s cap reaches the middle of the map; the forced exit is at 27 s (the insertion's 54/60). Sortie. The per-player state machine (warfare_core.h) takes a warfare_sortie instead of "phase 1": the insertion is sortie 0, the wave that parks before departure k is sortie k. A rider stays aboard only the sortie they boarded, so an insertion rider still seated at combat start leaves even though a reinforcement Pelican is parked. Boarding. After death the player respawns at home (Megalo's five seconds) and is boarded while their team's Pelican is parked at pwr_<team>_flight_start. Only a player still waiting where they spawned is taken: on foot within 40 m of the home flag. Someone who walked off or took a vehicle is never pulled out. Every machine checks "parked" itself (the transport near its flight start), so a client never tries to board a Pelican that is not there. Late joiners and players not admitted at roster lock take the next wave. A seat is allocated at boarding (late joiners have no roster seat).

A boarding the host never completes fails quietly and retries on the next wave; a client that loses the race with its host's boarding adopts the seat it finds itself in. Transport. The host holds the parked Pelican at its flight start with a bounded correction (about 2 m of sag in 55 s), flies it on schedule, and once it is empty after a flight makes it anew at its flight start. The first one replaces the insertion Pelican after the usual cleanup delay. Empty Pelicans fly their waves too, which keeps the schedule identical everywhere. Jumping while parked leaves at once by the normal exit (host detach, cabin clearance, canopy). The parked Pelican hovers over the team's base, so this is how to stay home. A first version that detached and teleported the rider home left a remote rider hanging at 550 m on three copies: the client's HS teleport never took. A body detached from a stationary Pelican also sleeps, so the fall starts with object_wake_physics (WF_WAKE). Spectating (warfare_spectate.lua). While seated in a parked wave with more than three seconds to go, the view follows a teammate on foot through a CameraActor attached behind their biped (SetViewTargetWithBlend), and the line adds "WATCHING ". Restoring the cabin view is the default on any other tick.

The game hides actors outside its own player's view, so the watched body is un-hidden while watched and given back its own state after. There is no key to change teammates yet; with nobody to watch the cabin view stays. Verified 2026-11-22: solo (board on respawn, parked countdown, departure on the minute, forced exit mid-map, re-park, parked jump with an immediate fall) and on three copies (host and client boarding, the host spectating its red teammate with the body drawn, a client's flying jump and parked jump through the host relay). Not yet seen: the wake on a client's parked jump (that branch is covered by test_warfare.c only), a full match on two PCs, and more than one teammate to watch. On three copies on one PC the simulation ran at about a third of real speed and no descent ever registered a landing (all timed out at stage 6); the solo run landed normally, so that looks like the rig, not the mode.

Markers. Each site may have up to six candidate koth_hill markers. A marker's spawn order is site + 3 * candidate, so the classic 0, 1 and 2 are candidate 0 and a map with one marker per site plays exactly as before (including today's published PWR). The pick (warfare.rs). Every warmup tick draws a Random Number (action 25) to stir the host's LCG, whose seed may repeat between launches. At launch each candidate draws a number and the highest wins per site. The last site then takes the first site's candidate index when it has one: on PWR, C's candidates mirror A's across the line between the homes, so every draw is equally fair to both teams. From insertion on the unchosen markers are deleted; only the chosen ones capture and score. Publishing. Each site's slot adds 1024 * candidate to its packed state (SiteState.candidate), from insertion on, so riders can steer toward where the zones went. Positions. layout.json capture_candidates_m holds each site's extra spots (metres). prepare_runtime.py turns them into the extra markers and warfare.capture_candidates (Unreal cm) in the level file, which the HUD reads for the holo fields, waypoints and zone tiles. The native layout header carries them for the tactical map. Choosing spots (plan_capture_candidates.py).

It searches the accepted runtime terrain's masks for 20 m discs that are flat (under 3 m of rise over 26 m), walkable, dry, off the shore and nearly tree-free, at least 150 m from other sites, 100 m from the site's own candidates and 160 m from both homes. A is searched on red's half and mirrored for C; B runs along the centre line. It writes capture_candidates_m with --write and a preview map. The map. The candidates are scenario markers, so the map needs one rebake. Only the scenario tag changes: a standalone bake of river-basin/native/native-level.json (patched by prepare_runtime.py) with the release's own pwr.sbsp and LPE.umap, against the rehearsal Paks, differed from the sealed chunk 997 in PWR-scenario.uasset/.ubulk only. The map registry DLL must be rebuilt too: it validates variants with its own copy of the Megalo crate, and an old one refuses a variant that uses Random Number. Verified 2026-11-22 in a solo match on the rebaked scenario: A took candidate 3, B candidate 2 and C candidate 3 (following A), announced at launch; the tactical map and all three holo fields stood at the new spots and nothing remained at the classic ones. Not yet played: a full match across several draws, two machines, and the zone tiles' "you are here" rim at a moved zone.

A cloned Spirit (pwr_spirit, from tuning_fork) per wave, flown by the native host like the Pelicans, from a map edge to a hover point near a zone. AI are placed with ai_place (the lobby DLL's Megalo gate is already shipped), loaded into the Spirit's fork_p_* seats, and unloaded over the zone. Both teams are enemies: the player-team table gives red and blue campaign teams that Covenant fight (for example human and player) instead of the team-bot mapping of red covenant and blue flood. Contest: the capture scan counts AI as a third presence. Megalo cannot see AI bipeds through EachPlayer; the candidate routes are a Megalo object loop over the biped or a labelled marker the host keeps on each AI. A spike decides. Prerequisites, in order: bake pathfinding and an objective for PWR (and measure it), check the Havok proxy budget with 16 players, the fleets and a wave, clone and cook the Spirit.

Each rule gets a warfare_behavior.rs case and each native change a test_warfare.c case. Live proof needs two game copies (tools/remote/instances.mjs up 2), then PC 2. Nothing is released until the owner has played it.

Research for pelican_warfare_waves.md section 4 (Covenant waves), 2026-11-22. Nothing here is shipped code. The measurements were made offline on the released map's sealed inputs (map 0.1.1, saturday.45/map-input) and the shipped campaign scenarios. The game was not run. Tools and outputs are in out/pwr-ai/ (listed at the end).

Feasible, but not with the bots lane as it stands. PWR's walkable ground is not in the BSP's collision shell. It lives in 151 instanced-geometry definitions: 1.2 million unwelded triangles. The bots lane only reads the shell, so on PWR it "succeeds" while producing nothing usable: one sector on a box floor 42 wu under the map. Bungie's own pathfinding has the shape PWR needs. Every shipped campaign BSP keeps its sectors on instanced geometry (object refs), merges many collision triangles into each sector, and goes past 32,767 links. The terrain is also friendly: one connected area joins both bases, all three sites and both flight-start grounds, and the routes are close to straight lines. The work is a new pathfinding generator, an "instances" mode that builds coarse convex sectors over the welded terrain. That is the first step and the biggest risk, because the one earlier attempt at object-ref pathfinding crashed the game. After it, the AI side reuses what Bungie's own missions do: a Spirit loaded with vehicle_load_magic, objectives and tasks over zones of firing positions, and ai_set_task when the target changes.
1. Can the bots lane generate pathfinding for PWR?

It runs, and the result is unusable. The bake input was the shipped pwr.level.json with the loader-only keys removed and defs/level/bots.json added as blam.bots, exactly as tools/level/add_bots.py builds it. It was baked into out/pwr-ai/bake/ from the shipped map container's BSP and world. Wall time 51 s (level bake, release build, PC 1) Exit 0, with no warning Pathfinding 1 sector, 4 links, 4 vertices, 9 surface refs, 151 instance refs (all -1) Spawns "16 of 16 on the main walkable ground" (false: see below) Firing positions 1,849, widened to a 15.38 wu grid to fit the 2,048 cap Squads 180 (12 kinds x 15) Output pakchunk997-MJOLNIRMAP-PWR_P 397.4 MB (shipped 402.7 MB). Package-by-package, only PWR-scenario.uasset/.ubulk differ (scenario bulk 237,714 -> 453,373 bytes). The BSP, world and lighting packages are byte-identical; the smaller .ucas is compression. Why the result is useless:
1. Can the bots lane generate pathfinding for PWR?

The shell is a 9-surface box. Its only floor is at z -6.56 wu (-20 m, the scenario's lower bound). pathfinding::shell_collision reads only that, so the lane makes one sector there. Every spawn "stands on" it because sector_at takes the highest floor under the point, and that floor is 42 wu below the actual ground. The firing positions all lie under the terrain. The ground is in instances. There are 151 instances, each of its own definition. Instance 0 / definition 0 is a copy of the box. The other 150 hold the terrain, the bases and the rocks, in definitions of up to 8,192 surfaces each, 1,199,995 in all. Edges and vertices are both exactly 3 x surfaces: every triangle has its own three vertices and edges, so no two triangles share an edge. 268,595 triangles are walkable (normal z >= 0.65). By count, 20.8% of the triangles face down, 34.6% are walls, 22.2% are steep and 22.4% walkable. By area, 38.8% are nearly flat floor. Most of the downward and wall area is the box (definition 0, a 656 x 656 wu floor, ceiling and walls). Every definition's surfaces have an edge loop (first_edge >= 0 on all of them). Every instance ref is -1, so an AI standing on the terrain is on no sector. That is the Blood Gulch "copy" failure (path follower state 3, cannot plan a path; docs/re/ai_in_multiplayer.md), but over the whole map.
1. Can the bots lane generate pathfinding for PWR?

The current generator could not do it even if pointed at the definitions. One sector per walkable triangle, summed over the definitions, gives 268,595 sectors, 1,089,160 links and 810,929 vertices. That is 4 to 17 times over the engine's limits, and the triangles are unwelded, so the sectors would not connect to each other. The lane should refuse this case loudly instead of passing. For example: stop when the chosen spawn sector lies more than about 2 wu below the spawn, or when the shell has under some minimum of walkable area while instances hold more. Engine limits, checked against shipped data (census of the 13 shipped Halo 1 scenarios, out/pwr-ai/census.txt): Block Limit Largest shipped sectors 65,534 (tag max) A30 BSP 3: 17,301 links 16-bit indices A30 BSP 3: 59,826, forward/reverse up to 59,356 vertices 65,535 (tag max) A30 BSP 3: 42,028 object refs 8,192 44 (C45) instanced geometry refs 16,384 11,813 (D40) bsp2d refs per object entry 262,136 9,228 hints 32,767 1,335 Bungie's link indices go past 32,767, so the sim reads them as unsigned 16-bit numbers. The generator's cap of 32,767 (pathfinding.rs, i16 types) is half the real budget of about 65,535 links and vertices. Two more facts from the census decide the generator's design:
1. Can the bots lane generate pathfinding for PWR?

No shipped BSP uses the structure's own refs (bsp2d refs = 0 everywhere). Every sector sits on instanced geometry through object refs (one per definition, each with its own bsp2d refs, one per collision surface, and a vertex offset). Every instance maps to an object through instanced geometry refs. Sectors merge triangles. A30 BSP 3's object 9 has 9,228 surface refs: 4,614 none, 426 into bsp2d nodes (a surface split between sectors), and the rest naming only 1,706 sectors. B40 BSP 8 has 632 sectors and 2,377 links in all. Sector flags are mostly 0x11. 0x15 (adds mobile) is rare on A30 but about a quarter of B40 BSP 8's sectors (149 of 632), and B40 also has step sectors (0x1045, 0x1085, 0x1105, 0x1205). Which definitions own the ground. Measured on the raster below: 18 large terrain tiles (instances 126-143) own 96.5% of the main walkable top, each as one big patch or two. So the definitions are spatial tiles. Their bounds look wide only because a tile's box reaches across its neighbours. 131 other instances (rocks, the bases, props) own the rest, in 1,419 patches under 10 cells: mostly rock tops. Tile-to-tile seams total 8,387 wu. Seams that involve a smaller owner total 9,908 wu.
1. Can the bots lane generate pathfinding for PWR?

So a generator that works per definition and joins seams with intersection links (Bungie's way) fits PWR's layout, at a cost of a few thousand intersection links and hints (the hint limit is 32,767). Small rock tops should get ref -1, which removes most of the second kind of seam. The BSP itself does not need re-chunking.
2. Is a graph usable on a 2 km heightfield?

This was measured on a 1 wu (3.05 m) raster of the topmost upward-facing instance surface: out/pwr-ai/probe/probe.txt, with a walkable map in probe/walkable.pgm. A raster is a stand-in for the real graph: it misses tree trunks and anything thinner than 3 m, so its obstacle count is a floor.
2. Is a graph usable on a 2 km heightfield?

Slopes. Of the top surface, 55.8% is under 10 degrees, then 15.5% (10-20), 13.9% (20-30), 10.9% (30-40), 2.4% (40-50) and 1.2% steeper. 99% of covered ground passes the 49-degree walkable rule. Connectivity. 423,967 wu^2 is walkable. One component holds 420,635 cells (99.2%). There are 291 components in all, 223 of them under 10 cells. Both homes, all three sites (on their layout positions, with the raster height matching the layout height to within 0.01 wu) and the ground under both flight starts are on the main component. Routes (Dijkstra on the raster). Home to near site: 121 to 123 wu, 1.03-1.04x the straight line. Home to far site: 277 to 298 wu. Site to site: 157 to 255 wu, 1.01-1.08x. Base to base: 392 wu. Water. The simulation has no water: Fluid Flux is Unreal-only, so the river and lake beds are ordinary walkable collision. Estimated from the flux sources' heights and the lake level (55 m), 35,080 wu^2 lies under water and 30,330 wu^2 of it deeper than 0.5 wu (1.5 m). The shortest route crosses water on 6 of the 10 pairs tested, up to 1.1-1.3 wu (3.4 to 4 m) deep: an AI would walk along the river bed under the surface. Each of those pairs also has a dry route, 2% to 14% longer. The dry routes pass the river at two places only: around (-23, -84) m and (-75, 209) m, on terrain tile 143, where the ground is about 20 m above the nearest flux source's height.
2. Is a graph usable on a 2 km heightfield?

So the navmesh must leave out water deeper than about 0.5 wu, taken from the flux state, which the level already ships. Bridges and roads: unverified. layout.py puts the three main bridges at y -350, 0 and 350 m and fords at y ±800 m. The two dry crossings above do not obviously match, so they may be a bridge deck merged into the tile, a high bank, or a gap in the water estimate: it only knows water within 15 wu of a flux source point. No bridge deck shows as a separate layer in the core. The 10,186 cells with a walkable floor more than 2 wu under the top cluster at the map's edges (around x or y of 450 to 840 m). Before the navmesh cuts water out, the bridges must be confirmed in collision (pf_where dump at the bridge positions), and the water mask built from the baked height fields rather than source points. Roads are part of the terrain surface. Obstacles. The play area has 2,215 blobs of non-walkable ground (rocks, steep bumps, cut-offs): 1,977 of 1-2 cells (1,931 of those cells steep), 176 of 3-20 cells, and 62 larger (largest 2,079 cells).
2. Is a graph usable on a 2 km heightfield?

Graph size. A coarse navmesh fits the engine, though not the generator's present cap. These are estimates on the raster, made with a right-triangle bisection (RTIN): a triangle splits until it is all main walkable ground and its heights fit one plane. RTIN is about 2x worse than a proper polygon or Delaunay decomposition, so the real counts should come in lower: Coverage Sectors Links (~1.6x) Whole map, every obstacle, plane fit 1 wu 34,417 ~55,000 Whole map, every obstacle, plane fit 2 wu 30,388 ~48,600 Whole map, 1-2 cell bumps ignored, 2 wu 20,578 ~32,900 Central band \ x\ <= 450 m (sites, not bases), bumps ignored, 2 wu 7,723 ~12,400 A quadtree is worse: 26,600 to 36,900 sectors and 72,000 to 94,000 links, which is over budget. What drives the count is the obstacle edges, not the terrain's curvature. Recommendation: a polygonal navmesh (welded walkable triangles, deep water and obstacles cut out, then merged into convex regions under a height tolerance), aiming at 10-25k sectors and under 50k links. The central band can be the first cut. Two things are open:

Height tolerance of a coarse sector. The AI finds its sector through the collision surface it stands on (bsp2d refs), so a sector need not be flat. How far its vertices may stray before paths or firing positions look wrong is not known; Bungie's sectors follow their surfaces exactly. A sector is a union of whole collision triangles, or the triangles it cuts need bsp2d nodes (Bungie uses both). The estimates above ignore that constraint.

What is known for certain (Ghidra on HaloSimulation_tag_release.dll, project C:\ghidra_proj\sim): FUN_180375470 creates the data array "havok proxies" with a fixed maximum of 16 (0x10) entries of 0x50 bytes, stored at [TLS+0x268]. This matches the memory note. game_performance_throttle (globals\default, referenced by the scenario) has one profile, for 3 or more players: maximum havok proxy count 0, ragdolls 3, impacts 10. Proxies are a throttled resource like ragdolls. A physics model material has a proxy collision group. The Spirit's (tuning_fork) material 0 is machine, the grunt's NONE. What is not known: which objects take a proxy, and what happens when all 16 are in use. The allocation sites were not found within the time box. Leading hypothesis: proxies are switched off in any real match. The throttle profile is restrictive (3 ragdolls, 10 impacts) and sets the proxy maximum to 0 from 3 players up. That would explain both readings: the Blood Gulch reading (4 Warthogs plus one per live biped = 13, with eight bots and a host) was taken with one human player, below the profile's threshold; PWR places 18 vehicles (8 Warthogs, 4 Scorpions, 4 Banshees, 2 Pelicans) and plays with players on top, which would be over 16 if every vehicle and biped held one.

Whether bots count toward "player count" is unknown, and "0" could also mean "no limit". Nobody has seen a failure caused by proxies either way. A safe wave size cannot be derived from "16". Until it is measured: one Spirit carrying 8 AI (two squads of 4: 2 elites and 6 grunts or jackals), and at most 12 live Covenant on the map; the first live test reads the proxy array (the [TLS+0x268] data array: count, then each datum's object handle at +0x44) across the throttle threshold: a PWR match with 2 players, then with 3 or more. In each, read it with no AI, then 8 and 16 AI plus the Spirit. Check that the last AI placed still stands on the ground and is hit by vehicles; raise the cap only on that evidence. Shipped missions run dozens of AI (B40 loads 2-3 squads per Spirit), so AI count is not otherwise the limit.

An AI marks a unit an enemy when either campaign team is -1 or the allegiance matrix says so. Players have campaign team -1 in a Megalo game unless the lobby DLL's team table gives them one. Our object-ref writer is unproven. Object refs as such work in a Megalo match: the first bots spike (BOT, on B40's stock BSP 8) ran Bungie's own object-ref pathfinding in Slayer. What crashed on Blood Gulch was our attempt: an object for the shell copy, reusing the shell's refs, with no sectors or vertices of its own, crashed 2-5 s after the bots moved. The risk is getting Bungie's layout exactly right (own sectors, a vertex offset, node trees), and BOT is the control to test against. The fallback is decimated terrain in the shell, but the collision-source notes say that route needs the kd hierarchy and structure physics rebuilt for a 2 km world. Unsigned 16-bit indices are inferred from shipped data (A30 has 59,826 links). The generator's types are i16 and need widening, and the sim's treatment of 0xFFFF as "none" must hold. The proxy budget is unknown (section 3). Activation at 2 km. AI far from every player go idle; ai_force_active covers that. Perception and engagement ranges are campaign-sized, which may suit PWR's open ground poorly. AI pilot and command scripts in Megalo are untested. So is compiling the point sets and scripts into PWR's generated scenario. Water looks wrong if deep water is not cut out of the navmesh (AI walking under the Flux surface). Network. AI far from a joiner lag a few metres (two-PC test, 2026-10-25).

With 16 players and 12 AI over 2 km this is unmeasured. A map republish is needed. All AI data lives in the scenario, and every machine needs the same scenario. The bake changes only the scenario packages (verified above), so the map container changes in the add_bots.py style, plus the HUD and native changes. The release also needs the bot character containers (CE runtime 1.16.0 or later) and a container for the cloned Spirit. The bots lane's silent pass on maps like PWR (section 1) could ship broken data by accident.

Template from B40 (offline). Run pf_dump raw and summary on B40 BSP 8 with its sbsp, to confirm whether object vertices are definition-local (vertex offset), how sector rings cross definition seams (intersection hints), the node trees and flags 0x11/0x15. Test: write B40's own pathfinding back through the new writer and compare byte for byte. Widen the indices in blam_sbsp::pathfinding to u16 (65,535). Test: unit tests, plus a round-trip of A30 BSP 3's 59,826-link block. "Instances" generator. Weld each definition's triangles; take the walkable ones; cut out water deeper than 0.5 wu (from flux state) and obstacles; merge into convex sectors per definition; write object refs, bsp2d refs/nodes and vertex offsets; join definition seams with intersection links; point instanced refs at their objects; give definition 0 (the box) none. Test: offline. Every sector ring closes (check_rings). Homes, sites and flight-start grounds are on one component. Route lengths are within 15% of the raster's. The counts fit. Guard the bots lane. Refuse when spawns stand far above their sector, or when instances hold the walkable ground. Test: PWR fails loudly, and the 48 hub maps bake unchanged (the add_bots.py --bake-only sweep). First live run, the crash gate.

A private PWR test install, one player, one placed grunt squad ordered between two far areas, with BOT (Bungie's own object refs) as the control. Test: solo, the Spirit reaches its hover point, unloads 8 AI on the ground, and leaves; then on two game copies, the joiner sees the drop. Native wave director and contest. The lookup is traced. An instance's sectors are read only when its pathfinding policy is static. All 151 PWR instances say none, so the terrain tiles must be set static in the BSP (a change to the BSP package, not only the scenario). Objects are per instance, not per definition. Each static instance gets its own object ref, with one ref per surface of its definition. The writer is proved. B40 BSP 8's object refs rebuild byte for byte. On PWR it gives one connected ground over all 18 terrain tiles in 8 seconds: 15,197 sectors and 51,844 links with sector borders allowed to move by 1 wu, or 19,290 and 62,109 at 0.6 wu. With exactly convex sectors of whole triangles PWR does not fit (about 98,000 links). Three structures are separate pieces: the two bases (near (-590, -80) m and (600, -80) m) and one more of the same size at (0, 690) m. They sit on the terrain without sharing its edges, so nothing joins them to it yet. Covenant waves that land at the sites do not need them; AI that should walk into a base does. A player who joins a server on a map they don't have, or whose host or post-game vote picks one, gets a prompt with the map's hub screenshot and details. DOWNLOAD installs the map and loads it into the running game, and the join (or the lobby) carries on. There is no restart. The same screenshots now appear on the map select, the lobby card, FIND GAMES and the post-game vote. Verified on CU4, 2026-10-09: Wizard was uninstalled (launcher state, cache, Paks, MJOLNIRMaps, and the registration container rebuilt without it). From the running game's download screen it then downloaded, verified, installed, mounted and registered in under six seconds, and hosted and played. Reactor, a halomaps.org conversion that was never in the registration container or in Paks at boot, was registered and mounted by hand while the game ran, then hosted and played. The game exited cleanly afterwards. Then on two PCs (PC 2 without Wizard: launcher uninstall, so its registration container lacked it too):

FIND GAMES: PC 2 used DOWNLOAD AND JOIN on PC 1's Wizard game. It downloaded, mounted and registered the map, joined the lobby, and both played it. The host's pick: PC 1 changed the lobby to Hang 'em High. PC 2 got the prompt, PC 1's lobby showed "WAITING FOR 1 PLAYER TO DOWNLOAD", PC 2 downloaded it, and both played. The vote: the post-game vote chose The Longest. PC 2's option read / DOWNLOAD, it got the prompt, PC 1 held its countdown until PC 2 was ready, and both played. Two things only a second PC could show, both fixed: The map's index in the campaign list must match on every machine (next section). The live row's MapGuid has to match the cooked one. The C copy of map_guid upper-cased all of "MJOLNIR map CODE", not just the code. A host alone never notices: it only has to agree with itself. A client whose row disagrees with the host's loads the world, and the game never starts.
Every machine needs the same index for the map

SetAndBeginCampaign (0x7B446E0) finds the map by a linear scan of DA_FirstPlayableCampaign.ScenarioList and keeps its index (BlamCampaignFlowGameSubsystem+0x38). A fireteam only starts when every machine's index agrees: PC 1 has two local maps (CSN, YOY) that PC 2 lacks. Danger Canyon is index 15 on PC 1 and 14 on PC 2, and both loaded the world and stayed "not in a game". Blood Gulch sits before both local maps, at 12 on each, and started. Installed map sets differ from player to player, and a live install appends at the end, so this has to be handled: The host sends its index with the map: field 4 of the lobby message, field 6 of the vote message. A guest joining a match under way asks for it (where / mapindex). Clients call MapLive.follow, which uses mjolnir_scenario_place (native/map_registry) to swap the handle to that index. When the list is shorter, it pads with copies of B40's handle; the scan finds the real B40 first, so a filler never answers for anything. The map registry logs the move, e.g. place DCN: index 14 -> 15.
What a converted map needs, and when each step happens

Step At boot (the launcher's install) While the game runs Containers in Paks hub::materialize copies them; the engine mounts them at startup the launcher's live install copies them under the same names; mjolnir_mount_paks mounts them Short world name resolves mjolnir_map_registry indexes Paks/*.utoc at load the mount re-reads the indexes DT_Scenarios row and campaign ScenarioList handle cooked into pakchunk996-MJOLNIRREG_P mjolnir_scenario_add clones the B40 row in memory Frontend levels cache entry built at boot from every DT_Scenarios row the same insert, called by mjolnir_scenario_add Level data and the menu list maps::sync writes MJOLNIRMaps/<CODE>/ and maps.json maps::add_live writes the same; the lobby re-reads it every time The frontend levels cache was the missing piece. The 2026-09 notes put the boot-time gate in the simulation's own levels registry. That registry is the data arrays campaign levels (64) and multiplayer levels (50) in HaloSimulation_tag_release.dll at 0xbd5738 and 0xbd5748, and on CU4 they are empty. Nothing reads them, and their caps limit nothing.
What a converted map needs, and when each step happens

The real boot-time step is in the exe: UBlamFrontendLevelsEngineGlueSubsystem::BuildRuntimeCachesFromBuiltInMapInfoDataAsset (0x7B7D180). It passes every row of the tables BuiltInMapInfoData names to a per-row insert (0x7BAC140). That insert builds the subsystem's per-map entries: 0x14c bytes each, keyed by MapGuid, in a sparse array at subsystem+0x138. It then stamps each campaign map's entry with its campaign's id (+0x120). A row added without that entry loads the world, but the simulation stays "not in a game" (mjolnir live arrays). With the entry, the map plays. So there is no limit on how many hub maps a player can install. Only maps registered at boot or added this session can start, and every start path adds the map first.

Launcher, --install-map <CODE> [--release <id>] --progress <file> (hub::run_live_install). This is the ordinary install (install_one), run with no window: It checks the hub's sha256, the platform signature when there is one, and the author signature. It writes the same cache, hub_state.json and active profile, and uses the same Paks file names. The next launch therefore copies nothing and rebuilds the registration container, because its record lacks the new code. Since launcher 0.14.0 it writes every file under the pack's map/ (a remastered map's foliage file and decals/). Since 0.14.1 a map that is installed but missing one of the files its level names is fetched again at the release it has, and its containers in Paks are left as they are. What it leaves out, because the game is running: It never rewrites a container the game holds open: an update of a mounted map is written beside it under a patch name, and the game swaps them (below). It doesn't install or update code mods: their DLLs are loaded. It treats a missing dependency (the CE runtime pack) as an error, and since launcher 0.14.0 one older than the floor of the pack's range too, naming the range and the installed version. It doesn't rebuild the registration container: it is mounted.

It decides everything that can stop it before it writes a container, so a refusal leaves Paks as it was, and a write that fails takes back what it wrote. A map that downloaded but cannot be loaded into the running game (a pack it needs is already loaded in another version, or Paks written for another profile holds another mod's shader library under its number) stays installed and enabled. The message then says to quit and start the game again from the launcher, and that launch writes the map with everything else. A container that only shares a chunk number with one already mounted is not such a case (docs/chunk_numbering.md). Progress goes to <file> as one JSON object, replaced as it changes: {"stage":"start","code":...} first. {"stage":"download","received":n,"total":n}, where the total comes from the hub listing, since the archive is streamed without a length. Then {"stage":"done","mount":[...],...} or {"stage":"error","message":...}. The launcher records its own path in launcher_exe.txt in its config folder each time it starts. A launcher from before live installs records nothing, so the game says to update it instead of opening it. MJOLNIRLobby's native half (native/lobby):

mjolnir_map_install starts the launcher for a code ([A-Z0-9]{3} only). mjolnir_map_install_status says whether the launcher is still running. mjolnir_hub_call gained a FILE method that saves a hub response to MJOLNIRMaps\_covers\<name>; the name is a plain file name. MJOLNIRLevelLoader's native half (native/map_registry): mjolnir_mount_paks calls FCoreDelegates::MountPak. The storage is at exe 0xD349040; the bound instance holds the FPakPlatformFile at +0x18 and HandleMountPakDelegate (0x4694C00) at +0x20, and the method is checked before the call. It mounts each .pak, then its IoStore sibling with the IoDispatcher and the package store, and fires OnPakFileMounted. Then it re-reads the world index. mjolnir_scenario_add does the following: clones a template row (B40, as the cooked rows do) with the codename's world, ScenarioName and MapGuid (blam_pack::scenario::map_guid); adds it to DT_Scenarios' RowMap; appends the ScenarioList handle; calls the frontend levels insert and copies the campaign id from the template's entry. Every allocation goes through GMalloc (exe 0xD4B7428: Malloc at vtable +0x28, Free at +0x48), so the engine frees them at shutdown like its own. An FText copied by value takes a reference (+8 of its text data).

Both are CU4-only, with one set of exe addresses per build picked by the exe's PE timestamp (exe_profiles). The exe RVAs in this note are the Steam exe's; the Xbox app's CU4 exe has its own set (PR #179, game_pass.md). MJOLNIRLobby (Scripts/maplive.lua, wired into main.lua): MapLive.refresh / info read the hub listings (GET /maps, /maps/{code}). MapLive.cover / texture keep each map's cover on disk and read it with KismetRenderingLibrary.ImportFileAsTexture2D. Textures are kept by name and found again with StaticFindObject, never kept by reference: a transient texture no brush holds any more is collected. MapLive.install starts the launcher, polls its progress, mounts, then registers. MapLive.register adds a map's scenario records unless they are there already. It runs before every start (startGame), before a join from FIND GAMES, and when a client hears the host's map.

FIND GAMES: A game on a map you lack offers DOWNLOAD AND JOIN. The download screen explains why, and once the map is in, the join runs as usual. The details panel shows the map's screenshot and download size. QUICK JOIN still only picks maps you have. The host picks a map a client lacks: The client's lobby offers the download once; after that, the lobby's START button reads DOWNLOAD MAP. The client reports mapstate <code> prompt download <pct> ready declined error to the host. While someone is deciding or downloading, the host's lobby footer says so. A first START warns; a second START within ten seconds starts without them. The post-game vote picks a map a client lacks: Vote options on maps you lack read / DOWNLOAD. When the vote ends on one, the client gets the download screen. The host's countdown waits while anyone is deciding (up to 25 s without word) or downloading (Live.DOWNLOAD_WAIT, 180 s), and the post-game footer says who it is waiting for. Test verbs: mjolnir_auto download <CODE> opens the screen. mjolnir_auto install <CODE> installs with no screen. mjolnir_auto join downloads the listed game's map first.
Versions, and updating a map the game has loaded

Every player has to run the host's release of the map. The host sends it, as its hub release id and version (read from the launcher's hub_state.json, MapLive.release): in the lobby message (fields 5–6); in the vote message (fields 7–8); in starting; in the hub listing (map_release_id / map_version, migration 0016). A guest with another release, older or newer, gets the download screen as an update: "ANOTHER VERSION OF THIS MAP — The host runs WIZARD 1.4.0; you have 1.1.0", with UPDATE (or UPDATE AND JOIN in FIND GAMES). It installs the host's exact release (--install-map <CODE> --release <id>), even one older than the newest. A guest that won't update is treated like one without the map: named on the host's first START, sent back on the second. The swap happens in the running game.
Versions, and updating a map the game has loaded

The engine holds a mounted .ucas open, so the launcher writes the new release beside it as <name>_2_P, _3_P, and so on. FPakPlatformFile::Mount gives a _<n>_P pak 100·n more order than a plain _P one, so the update wins even where a later Steam launch mounts both. The next launch from the launcher removes the patch files (paks_strays) and writes the release under its usual name. The launcher also removes, or lists for unmounting, any other copy of the map in Paks: an earlier patch, or a load-order number the profile no longer uses. Two releases mounted together mix their packages. The game unmounts the old containers through FCoreDelegates::OnUnmountPak (exe 0xD349248 → 0x4694CC0, mjolnir_unmount_paks). That drops each pak and its IoStore container from the package store and the IoDispatcher. The game then collects garbage, mounts the new release, and rescans. Verified on one PC: Wizard 1.1.0 was played, then updated to 1.4.0 from the frontend. Before the update, a texture only 1.4.0 has (…_sunshare) didn't load; after it, it did. The updated map then played with its baked lighting. Verified on two PCs: PC 2 downgraded live to 1.1.0, joined PC 1's 1.4.0 lobby, got the update prompt and updated. A 1.1.0-only texture no longer resolved there, and the 1.4.0 one did. Both played.
Versions, and updating a map the game has loaded

Not tested yet: FIND GAMES comparing releases before the join. The listing fields need the hub deploy and migration 0016. Until then a joiner compares once the host's lobby message arrives, which the two-PC test used.

A website links a listed game as mjolnir://join/<lobby id> (the hub's lobby id). The launcher registers the mjolnir scheme (its src/links.rs also takes mjolnir://mod/<slug> and mjolnir://map/<CODE>, which only open the launcher's pages, and mjolnir://update, the game's out-of-date prompt, update_check.md). A join that has to start the game runs the launcher's launch check first, as Launch does. The launcher (hub_join_lobby) checks multiplayer is installed: the four map code mods present and on, and the CE runtime pack installed and on. If not, it offers Install multiplayer instead. Otherwise it writes MJOLNIRLobby\native\pending_join.txt (a temporary file renamed over it) and starts the game if no game process is running: lobby= at= MJOLNIRLobby reads the file from the main menu's poll (every 1.5 s), only once the player is signed in (a main menu has been up) and in the frontend. During a match the file waits. It deletes the file on reading, and drops a join older than ten minutes or one it can't read. It then opens FIND GAMES and, when the list arrives, chooses the game with that id and joins it as JOIN does, so DOWNLOAD AND JOIN, a full game and another version are handled as usual. A game that is not listed reads "That game has ended or is no longer listed." Not tested yet: all of it in game. The launcher side is unit-tested.

Update 2026-10-21: both items below are done; they were verified on two PCs on 2026-10-09 (eced8a14). A guest that can't get the map. One left in the fireteam holds everyone's start. Two PCs showed the host waiting forever on Gephyrophobia because the guest had declined it. So: The host's first START names who doesn't have the map. A second START sends them back to their own menu, and the post-game vote does the same once its wait is over. A guest told starting <code> for a map it lacks leaves by itself. In the lobby the leave is MeteoritePlayerViewModel.LeaveFireteam. BlamCampaignFlowGameSubsystem.LeaveGame, which the kick used, only leaves a match. Verified: the guest left before the countdown, and the host's match started alone. Joining a match under way on a map this PC lacks works. On two PCs, PC 2 used DOWNLOAD AND JOIN on PC 1's running Gephyrophobia game. Its held join asked where, got mapindex back at once, moved the map from index 18 to 19, and joined: the host's game had 2 players. A match started private with the host alone used to play offline and could never be listed later. Since MJOLNIRLobby 0.24.0 a host stays online alone, and the match can be made public mid-match (multiplayer_servers.md).

Three pieces keep a player's game in step with what the hub ships, so a fireteam is never split by versions or by somebody else's mods: The launch check. Launch in the launcher checks for updates, checks the installed files, looks for mods MJOLNIR did not install, and only then starts the game. The in-game prompt. At the main menu, the game asks the launcher what is out of date. If anything is, it offers UPDATE AND RESTART. Unsupported mods. Pak and UE4SS mods from elsewhere are found and, on the player's say-so, moved aside for the session and moved back after.
What counts as out of date

preflight::check (apps/launcher/src-tauri/src/preflight.rs) asks four sources side by side and reports each one it could not reach: Source Compared Out of date when The launcher (check_launcher) this launcher's own version /api/releases/latest (what the Tauri updater reads) names a newer one. A newer build on disk is not out of date. MJOLNIR_LAUNCHER_LATEST_URL points it elsewhere, for testing. Code mods (hub::code_mods_outdated) each MJOLNIR mod in ue4ss/Mods that is in the signed set: its own mod.json version the signed set's version is newer. A newer version on disk (a development build) is not out of date. Runtime bundle (modpack_update) the cached runtime manifest the bucket publishes another version Hub mods (hub::check_updates) each installed hub mod: the CE runtime pack and every map the hub has a newer release, or a map's install is missing files (the same release again) The Updates screen asks the same sources. It judges code mods by this launcher's install record, not by mod.json, so it can offer a few more.

Any run that includes the launcher installs the launcher alone, first. The updater plugin's NSIS installer (update mode) closes the launcher and starts the new one, which checks again and installs the rest with its own code. So a fix to how updates are installed reaches players before it is needed. The run is handed over through resume_after_update.json in the launcher's config folder, written just before the launcher installs and read (and deleted) by the next launcher at startup (App.tsx): { "launch": true } from a launch or the game's update link: the launch check runs again in update mode (as for mjolnir://update): it installs what is still out of date and starts the game. { "launch": false, "keys": [...] } from the Updates screen: it opens Updates and applies the rest of what was selected, if still offered. It is never a replay: what is out of date is checked afresh. A failed launcher install deletes the note, and a note older than an hour is ignored.
A mods release waits for the launcher

Because the launcher updates first, a mods release only has to suit the launcher players are offered, but it does have to suit that one. A launcher compiles in its variant validator: check_mglo (apps/launcher/src-tauri/src/hub.rs) runs Variant::validate from the crates/blam-megalo it was built with, and refuses a mod holding a .mglo that validator cannot read. A mods tag built from newer Megalo code can therefore ship game types that launcher refuses, and the launch check has no way to launch out of date. mods-v0.44.0 did this on 2026-11-05. Launcher 0.21.0 refused 8 of its 13 game types (not modelled: number operand kind 1/6), so players could start the game from Steam but not through the launcher. So release-mods.yml tries it first. Once build-game-types has written the game types, it checks out the released launcher's tag and runs that tag's own validator over every variants/*.mglo, through the validate_mglo example in crates/blam-megalo. A refusal fails the job, naming each file and the error, and the release job that signs and publishes never starts.
A mods release waits for the launcher

Released means offered to players. The check asks /api/releases/latest, the endpoint the updater and check_launcher read, rather than taking the newest launcher-v* tag. A tag exists from the moment it is pushed, and its GitHub release goes public before the R2 upload that reaches players, so if that upload failed GitHub would show a fix players cannot get. A stale answer names the older launcher, so it can only hold a release back, and no answer stops the release as well. When it fails, the launcher goes first. Nothing was signed or published, so the mods tag can stay. Tag the launcher, wait for /api/releases/latest to name it (a minute or two after its release workflow finishes), then re-run the mods workflow, which checks against whatever is released by then: gh run rerun --failed

Every Launch goes through launch/PreflightProvider.tsx. So does a mjolnir://join link that has to start the game. A join the running game picks up skips it, since nothing can change under a running game. If the game is already running, it launches at once. Steam only brings the game forward. It runs preflight_check (above) and preflight_verify together. preflight_verify needs no network: runtime bundle: each file against the cached manifest (verify_install). The player's own config files are skipped. hub mods (maps, the CE runtime pack): a quick pass, hub::verify_quick. Hashing every map's containers on every launch read gigabytes, and it took minutes on a slow disk. The launcher keeps each cache file's size and modification time from when its hash was last known good (verify_stamps.json, written by every install and by the Library's full Re-check). A launch only looks those up, and reads a file only when either changed: it is re-hashed against container_hashes, and a mismatch is reported. A file never stamped (installed before launcher 0.17.0) is stamped as it stands on first sight. Its download was hash-checked; from then on it is watched. Missing files are always caught. On this PC (25 hub mods, 248 cache files): 0.4 s, against 29 s for the full hash.

The Library's Re-check still reads every byte (hub::verify_installed). code mods: each file the release shipped against the hash recorded when this launcher installed it (hub::code_mods_verify, the record's shipped list). Files a mod writes into its own folder while the game runs (MJOLNIRBlamConsole's native\status.txt) are not looked at, so a mod that has been used does not read as damaged. Mods installed by a launcher before 0.17.0 have no list and are skipped, as is a mod whose mod.json names another version than the record. When nothing is found, it launches. Otherwise a dialog lists: the updates; the damaged installs (a repair reinstalls the same release); the unsupported mods, with Move them aside while the game runs ticked; any source it could not check. The buttons are Update and launch (Update the launcher when the launcher is behind: see above) and Cancel. There is no launching out of date: one player on old versions splits the fireteam. When only unsupported mods or unreachable sources were found, the button is Launch. The steps run one at a time, since they write to the same game folder, each with its download's bytes as they arrive. A failure stops the launch and offers Try again, which runs the whole check again. When anything was installed, the installed files are checked again, item by item, before the game starts. A file that still differs offers Try again too.

The gate covers launches through the launcher. A game started from Steam directly gets the in-game prompt below, which can be put off, but cannot play multiplayer with unsupported mods (see "Multiplayer needs an unmodified game"). While it checks, the dialog shows every item it looks at as a live checklist under one progress bar (launch/Checklist.tsx): the core, each code mod, each hub mod's update, each hub mod's files, and the unsupported mods scan. The backend reports each item as it is queued, started and finished (preflight-progress events, preflight::Step). Hub mods are asked about four at a time, and the active row stays scrolled into view. With the quick file pass, the slowest part is waiting on the hub's answers. Being offline never blocks a launch. A source that can't be reached is listed, and Launch still works. Paks gaps (a hub container deleted by hand) are not reported. launch_game puts them back from the cache anyway (hub::prepare_launch).
mods/MJOLNIRLobby/Scripts/outdated.lua runs from the main menu's poll in main.lua. That poll runs every 1.5 s in the frontend and not at all in a match.

When it checks. A poll after a gap of more than 10 s starts a new visit: the first main menu after start, or the return from a match. A visit asks for a check unless the last answer is under 10 minutes old. How it asks. It writes check to native\launcher_request.txt and calls the native export mjolnir_launcher. The native half starts the launcher with no window: --check-updates --out native\update_check.json. The launcher writes the preflight::check answer there, whole (a temporary file renamed over it). The game polls for it and gives up after 180 s. What it shows. When there are updates or unsupported mods, it pushes a screen with the campaign-menu kit (UI.push, no cooked widget needed), at most once a visit, and only while the main menu is the top screen. The screen lists up to six items and counts the rest. Its buttons are UPDATE AND RESTART (OPEN LAUNCHER AND RESTART when only unsupported mods were found) and NOT NOW. UPDATE AND RESTART. It writes update and calls mjolnir_launcher, which starts the launcher with the link mjolnir://update. That reaches a launcher that is already open too (the single-instance hand-over). The game quits 2.5 s later, from the frontend only: quitting from a match hangs. In the launcher, the link goes to Updates and runs the launch check in update mode: It waits for the game to close. It applies every update and repair without asking.

It asks only when there are unsupported mods to move. It starts the game again. The game reaches the network only through the launcher, which already holds the signed sets' keys. The game process gains no network client.

An older launcher would ignore both requests and open its window. So hub::record_exe_path now also writes launcher_features.txt beside launcher_exe.txt, one word a line: check-updates, update-link. The native half starts the launcher for a request only when its word is listed; otherwise the request fails with "the MJOLNIR launcher is too old". It is a separate file because an older MJOLNIR Lobby reads launcher_exe.txt whole as the path.
The in-game prompt › The check's file

{ "checked_at": 1792825712, "items": [ { "kind": "code", "id": "MJOLNIRLobby", "name": "MJOLNIRLobby", "installed": "0.14.0", "latest": "0.15.0", "release_id": null, "repair": false } ], "unreachable": ["the hub: ..."], "unsupported": [ { "kind": "pak", "name": "z_Mod_P", "files": ["Meteorite/Content/Paks/z_Mod_P.pak"], "bytes": 123 } ] } kind is launcher, core, code or content. release_id is the hub release to install, for content. MJOLNIR Lobby shows a kind it does not know by its name alone.

apps/launcher/src-tauri/src/unsupported.rs. In Meteorite/Content/Paks, every .pak, .utoc, .ucas and .sig is looked at, subfolders included: the engine mounts ~mods and LogicMods too. Names are compared case-insensitively. These are known: the game's own: pakchunk<N>[optional]-Windows or -WinGDK, and global.utoc/global.ucas, in Paks itself only. No store puts a file list in the install, so this is a name rule, and both stores' paks follow it. MJOLNIR's: pakchunk<N>-MJOLNIR…, in Paks itself only (MJOLNIR installs and mounts nothing in a subfolder; a pakchunk1-MJOLNIRx in ~mods used to pass). That covers the hub's containers (pakchunk9NN-MJOLNIRHUB-<slug>-<j>_P, and their _<n>_P patch names) and those MJOLNIR's tools place (MJOLNIRREG, MJOLNIRMENU, MJOLNIRLAND, …). Everything else is unsupported. A container's files are grouped by name. In ue4ss/Mods, a folder UE4SS would start (mods.txt says 1, or it has enabled.txt) is unsupported unless it is one of these: named MJOLNIR…; a code mod this launcher installed; a folder of the runtime bundle (from the cached manifest); one of the mods UE4SS itself ships (BPModLoaderMod, Keybinds, shared, …). Moving aside is a rename into <install>/MJOLNIR-set-aside/<unix time>/<same relative path>:

It stays on the game's own volume, so it is instant and cannot half-copy a large container. Nothing in the game reads that folder. Each move is written to set_aside.json in the launcher's config folder (%APPDATA%\com.devnull9090.mjolnir-launcher) before the next one, and logged to set_aside.log there. A file the game holds open is left in place and reported. Nothing is ever deleted. Moving back happens three ways: When the game exits. launch_game starts a watcher whenever the ledger has entries. It waits up to 5 minutes for the game to appear, then for it to go. On the next launcher start, if the game is not running. This covers a launcher that was closed or crashed while the game ran. Before every launch check, with the unsupported_restore command, so the check sees the mods and no late watcher moves them back under the next game. Moves aside and back hold one lock, so two never overlap. A move back that would land on a file of the same name (the player put the mod back by hand) keeps the set-aside copy and its ledger entry, and says so. Folders the moves emptied are removed with remove_dir, which only ever removes an empty folder.

A mod works in a match: in the 2026-11-21 playtest players with a faster-firing weapon mod fired faster in matches. So in game the unsupported-mods finding is a gate (mods/MJOLNIRLobby/Scripts/outdated.lua, Outdated.mpBlock): No joining and no public listing (Games.join, Games.setPublic) while the last check found unsupported mods, or before a check has answered. The check is asked for if none is running; one that cannot run (no launcher) keeps the player out with a line saying to start from the launcher. The host sends back (its 5 s watch, Live.modsToRemove) a member whose game reports mods, one that sends no report for 90 s, and one still "unchecked" after 240 s. Every client sends its verdict (modcheck clean, modcheck unchecked, modcheck mods:<n>) each 20 s and whenever it changes. This is what covers joins that skip FIND GAMES (Steam invites). A client leaves a host with mods. The host tells each member its own verdict (hostcheck …) when it changes. Limits: the kick is the lobby's own (the kicked game's MJOLNIR Lobby leaves), and the verdict is what the player's game says about itself. This stops paks and UE4SS mods dropped into the game folder, which is what the launcher sets aside. It does not stop someone who edits MJOLNIR Lobby's scripts or its answer file, or changes the game's memory.

cargo test in apps/launcher/src-tauri. The unsupported tests cover the name rules against this PC's real Paks listing, a scan, and a move aside and back that will not overwrite (with a scratch ledger). links covers mjolnir://update. lua5.4 tools/tests/test_outdated.lua. It checks when the prompt asks, what it shows, that it shows once a visit and not over another screen, and the update request. By hand: run mjolnir-launcher.exe --check-updates --out check.json and read the file.

When the game crashes, the launcher notices, asks the player whether to send a report, and uploads a small bundle to the hub. The hub groups reports by where the game crashed, and asks for the full memory dump only for crashes it has not seen enough of. Status as of 2026-10-17: both sides are built, the launcher in apps/launcher/src-tauri/src/crash.rs and the hub in hub/src/lib/api/crashes.ts (migration 0019, admin section on /moderation). Tested end to end against a local hub with this PC's real crashes; not deployed, and the real launcher has not run it yet. Update 2026-10-21: shipped. The launcher side is in launcher-v0.15.0 (PR #196); the hub side reached main with PR #194, and the hub deploys from main. Migration 0019 was applied to production during PR #194's deploy, and the mjolnir-mods bucket expires crashes/ after 100 days (c05e2de4).

Location What is there %LOCALAPPDATA%\Meteorite\Saved\Crashes\UECC-Windows-<GUID>_<n>\ One folder per crash, from UE's crash handler: CrashContext.runtime-xml, UEMinidump.dmp, CrashReportClient.ini, for GPU crashes Breadcrumbs_*.txt and a .nv-gpudmp, and an 8-byte .film-unreal whose name carries the mode and map %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Microsoft.198377053870B_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache\Local\Meteorite\Saved\Crashes\ The same, if the Xbox app's build is sandboxed. Unverified: the dev box has the Xbox build's Saved\Config\WinGDK in the plain folder above, so both are scanned ...\Binaries\Win64\ue4ss\crash_*.dmp UE4SS's own dump. Not collected: UE's folder has the same crash C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WER\ReportArchive\AppCrash_HaloCampaignEvol_* Windows' record of the crashes UE's handler missed, no dump. Not collected ...\Binaries\Win64\ue4ss\UE4SS.log The only useful log (Saved\Logs\Meteorite.log is near empty in Shipping). Overwritten on every launch UE never deletes crash folders: the dev box had 117 of them, 19 GB. The game's own crash reporter posts to 343's BugSplat (DataRouterUrl in CrashReportClient.ini); the launcher leaves that alone. Whether a successful BugSplat send deletes the folder is unverified, since every send on the dev box failed. What the files are worth:

The XML call stack is junk: frame 0 is "UE4SS", then ntdll+160e44 over and over. The useful facts are CrashType, ErrorMessage, BuildVersion, SecondsSinceStart and TimeOfCrash (UTC .NET ticks). The minidump (~172 MB, flags 0x201045: data segments, indirectly referenced memory, handle data) is almost all MemoryList. The thread stacks are about 0.6 MB of it. Its exception record and module list give the faulting module and offset, which is what groups crashes. It also carries the XML again, as a UTF-16 user stream (type 0x10000). Asserts and GPU crashes fault inside KERNELBASE.dll (UE raises them with RaiseException, codes 0x4000 and 0x8000), so their address says nothing; their ErrorMessage does. The XML carries MachineId, LoginId and EpicAccountId.

tools/crash/analyze.py reads the dumps with no debugger and no symbols: python tools/crash/analyze.py --last # the newest crash, in full python tools/crash/analyze.py # one crash (or an unzipped report) python tools/crash/analyze.py --since 2026-11-14 # every crash since, grouped For each crash it finds the thread that failed (the exception's, or for an assert the one that raised it), takes the return addresses on its stack that follow a call instruction in a module's code (checked against the module's file on disk), drops the crash handler's own frames above the raise, and names each frame by its function: FUN_<address> from the module's unwind table, as Ghidra names it in the analysed exe (tools/ghidra/decompile.ps1 decompiles one), or a name from tools/crash/names.json. Crashes group by error message or exception code plus the first frames below the fatal-error helpers (_skip in names.json). Stack scanning can keep a stale address; the call check drops most of them. Some dumps carry no thread records at all (zero stacks and registers: 12 of the 2026-11-14 crashes); for those only the exception record's address is known, and the census marks them "no stack in dump".

The Level Loader's breadcrumbs (MJOLNIRLevelLoader 0.13.16, breadcrumbs.lua): ue4ss/Mods/MJOLNIRLevelLoader/breadcrumbs.txt, started afresh at each map load, one line before every load step and every asset it loads from disk, written unbuffered so the last line survives a crash. A Blood Gulch load writes about 315 lines (185 assets). analyze.py prints the last lines beside a crash written within a minute of the file. Shipping compiles Unreal's own log out, so this is the only record of what a load was doing.

Detection. The launcher starts the game through steam:// or the Xbox app, so it has no process to watch. It scans the crash folders instead: once at startup and every 10 seconds while open. A folder counts once its files have stopped changing for 15 seconds. Crashes are remembered in crash_reports.json in the launcher's config folder. On the first run every crash already on disk is recorded as old, so only crashes after that prompt. The log. UE4SS.log is copied into crash-reports\<crash id>\ as soon as the crash is seen, and again checked in launch_game before the game starts. It is taken only when it belongs to the crashed session: its first line (local time, converted with the offset between its last line and its modified time) is no later than the crash, and it was last written after that session started (TimeOfCrash - SecondsSinceStart). The prompt. A banner names the crash ("The game crashed 3 minutes into a multiplayer game on BCK") and offers Send report and Not now. Nothing is sent without that click. Sending needs the launcher signed in to the hub. Settings lists recent crashes with a Send button each, for one dismissed earlier. The bundle (crash-<id>.zip, typically well under 1 MB):

File Contents report.json The summary below, plus launcher version, installed hub mods (slug, version, enabled), code mods and versions, mods.txt CrashContext.runtime-xml With MachineId, LoginId, EpicAccountId and UserName emptied and Windows user names masked in paths UEMinidump-slim.dmp The dump with every memory range dropped except thread stacks, the handle data and the XML user stream removed, and user names masked in module paths. Same layout and size, the dropped bytes zeroed, so it still opens in WinDbg and compresses to almost nothing UE4SS.log The crashed session's log, last 4 MiB, user names masked Breadcrumbs_*.txt GPU crashes only User names are masked as C:\Users\<user>\ (either slash) in the text files, and as underscores of the same length inside the dump (module paths, and path strings found on the kept stacks, ASCII or UTF-16). The bundle is built as soon as the crash is seen and kept in crash-reports\<id>\ with the crash's summary in crash_reports.json. If the game's crash reporter deletes the folder before the player answers, the report can still go; only the full dump cannot. While the folder is there, sending builds the bundle again, since the log may have been kept since. The signature groups crashes: build_version crash_type fault

fault is MODULE.dll+0xOFFSET (0xCODE) for a Crash outside KERNELBASE.dll, and otherwise the ErrorMessage with user names masked and hex numbers replaced by 0x? (asserts and GPU crashes). signature is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of that string. The game's offsets move every CU, hence the build.

hub/src/lib/api/crashes.ts. All under /api/v1, with the launcher's paired key. Any valid key will do: there is no crash scope, so every launcher signed in before this existed can send. Each key has an hourly budget: 20 reports, 40 bundle uploads, 6 dump uploads (admins have none).

{ "crash_id": "UECC-Windows-A13FF88D473CDE7854D7F18E02EFDA14_0000", "signature": "ccfab15f14e59877", "build_version": "2026.08.11.1121610.2-Rel-i343-Meteorite-2607-CU4", "crash_type": "Crash", "fault": "UE4SS.dll+0x2580d7 (0xc0000005)", "error_message": "Unhandled Exception: EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION reading address 0x0000000000000018", "crashed_at": "2026-10-17T04:28:33Z", "seconds_since_start": 175, "mode": "multiplayer", "map": "bck", "role": "server", "launcher_version": "0.14.0", "bundle_bytes": 327222, "bundle_sha256": "", "dump_bytes": 176604251 } error_message, mode, map, role and launcher_version are cut to length rather than refused. crash_id is the folder name, unique per crash, so a retried send gets 200 with the report already made instead of a second one. A new report gets 201: { "id": "", "bundle_upload": { "method": "PUT", "url": "/crashes//bundle", "max_bytes": 8388608 }, "wants_dump": true, "dump_upload": { "method": "PUT", "url": "/crashes//dump", "max_bytes": 94371840 } }

bundle_upload is left out when the bundle is already stored. wants_dump is true when the launcher has a dump (dump_bytes > 0) and the hub holds fewer than three full dumps for that signature and build. A dump a player declined does not count, so the next player is asked. dump_upload is present only then. Its url is a hub path (the launcher adds its key) or an absolute presigned URL (sent without the key); the hub uses paths today.

The zip, Content-Type: application/zip, at most 8 MiB. Only the report's owner may upload it; anyone else gets 404. Refused with 400 when it is not a zip or its SHA-256 is not bundle_sha256. 200 {sha256, bytes}.

The untouched UEMinidump.dmp zipped (deflate, about 30% of its size: 52 MB for a 176 MB dump), at most 90 MiB (MAX_ARCHIVE_BYTES). The launcher sends it only after a second, separate yes from the player, because the full dump is a copy of the game's memory. 409 when the hub did not ask this report for it or already has it. 200 {sha256, bytes}.

GET /admin/crashes: signatures grouped by signature and build, most recently filed first, with report, player and dump counts, maps, first and last seen. ?build= narrows to one build. GET /admin/crashes/{signature}?build=: its reports, newest first. GET /admin/crash-reports/{id}/bundle and /dump: the files, as downloads. Admins only, not moderators: a bundle carries a player's log and a dump is their game's memory. The page is the Crashes tab of /moderation (/moderation#crashes), shown to admins.

A crash_reports row per report (migration 0019), and R2 objects in MODS_BUCKET under crashes/<id>/bundle.zip and crashes/<id>/dump.zip. Nothing serves that bucket directly. Each new report also sweeps up to 50 reports older than 90 days, rows and objects. An account deleted from users takes its rows with it (cascade) but leaves its objects, so an R2 lifecycle rule on the crashes/ prefix (about 100 days) is the backstop, set on mjolnir-mods since the deploy (c05e2de4).

pnpm db:migrate, seed a user and an API key into the local D1, run pnpm dev, then send this PC's newest crash from the launcher code: MJOLNIR_CRASH_HUB=http://localhost:3000/api/v1 MJOLNIR_CRASH_KEY=mjc_... cargo test --lib real_crashes -- --ignored --nocapture Without the two variables the same test sends to a stand-in hub inside the test and checks every request against this contract.

MJOLNIR publishes its current game to the running Windows Discord desktop client as MJOLNIR Core, using application 1533237469259104458. The game owns the connection, so closing the launcher does not stop presence. The launcher registers Discord's launch protocol so an invite can start MJOLNIR when the game is closed. The code-mod update consists of MJOLNIRLobby 0.17.0 (including its rebuilt native DLL) and MJOLNIRHud 0.12.0. Ship them together, plus the launcher change for cold starts. These version increments let the existing updater recognize the changed code mods.

There is no Social SDK download, bot token, OAuth client secret, redirect URI, or Public Client setting required for this implementation. It uses Discord's documented local RPC over IPC transport for Rich Presence and the ACTIVITY_JOIN event. The app's existing Hub OAuth configuration can stay as it is. The activity explicitly sends name: "MJOLNIR Core"; the developer portal application can remain named MJOLNIR Hub. Players need the Discord desktop application running and signed in, with activity sharing enabled for their intended audience. The browser-only Discord client cannot receive the game's local IPC connection. They also need the MJOLNIR launcher installed and run once to register the launch protocol. Joining continues to use MJOLNIR's existing Hub sign-in and map installation/version checks. The app's Rich Presence Art Assets page initially contains no assets. Map names and stats work without uploaded artwork. Artwork is optional and must use asset keys actually uploaded to this application; do not publish guessed map keys. Custom artwork is unset by default. To enable it, create MJOLNIRLobby/native/discord_assets.json with a default image and optional lowercase map codes mapped to uploaded keys (or supported external image URLs), for example: {"default":"mjolnir_logo","bgl":"blood_gulch"}

If a future feature needs the full Social SDK (for example an in-game Discord friends list), complete Games > Social SDK > Getting Started in the developer portal, accept Discord's terms, download its Windows C++ SDK, and integrate/package discord_partner_sdk.dll. That is a separate integration; adding the SDK DLL alone does not enable new features here.

The lobby publishes the current menu, public/private lobby, loading, match, and post-match state. The HUD contributes the current map, game type, local player's observed kills/deaths, and session start time through a bounded, fresh snapshot. Kills for presence are counted separately from the Team Slayer score's betrayal penalty. These are observed local-session statistics, not a replicated authoritative match total; a late join cannot reconstruct earlier incidents. Lua refreshes MJOLNIRLobby/native/discord_activity.json and calls the native export mjolnir_discord_update once per second. The native half copies the snapshot, then handles Discord I/O on a worker thread. It coalesces routine changes, reconnects when Discord starts/restarts, and clears stale presence if the game stops refreshing it. The payload uses the game process ID, never the launcher's PID. To opt out locally, create MJOLNIRLobby/native/discord_disabled.txt. Remove that file to enable presence again. Discord's own activity-sharing settings also control its visibility.

Only a confirmed public, fresh, non-full, joinable session publishes a join secret. The host's public session identity is shared with its participants so their cards can expose the same game. Private/offline sessions, stale listings, full games, and matches with joining disabled do not advertise Join Game. The secret is mjolnir:v1:<public hub lobby ID>. It contains no account key, host token, or PlayFab connection string. A received secret is validated, then queued as MJOLNIRLobby/native/pending_join.txt using the same lobby=... / at=... format as website join links. No secret is executed as a command. The game's existing main-menu consumer fetches the current public list and joins through the authenticated Hub endpoint; an old invitation cannot bypass private/full/stale session checks.

The launcher registers discord-1533237469259104458:// as a launch-only protocol. Discord retains the actual join and delivers it over IPC once the game connects. Launch intent passes through the normal launcher preflight; a running game is not started again. If the player is already in a match, the existing pending-join consumer waits until they return to the signed-in main menu. It does not interrupt their match. Discord holds a cold-start invite for about 180 seconds: if installation/preflight or startup takes longer, click Join again after the game is ready. Once received by the game, the existing pending-join queue expires after ten minutes.

Run the Lua presence/session tests, native Discord transport tests, and launcher link tests before shipping: lua54 tools/tests/test_discord_presence.lua ./native/lobby/test-discord.ps1 cargo test --manifest-path apps/launcher/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib links::tests cargo test --manifest-path apps/launcher/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib discord The native tests use a private mock pipe and do not change a real Discord account's activity. CI runs the Lua, native transport, and launcher tests; a production lobby build includes the Discord source in the existing DLL and release artifact, with no additional runtime DLL to distribute. Live acceptance requires two Discord accounts on two machines:

Run the updated launcher once, then start the updated game with Discord open. Inspect the profile from the second account for MJOLNIR Core, current map/mode, observed kills/deaths, player count, and elapsed time. Host a public game with space. Join from the host's card and from a participant's card. Verify the usual sign-in and map-download/version prompts still work. Repeat with the joining game closed and with the launcher already open. Verify only one game starts and the pending join survives startup. Make the game private, full, or unavailable for joining during a match; verify the join action disappears after the presence update and an old invite cannot bypass the current Hub checks. Restart Discord, return to the main menu, leave the session, disable presence, and exit the game. Verify recovery and removal of old stats and join availability. Automated tests do not establish Discord's visual presentation or an end-to-end Steam/Xbox network join. Record those two-account results separately before announcing live verification.

On 2026-10-24, a live local Discord desktop IPC check accepted application 1533237469259104458, acknowledged the ACTIVITY_JOIN subscription, and echoed name: "MJOLNIR Core" and supported_platforms: ["desktop"] in its successful SET_ACTIVITY response. The temporary activity was labeled "Integration test" and then cleared with an acknowledged null activity. This verifies these wire fields against the desktop client; it does not replace the two-account game test above.

Discord RPC over IPC, SET_ACTIVITY, SUBSCRIBE, ACTIVITY_JOIN Rich Presence fields and unauthenticated desktop presence Invite configuration, launch registration, and pending joins Discord's Windows launch registration implementation

The Xbox app ships the same version of Halo Campaign Evolved as Steam (CU4, 1.112.1610.0), built for the WinGDK platform. MJOLNIR's Lua mods and cooked containers run on it unchanged; the native halves did not until 2026-10-10, because they call into the exe at addresses measured on the Steam build.
