The simulation DLL is the same code. The two copies differ in 29 bytes (timestamp, checksum, debug id) plus Steam's signature. Every simulation RVA and byte patch holds for both. The exe is a separate link of the same engine code. Engine functions match instruction for instruction at other addresses. Platform code differs: the Xbox app's exe has no Steam subsystem. The exe cannot be read on disk. The Xbox app's file protection refuses even an administrator. The DLLs beside it can be read. To study the exe, dump it from the running game: OpenProcess + ReadProcessMemory over SizeOfImage from the module base. The image comes out relocated to the load base, so for Ghidra rewrite each section's raw pointer and size to its virtual ones, and set ImageBase to the load base. The game is a packaged app. It starts through shell:AppsFolder\Microsoft.198377053870B_8wekyb3d8bbwe!AppHaloCampaignEvolvedShipping. The launcher derives that id from the install's appxmanifest.xml. No ms-xbl-<product id>:// link is registered for it. C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\Microsoft.198377053870B_… is a junction to the XboxGames folder, so files installed there are what the game sees.

native/map_registry keeps one address set per exe (exe_profiles, keyed by the PE timestamp). The Xbox app's set was found from Steam's with native/signatures/port_rvas.py: python -P native/signatures/port_rvas.py --dump 36D29F0 ... gD349040 ... All eight functions matched whole. The three globals were read back from 5 to 8 functions each. FModuleManager::Get needs a longer pattern than the script's first try, because it differs only in a thread-local slot index (0x154 on Steam, 0x13c on the Xbox app). Do the same after a game update. Steam Xbox app FModuleManager::Get 0x36D29F0 0x32EBF10 FModuleManager::GetModule 0x36D3540 0x32ECA60 FName hash 0x3709650 0x33214B0 FName from a view 0x36FCC60 0x3316080 FCoreDelegates::MountPak 0xD349040 0xC31C940 HandleMountPakDelegate 0x4694C00 0x4239420 FCoreDelegates::OnUnmountPak 0xD349248 0xC31CB48 HandleUnmountPakDelegate 0x4694CC0 0x42394E0 GMalloc 0xD4B7428 0xC47DF60 levels glue Get 0x7B7DFC0 0x7749E60 levels glue row insert 0x7BAC140 0x7777F20 The AssetRegistry's GetFirstPackageByName is slot 30 on both builds.

native/lobby finds everything by code pattern. On the Xbox app every pattern matches once, as on Steam, except two. One is the Steam join hook, replaced as described below. The other is the presence session's 4-player literal, which does not exist on the Xbox app, so the lobby DLL searches for it only on Steam. The fireteam still shows 16 slots there.

On Steam a join is the task manager's own GameRichPresenceJoinRequested_t handler, called from OnlineTick (docs/multiplayer_servers.md). The Xbox app's counterpart is the invite handler that FOnlineSessionGDK registers with XGameInviteRegisterForEvent: The handler (0x663bf40, (session, const char *uri)). It reads connectionString, sender (or joineeXuid) and invitedUser (or joinerXuid) from the URI's query: name= up to the next &, with no URL decoding. It then queues the join on the subsystem's next tick. That path is taken while a console variable reads true (it does in CU4). The other path reads an MPSD handle. The invited user must be a signed-in user. The queued task looks the XUID up with XUserFindUserById. A miss starts XUserAddByIdWithUiAsync and waits for it on the game thread. The queued task stores a pending invite (sender, the user handle, the connection string), which the session acts on later. The sender XUID is only stored. mjolnir_lobby delivers the request from the GDK subsystem's own tick: FTSTickerObjectBase::Tick at subsystem+0x70 (0x6686270), whose first act is to service the invite's task queue. The session is at subsystem+0xF8, and points back at +0x2D8. The player's XUID is the first live key of the subsystem's XUID → XUserHandle map at +0x208 (0x38-byte elements).
The URI it sends is ms-xbl-mjolnir://inviteHandleAccept/?invitedUser=<xuid>&sender=<id>&connectionString=<string>. PlayFab connection strings (cv2:<lobby> <n> kv1:<key>) contain no &.
Joins by connection string › Why a delivered invite went nowhere

Delivering the invite was not enough. Every join from the Xbox app stopped after join: delivered, with no PFMultiplayerJoinLobby and no error, and the player saw nothing happen. The GDK subsystem does its whole part, all in one tick: the task parks the invite (0x664bb80), the tick builds a search result and hands it on (0x664bd60), and the session raises OnSessionUserInviteAccepted (IOnlineSession vtable +0x348) with success. Two things then lose it: Nobody listens there. The GDK session's only listener is its Online Services adapter, and nothing subscribes to the join event that adapter re-raises. The game listens on the other session interface, PlayFab's. Its adapter is bound with the same delegate type, and its join event has one handler. The key is the GDK one. The result carries the connection string as CUSTOMJOININFO. PlayFab's join reads CONNECTIONSTRING. Raised on the PlayFab session with the GDK key, the game left its fireteam and showed FAILED TO JOIN without calling PlayFab.
Joins by connection string › Why a delivered invite went nowhere

So for a join it delivered (within 30 s), mjolnir_lobby hooks the GDK session's trigger slot and does two things instead. It renames the setting in place. That is safe while the settings map has a single hash bucket (fewer than four settings), where a lookup walks every element. Then it raises the invite on the PlayFab session. It finds that session by its adapter's delegate instance: a heap scan for the vtable of the GDK session's own listener, once per game. The adapter is the instance's +0x18, and the session is the pointer the adapter holds whose invite listeners include that instance. Every other invite reaches the GDK session as shipped. A real Xbox invite raises the same event on the same session, so it probably goes nowhere in the shipped game either. That is untested. Verified 2026-10-10 on the Xbox app with a dummy connection string: the game left its fireteam, called PFMultiplayerJoinLobby with the string (returned and showed its own FAILED TO JOIN when PlayFab refused the fake key. That is what the Steam build does with the same string. Verified 2026-10-10 between two real players: a Steam player joined a game hosted on the Xbox app.

Steam and Xbox app players share one PlayFab lobby service, so either can host and the other joins from FIND GAMES or a link. The game refuses a player from another platform when crossplay is off for either side. On the Xbox app that follows the Microsoft account's "You can join cross-network play" privacy setting. A Steam joiner dropped a few seconds after connecting to an Xbox app host points at that setting.

Question: can players join a host's converted-map game from our own lobby service, on Steam and Game Pass alike, and can a game hold more than four? Short answer: yes on joining. The PlayFab join needs only the lobby's connection string, not an invite. Toward 16 players there are four separate caps to raise, none of them known to be impossible. Measured 2026-10-01 on CU4, statically (the exe disassembled with capstone) and by live reflection. Nothing was patched or tested with a second player. Exe RVAs are relative to 0x140000000, the simulation DLL's to 0x180000000. They move with each update. The CU3 study before it is on the mjolnir/coop-lobby-8-players-de2bcd branch (docs/coop_player_cap.md, tools/pe/lobby_size_hook.py). Update 2026-10-21: the caps were raised and tested on two PCs on 2026-10-02 ("Raising the caps in game" below). Fireteams of up to 16 shipped in mods-v0.10.0 (PR #120, #121), and the host's MAX PLAYERS in mods-v0.16.0 (PR #143). Our lobby service took route step 2: FIND GAMES hands the string to the game's own join handler (mods-v0.11.0, PR #127; multiplayer_servers.md).

The session layer is Microsoft's OnlineSubsystemPlayFab: DefaultPlatformService=PlayFab, NativePlatformService=Steam. Two PlayFab libraries sit under it: PlayFab Multiplayer lobbies carry membership and the connection string. PlayFab Party carries the network traffic. The Friends roster (WBP_Roster_C) lists Xbox, PlayStation, Steam and WinGDK friends, each Joinable or NotJoinable (ERosterJoinability). The game can join a friend's fireteam from the roster, without an invite. Invites are platform-native: PFMultiplayerSendInvite is not imported.

Route for our lobby service. The host publishes its lobby connection string. It can come from PFLobbyGetConnectionString, or from its Steam rich presence connect. A joiner's native mod hands the string to the game's own invite-accepted flow, the way a Steam invite does. UBlamOnlineSessionSubsystem then leaves and joins as it would for a real invite. The fallback is calling JoinSession with a search result whose settings hold CONNECTIONSTRING. The PlayFab half is the same on Game Pass. Joins there take the GDK invite route instead of Steam's (docs/game_pass.md); a Steam player joining an Xbox app host was verified 2026-10-10.

PFMultiplayerFindLobbies is called at 0x6f1a347, from FindSessions (0x6f19210). It builds OData filters (lobby/memberCount, lobby/amMember, search keys). Lobbies are created at 0x6f40aaf–0x6f40ade: owner migration: none; access: Private, unless the session is advertised, then Public (or Friends with presence-join friends only); search properties string_key1, string_key2, plus PlatformId, PlatformModel=WIN64, OWNERNICKNAME, _flags. Co-op lobbies are Private, so a search never finds them. A Private lobby can still be joined by its connection string, which is why our own service is the place to list games.

MJOLNIRLobby's native half (native/lobby, mjolnir_fireteam_open) now does three things at startup, all found at runtime by import name or byte pattern: hooks PFMultiplayerCreateAndJoinLobby (IAT) and raises maxMemberCount; hooks PartyCreateNewNetwork (IAT) and raises the Party limits; patches the presence session's two literal 4s (the unique 24-byte pattern at exe RVA 0x6f2007b). MJOLNIRLobby holds GameSession.MaxPlayers at 16. native\fireteam.log records each call: party: users 4 devices 4 users/device 2 devices/user 1 endpoints/device 3 (options 15) party: users 16 devices 16 lobby: maxMemberCount 4 -> 16 The incoming Party values match the shipped [OnlineSubsystemPlayFab] section (MaxUserCount 4, MaxDeviceCount 4, MaxUsersPerDeviceCount 2, MaxDevicesPerUserCount 1, MaxEndpointsPerDeviceCount 3), which confirms PartyNetworkConfiguration's field order. Both calls happen at sign-in. A user Saved/Config/Windows/Engine.ini is deleted by the game at startup, so the ini route is closed.
Raising the caps in game (2026-10-02, two PCs)

Results: More than four players join. PC 2 joined a host that already had three CreatePlayer guests: five players in GameState.PlayerArray, five player states, one PlayFabNetConnection. Keep Party's per-device limits as shipped. Raising users/device to 4 and endpoints/device to 5 made every remote join time out, with or without guests: ClientTravel to the Party address (0.0.0.0:5000) gives up after exactly 20 s with "CONNECTION LOST / Disconnected from host", although the lobby join, the Party connect, authentication and endpoint creation all return 0 on the client and the host's lobby sees the member arrive. The host has no net driver at the frontend. It creates a PlayFabNetDriver when the first remote player arrives. Local guests added before the first remote player block that join (the same 20 s timeout). Guests added after a remote player has joined do not block later joins, up to four local players. CreatePlayer guests never pass through UBlamOnlineSessionSubsystem::AddSplitscreenPlayerToSession; the game's own HaloOnlineGameInstance:LoginSplitScreenPlayer does nothing without a second input device. More than two local players on one PC freeze a match at its start: black screen on every machine, nothing responds, player_spawn still fires. This happens offline too (host plus two guests, no remote player), so it is a splitscreen limit, not the fireteam's.
Raising the caps in game (2026-10-02, two PCs)

Host, one guest and one remote player play Slayer normally. CTF with three players raised game_over (cause -1) about 15 s in; Slayer did not. So a five-player match needs five machines, or a fix for three local players on one; two PCs reach four players at most (two per machine).
Raising the caps in game (2026-10-02, two PCs) › The FIRETEAM panel

MeteoriteSquadLobbyViewModel.SquadMembers always holds four slots: the players, then blank INVITE + rows. A fifth player gets no row and the header reads "n/4". MJOLNIRLobby's squadpanel.lua rebuilds the difference after the panel's own BackingDataChanged and UpdateHeader: a row for every player in the game state, one INVITE + row while there is room, and "Fireteam n/16" (since 2026-10-04, on the host, n over its MAX PLAYERS). A row's widget class travels with its item in a native field. The list's EntryWidgetClass is only the fallback, read whenever the list builds the row, so a fresh item gets whichever class happens to be set by then. Player rows are therefore constructed with one of the view model's own player items as the template, which carries the class. An added row's MeteoritePlayerViewModel holds the name, platform and player state. CanKickFromFireteam returns true on it, so its menu offers Kick. Removing a CreatePlayer guest with GameplayStatics:RemovePlayer crashed the game.

The lobby's MAX PLAYERS row (-, the number, +; host only) narrows the fireteam below 16. Nothing raises it past 16: the simulation's players array is the ceiling, so a larger PlayFab lobby would only let a seventeenth player into a lobby the simulation then refuses. PlayFab lobby. mjolnir_lobby_max (native\lobby_max.txt) sets maxMemberCount on the lobby the host owns, through PFLobbyPostUpdate as its owner (PFLobbyGetOwner). It is kept for every lobby the game creates later (the create hook uses it), and an update the game posts with its own size is rewritten to it. This is the one layer every join passes, invite or FIND GAMES. PlayFab answers asynchronously; mjolnir_lobby_connection's max line shows what took. The choice never goes below the players already in the fireteam. Party and presence stay at 16: they only have to be at least the lobby. GameSession.MaxPlayers is held at the choice (it was raised to 16). The hub listing sends it as max_players on create and heartbeat, and reports full at that many players; /join refuses a full game. The choice is saved in MJOLNIRLobby\max_players.txt and applied at startup, before the game creates its lobby at sign-in. Not yet tested on two PCs: a join refused by a full lobby should reach the joiner as "This fireteam is full", the same message a locked lobby gives.

Forge lets you build with a map's palette, change object properties and save layouts for play. F3 selects physics modes, F4 sets the position grid and F10 selects rotation increments. Custom packs add modular building pieces and utilities. Forge editing is host-only. Use the mods the launcher installs (mods 0.45.0 or newer: MJOLNIRForge 0.4.2, MJOLNIRLobby 0.21.0), with the matching CE runtime and map dependencies. New to building? Start with Your first Forge build, a raised courtyard walkthrough with doors, lifts and teleporters. This page is the complete control reference. See how the engine works for implementation details. Halo Reach's Forge is still inside Halo: Campaign Evolved's simulation. MJOLNIR switches it on: you turn into the Monitor, fly around the map, and pick up, move, drop and delete its objects. The game's own Forge engine does the work; MJOLNIR gives it keys and a HUD. As the Monitor you can also place new objects from the map's palette: weapons, vehicles, equipment and scenery. Community model sets use Forge packs. Maps declare their supported pack pieces when baked; the Hub catalog and launcher handle their releases and dependencies. That guide includes the original Foundry set, authoring commands and saved-layout compatibility checks. For a model-to-pack walkthrough, see Community pack authoring.

After a fresh launch, press Enter at the title screen and wait for sign-in to finish and the main menu to appear. MULTIPLAYER → HOST GAME, pick a map. Pick FORGE as the game type. It is listed once MJOLNIRForge is installed and the CE runtime pack has the monitor fix. Start. A panel at the top left says FORGE. For scripts and tests: mjolnir_auto host <CODE> forge private at the console. Before issuing it after a fresh launch, wait for MULTIPLAYER is on the main menu in the current UE4SS.log. Starting before sign-in can load the Unreal world without starting the native simulation.

Top left: FORGE, whether you are the Monitor or your Spartan, and the map. Centre: the Monitor's cursor. Blue when it rests on nothing, white on an object, green while you hold one. Beside the cursor: what you aim at or hold. It shows the kind of object, its name, the game's own picture for a weapon, and what the keys do to it. While you hold something, a bar shows how far out it is (1 to 60 m). Bottom: the main controls, dimmed when they do nothing right now, and a short note of what the last key did ("DELETED Shotgun"). Right, as the Monitor: the palette. The category (WEAPONS, VEHICLES, EQUIPMENT, SCENERY) between its keys, the object Insert places with its picture, and the category's list around it. A dimmed entry is one the map cannot place right now. The HUD also shows the target's physics mode and keeps the grid and rotation settings visible in Monitor mode. The palette header shows the turn increment separately: snapping off still leaves comma and period turning by 22.5°. The HUD ships in the CE runtime pack (pakchunk980-MJOLNIRFORGEUI-Windows). Without it, a plain text panel shows the same things.

Key What it does B Turn into the Monitor, or back into your Spartan V Pick up what the cursor is on; press again to drop it Page Up / Page Down Push a held object away, or pull it in Delete Delete what you hold (or, holding nothing, what you aim at) N Duplicate the target at the cursor Insert Place the palette's selected object at the cursor; you hold it, ready to move Left / Right Previous / next palette category Up / Down Previous / next object in the category F5 Save this map's layout F6 Load the saved layout, replacing the objects on the map now. With no saved layout, the newest one in layouts\history comes back F2, twice Go back to the map's own layout (the saved one is kept in layouts\history). The first press asks; press again within 4 seconds K Team of the target: neutral, red, blue L Megalo label of the target (the map's labels in turn, then none) J Respawn time of the target: 0, 5, 10, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 180 s O Spawn order of the target: 0 to 9 P Teleporter channel of the target: alpha through zulu, then 26–31 , / . Turn what you hold or carry, or the next marker you place, left / right; 22.5° with rotation snapping off F3 Cycle the target's physics: Normal → Fixed → Phased F4 Cycle the position grid: off → 0.25 → 0.5 → 1 → 2 → 4 m F10 Cycle rotation snapping: off → 90° → 45° → 30° → 15° → 5°

As the Monitor you move with your usual movement keys and the mouse; jump flies up. To use other keys, create keys.txt in the MJOLNIRForge mod folder with lines like grab=H (actions toggle, grab, duplicate, delete, nearer, farther, place, prev_category, next_category, prev_item, next_item, save, load, revert, team, label, respawn, order, channel, rotate_left, rotate_right, physics, grid and rotation_snap; key names as UE4SS spells them, such as PAGE_UP or LEFT_ARROW). The defaults are keys the game does not use. G, C, Z and X are taken; MJOLNIRFlyCam uses F7–F9 and the square brackets.

A map's palette is its scenario's own Forge palette. Current converted maps can offer the CE arsenal: 13 weapons, 6 vehicles (not the campaign's flyers), grenades, power-ups, ammo and scenery such as spawn points, teleporters, flag stands and health packs. A map with a smaller palette only offers its baked selection. Adding installed assets does not change that selection. A converted map's own vehicles start in place: a FORGE game shows the ones a Slayer game on that map would place. Saving keeps them under the host's vehicle settings, so a match still places what its VEHICLE SET pages say. The blocks palette includes a Covenant crate and portable shield. Maps can also include original namespaced model sets such as Foundry through Forge packs. Per-kind quotas and overall object capacity still depend on the map and engine (Budgets and quotas).

Every object Forge places carries properties the game types read. K, L, J and O change the target's (what you hold, else what you aim at); the target card shows its team and label. Team: a red flag stand is where the red flag starts in CTF; spawn points with a team are that team's. Include neutral spawn markers for free-for-all Slayer; red/blue starts alone do not cover that mode. Label: what a game type looks objects up by. CTF finds flag stands by ctf_flag_return and team spawns by ctf_spawn_red / ctf_spawn_blue. The list is the map's own labels. Respawn time and spawn order for weapons, vehicles and equipment.

Aim at an object or hold it, then press F3 to change its physics mode. These are the game's native Forge object properties: Normal: uses the object's normal physics. An unsupported piece can fall when dropped. Fixed: stays where you place it, including in midair. Phased: stays where you place it and allows overlap with other geometry. For a platform that should remain suspended, choose Fixed or Phased before dropping it. The target card shows the selected mode; saved layouts keep the object's physics properties. F4 controls MJOLNIR's position grid. It starts off and cycles through 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 metres, then off again. On placement or drop, the object's origin aligns to the nearest grid point in world coordinates. The grid is anchored at the map's world origin; it does not connect model edges automatically. A Normal object can still move or fall after it lands on the grid. F10 starts with rotation snapping off and cycles through 90°, 45°, 30°, 15° and 5°, then off again. With a snap selected, comma and period request a turn to the next angle on that world yaw grid. With snapping off, they turn by 22.5°. Turning is around the vertical axis; pitch and roll controls are not available.

Use Phased for precise construction and check the angle after dropping. A held Fixed object can resist a requested turn when it encounters collision, and the game's hold motion can settle slightly off the requested angle even in Phased mode. Rotation snapping is not a guarantee of an exact final angle. The HUD shows the current grid, snap angle and turn increment. Grid and angle choices are editing settings for the current session; a saved layout records the resulting object positions and rotations.
Markers: flag stands, spawn points, health packs, teleporters

These have no physics, so the Monitor cannot drag them the way it drags a weapon. Forge handles them its own way: Insert puts one where the cursor is, facing the way , and . set. V on one picks it up: it leaves the map and the HUD shows you carrying it, properties and all. Turn it with , and . and press V again to put it down at the cursor. Delete while carrying throws it away. N copies one, properties included. They are invisible in game (the bases' stands are separate scenery). Aim close to the marker's position to select it. A flag stand made this way works in CTF: on Blood Gulch, a red stand placed, labelled ctf_flag_return, saved, and the map then hosted as CTF got the red flag.
Markers: flag stands, spawn points, health packs, teleporters › Teleporters

The scenery palette can include Teleporter Sender, Teleporter Receiver and Teleporter 2-Way. Place an entrance and exit with the same channel; P changes the targeted marker's channel, shown on its target card. The game's simulation handles travel, including the receiver's facing. Use different channels for separate routes. A two-way pair uses the same channel at both ends. New Insert placements start on alpha with a player-only cylinder about 1.07 m in radius, 1.83 m above and 0.30 m below the marker. Moving, duplicating and saving preserves the marker's channel and trigger dimensions. Keep the receiver clear of walls and leave room for the Spartan. The engine supports 32 endpoints in total, including both ends of each route. Foundry's portal frames and pads are visible architecture; place functional teleporter markers separately.
Markers: flag stands, spawn points, health packs, teleporters › Pack lights

Foundry's light strip and warm/red/blue pylons have optional catalog light data. MJOLNIRForge attaches a movable point light to each active piece's actor, so light follows placement and rotation and is removed when the piece disappears. This also runs in ordinary game modes and when a saved layout starts a match. The first 64 active lights receive illumination; additional fixtures still render. Lights currently cast no shadows. Colors and brightness are properties of the piece's catalog, so use the red or blue variant for team bases.
Markers: flag stands, spawn points, health packs, teleporters › Automatic doors and lifts

These utilities need MJOLNIRForge 0.4.0, MJOLNIRLobby 0.19.3 and MJOLNIRLevelLoader 0.9.8 at least; the mods the launcher installs today are all newer. Foundry Wide's door frames and moving panels are separate pieces. Place the panel in its closed position inside the matching frame. Use F3 to keep it Fixed or Phased for automatic opening; Normal disables automation. Leave the panel's full upward travel clear: 4 m for the infantry panel and 6 m for the vehicle panel. Return to your Spartan with B and approach the doorway to request opening. The panel waits two seconds after you leave before closing. Clear players and vehicles from the doorway before editing it. Entering Monitor mode attempts to close the panel, but a blocked closing path keeps it raised. Moving, copying, turning and changing that panel's physics wait until it can close; the HUD asks you to clear the doorway. Other objects remain editable. F5 saves the authored closed pose even while the live door is open. Door saves require the host's known closed pose; client saves containing enabled doors are deferred, and a migrated host must rehost before using them.
Markers: flag stands, spawn points, health packs, teleporters › Automatic doors and lifts

For a lift, place the station with open space above its central deck, then walk up its ramps as a Spartan and steer onto a nearby landing during ascent. Crossline demonstrates a landing at 4.5 m above ground, four metres above the station deck. A green teleporter frame or pad still needs the separate sender/receiver markers and matching P channel described above. Their metadata and current limits are in Forge pack utilities.

Forge editing is host-only. Start it without fireteam members; the lobby refuses a Forge session with members present. Forge sessions do not appear in Find Games. Save your layout, return to the lobby and choose the game type you want to play with your fireteam. The hosted map uses your saved layout. Players need the map's matching runtime and pack dependencies.

A map can limit what Forge places: a budget, a price per object, and a most of each kind. The simulation enforces them, as Reach's Forge did: an object over its quota or over the budget is refused ("THIS MAP CAN'T PLACE ANOTHER"). The palette shows placed/most and the price beside an object that has them, and the budget spent in its title. The text panel shows the same. Maps set them when they are built (blam.forge in the level file, level_format.md). A map without prices or per-kind quotas still has the engine's overall object capacity.

F5 saves what is on the map now, everything Forge can move, as a layout: layouts\<MAP>.mvar in the MJOLNIRForge mod folder (Blood Gulch is BGL.mvar). It works as the Monitor or as your Spartan, in a FORGE game. A map with a saved layout starts every game with it: FORGE, Slayer, CTF or any other game type on that map. Saving again replaces it; the one before moves to layouts\history with the time in its name. To play the map as it shipped, press F2 twice in a FORGE game (or move the file out of layouts). Objects you have not saved are gone after that, but the saved layout is not: F6 brings it back from layouts\history until you save again. F6 puts the saved layout back on the spot, undoing everything since the last save. Objects you are holding are dropped first. A layout file is a Halo Reach map variant (.mvar), the same format MCC uses, so cargo run -p blam-megalo --example mvar_summary -- BGL.mvar lists what is in it. Layouts belong to one map: the file name says which. Forge checks a layout file before loading it and refuses a malformed one with the reason, for example "FRB.mvar refused: it has more than 256 labels". The map then plays its original layout. Layouts saved in game always pass.

Several layouts per map, and picking one in the lobby. One saved layout per map for now; layouts\history keeps the older ones. Layouts for your fireteam. A saved layout is used when you host; players who join see the host's objects. A Forge menu (object lists, properties). Tilting. , and . turn about the vertical only. Markers are invisible: aim near where you put them. The cursor only reaches things in plain view: it stops at walls and the ground.

A Forge pack is a normal .mjolnir content release with a validated catalog of namespaced building pieces. The Hub lists them in its /forge catalog; the launcher downloads published containers and exposes their catalog to Forge. A map declares which pieces it supports when its scenario is baked. A saved layout records the pack releases and palette bindings it used. Packs can be updated without stranding the maps and layouts built with them, and the format leaves room for other kinds of content than building pieces. For a practical first contribution, see creating a community Forge pack. For placing existing pieces, use the Forge building guide. This page describes the release format, build pipeline and dependency checks. Reference pack Current version Contents Foundry 0.2.0 24 original pieces on a 2 m module, including portal frames/pads and warm/red/blue lights Foundry Wide 0.2.0 38 pieces on a 4 m module; the original 18 retain their exact geometry and catalog order, with 20 additions for larger floors, walls, ramps, junctions, glass, doors, a gravity lift and green teleporter housings Roadworks 0.2.0 Ten road pieces with 16 m clear decks, 24/48 m straights, R40 curves and 48 m ramps rising 4 m; open and guarded variants

Crossline 0.3 combines Foundry and Foundry Wide in a 96 × 160 m Red versus Blue arena and utility showcase. Raised decks remain 4.5 m high inside a 9 m perimeter. Its 300 authored objects include two stock Warthogs, eight team-owned starts and four neutral midfield starts; 351 native slots remain available. Original Foundry's lights retain their size. The Forge Canvas stays a blank 64 × 64 m deck using Foundry, while Roadworks Circuit 0.2 provides a roughly 731 m course on a 320 × 320 m recovery deck with three stock Warthogs. Road connectors describe exact source assembly; current Forge placement does not automatically dock them. Separate namespaces, and the rule that a compatible update keeps every existing piece, keep new geometry from silently resizing old builds. Historical Roadworks 0.1 used 8 m lanes, and Crossline 0.2 used the 18-piece Wide 0.1 kit in a 48 × 80 m arena; those layouts need an explicit compatible rebuild to use the larger sets. Design research explains the piece selection. The validation record records the tested artifacts, gameplay checks and remaining coverage. Full vehicle-route, surface-placement lifecycle and second-machine utility checks remain separate work; a representative live check is not an exhaustive review of every piece.

mjolnir.json keeps type: "content" so existing archive download and signature handling applies. Its optional forge_pack block identifies the catalog: { "schema_version": 1, "name": "Foundry", "version": "0.2.0", "type": "content", "summary": "Modular industrial construction pieces", "forge_pack": { "schema_version": 1, "id": "foundry", "blocks": [ { "id": "floor_2x2", "name": "Floor 2 x 2", "tag": "objects\mjolnir\forge\foundry\floor_2x2", "category": "floors", "dimensions_m": [4, 4, 0.5], "snap_m": 0.5 } ] } }

The pack ID must equal the Hub mod slug: 2–64 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, beginning with a letter or digit. Block IDs and categories are 1–64 lowercase letters, digits, hyphens or underscores, beginning with a letter or digit. IDs are unique within a pack. Names contain 1–80 characters and cannot be blank. Every tag is exactly objects\mjolnir\forge\<pack-id>\<block-id>, whatever the entry's kind. For a block it names a crate (bloc) with its associated model, physics and collision tags. A catalog contains 1–256 blocks. Dimensions and optional snap are finite, positive metres. They describe authoring metadata; they do not change engine collision or configure the editor's global snap setting. Release versions are exact SemVer, at most 96 bytes. Hub versions exclude +build metadata. A published version's bytes never change; see updating a pack for what each kind of new version may change. Optional deps use the existing { "slug": "other-pack", "range": "^1.2.3" } format. The launcher supports Rust SemVer requirements such as ^1.2.3, ~1.2.3 and >=1.2.3, <2.0.0; a bare complete version is an exact pin.

Each catalog entry may name its kind. Without one it is a block, which is all the format carries today. The names below are reserved so that packs can carry other objects once the bake, the launcher and Forge handle them: kind Object tag class Status block crate (bloc) Supported scenery scen Reserved weapon weap Reserved vehicle vehi Reserved equipment eqip Reserved biped bipd Reserved The Hub, the packer (mjolnir forge pack) and the launcher refuse an entry of any kind they do not support. A launcher meeting a pack built for a newer one says to update instead of installing it, so a weapon is never handed to Forge as a building block. Forge's light, lift and material code also skips entries that are not blocks. An entry's tag path stays objects\mjolnir\forge\<pack-id>\<entry-id> for every kind. The tags an object needs besides its own (projectiles, effects, sounds, animations, a weapon's first-person model) belong below objects\mjolnir\forge\<pack-id>\ too, and Unreal assets below /Game/MJOLNIR/Forge/<pack-id>/. A pack replaces nothing outside its own namespace. The Hub enforces this for catalog tags today; checking every package in a pack's containers against it is follow-up work before packs carry kinds with dependency tags.
Release contract › Required features and new fields

Catalogs stay at schema_version 1 while they only gain optional fields; 2 is kept for a change older launchers must not read at all, and they refuse it with a request to update. A pack lists in requires any feature it needs beyond what schema 1 readers understand, for example "requires": ["turrets"]. None are defined yet: the Hub accepts only features it knows, and a launcher refuses a pack that needs one it does not, asking for an update. A pack that uses no new feature stays installable by every launcher. The rule for extending the format: A new field that changes what MJOLNIR does with a pack (a new utility, a new surface profile, a field inside light, lift or door) comes with a requires feature name, added to the Hub, the packer and the launcher in the release that supports it. A field that only describes the pack (a credit, a preview hint) needs none; older readers ignore unknown top-level and entry fields.

Releases follow SemVer, and maps and saved layouts accept any later release in the caret line of the version they were built with: Line Same line New line 1.0.0 and later the same major version: 1.4.2 serves a map built with 1.2.0 2.0.0 0.x the same minor version: 0.2.7 serves one built with 0.2.0 0.3.0 Within a line, a release must keep every entry of the earlier ones: the same ID and kind, dimensions and snap, origin, and the heights where pieces meet. It may fix an entry's look and collision within that shape, and add new entries. In 0.x the patch number carries both fixes and additions. The Hub refuses a release that drops an entry of an earlier release in its line, or changes one's kind, dimensions or snap; origin and joins are the author's to keep. Anything else starts a new line, or a new pack: Foundry Wide is its own pack so that its larger pieces could never resize a Foundry build. Maps record ^<version> for each pack they were baked with. When the launcher has to download a pack it takes the newest release of that line, and updating an installed pack within the line is allowed while maps that use it are enabled. A saved layout records the version it was saved with and loads with it or any later release of the same line; the palette entry must still be the saved tag path exactly. Two maps or layouts that need different lines of one pack cannot be enabled together.

A block may also contain a data-only light object (omit it for ordinary pieces; null is also treated as absent): "light": { "offset_m": [0, 0, 3.1], "color_rgb": [1, 0.05, 0.03], "intensity_cd": 70, "radius_m": 8 } Offsets are relative to the piece's authored origin, in the same right-handed Z-up metres as its geometry. Each component must be finite and within −100..100 m. Linear RGB components are within 0..1. Intensity is positive and at most 10,000 candelas; radius is positive and at most 100 m. Unknown light fields are rejected. Hub, packer and launcher validate the same bounds. Forge derives the actor class from the pack/block IDs, attaches a movable inverse-square point light to its root, and converts metres to Unreal centimetres with Y reflected. It does not execute pack code or accept an arbitrary actor path. Illumination is capped at 64 active fixtures, is currently shadowless, and has no exposure multiplier. Deleted/pooled actors and world changes remove their attached lights. See Forge utilities. Optional lift, door and surfaces fields provide the additional bounded features used by Wide 0.2. See the utility contract for their schemas and runtime limits, and material authoring for pack-owned glass/portal assets and the shader chunk a pack's material container is cooked under. A portal surface is visual; native teleporter markers still perform travel.

The archive contains mjolnir.json, cooked .utoc/.ucas pairs under content/, optional docs/README.md and changes.json, and author signatures when signed. Source .blend, glTF and collision JSON files are authoring inputs, not directly installable content. The launcher generates container .pak stubs. The generated Foundry release uses original visual geometry and collision with game-specific actor/tag templates and shipped material references; its cooked outputs require the supported game installation. The Hub validates the catalog during the normal upload/scan/publish flow and stores it on the release. GET /api/v1/releases/{id}/forge-pack returns the published catalog, release version, archive SHA-256 and dependencies. The mod detail page displays piece names, dimensions and snap. Choosing the Forge category alone does not put an unvalidated archive in the Forge catalog. Publishing still uses the existing registered author-key requirements and review rules. Forge packs are live: the hub lists them at /forge, and launcher 0.21.0 or newer installs them with the maps and layouts that need them.

Run these commands from the repository root. $paks is a developer's installed game directory, and generated donors/cooked content remain local under ignored build/ directories. The examples use the debug tool builds for iteration.

$paks = 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Halo Campaign Evolved\Meteorite\Content\Paks' $cli = 'target\debug\mjolnir.exe' cargo build -p blam-cli cargo build -p ue-asset --example mesh_rewrite --example forge_actor cargo build -p blam-pack --example package_add python forge-packs/foundry/generate.py python forge-packs/foundry/validate.py & 'C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\blender.exe' --background --factory-startup --python forge-packs/foundry/build_blender.py -- --render & $cli extract --paks $paks --group collision_model --filter crate_space_a --shipped-only --verify --out forge-packs/foundry/build/donors cargo run -p blam-sbsp --example forge_collision -- forge-packs/foundry/source/geometry.json forge-packs/foundry/build/donors/objects/props/covenant/crate_space_a/crate_space_a.collision_model forge-packs/foundry/build/blam-collision python tools/forge/build_collision.py forge-packs/foundry/source/geometry.json forge-packs/foundry/build/blam-physics --mjolnir $cli --paks $paks --payload-out forge-packs/foundry/build/blam-collision python tools/forge/build_pack.py forge-packs/foundry --paks $paks & $cli forge pack forge-packs/foundry/build/game/all/mjolnir.json --content forge-packs/foundry/build/game/all/content --readme forge-packs/foundry/README.md --changes forge-packs/foundry/build/game/all/changes.json --out

forge-packs/foundry/build/foundry-0.2.0.mjolnir --sign --sign uses the existing local author device key registered with the Hub. --sign-seed <file> uses an explicitly supplied key instead. Omit signing for an offline build; the Hub does not accept an unsigned public upload. The packer validates the catalog, container pairing and basic IoStore structure before it writes the archive. The Hub independently scans the submitted archive. build_pack.py --only <block-id> produces a reduced diagnostic inventory in build/game/<block-id>/; package that directory only for local tests. Do not publish a reduced diagnostic build with the same version as the full set. Use a fresh output directory when changing the set's inventory: these builders retain prior outputs.

The visual cooker writes a namespaced mesh and synchronized actor per piece. Blender/glTF geometry is converted to the game's units; the actor restores each piece's authored transform after mesh normalization: Foundry uses a bottom-centre origin, while Roadworks uses its entry floor. Actor visual collision is disabled so the simulation owns collision. The collision cooker builds triangle collision BSPs/MOPPs and fixed Havok polyhedra from the same source hulls. Composite pieces keep separate hulls so doors and windows remain open. The pack builder then creates namespaced collision, physics, model and crate tags and packages their visual dependencies.
Add a pack to a map

Add the desired subset to the level JSON before a level bake --standalone build. Forge pack palettes currently require a standalone map; canvas overrides are rejected because they do not install the new package preloads. Keep the pack's cooked containers available in the bake's input Paks view so tag references and preload dependencies resolve. { "blam": { "map_variant": true, "forge_packs": [ { "slug": "foundry", "version": "0.2.0", "blocks": [ { "id": "floor_2x2", "tag": "objects\mjolnir\forge\foundry\floor_2x2" } ] } ] } } This is a fragment to merge with the existing level definition. The bake adds one custom Forge palette in the authored pack/block order. There is no global slot assignment: independent maps choose their own subset and order. At most 63 packs and 200 custom references are accepted, and the completed palette must fit the engine's 255-entry total including standard objects. The baker checks both limits. It also adds each custom crate to the scenario wrapper's preload list, dependency bundle and container package-store imports, preserving the donor wrapper. A declared crate absent from the input Paks fails the bake.
Add a pack to a map

Package the newly baked map with the existing mjolnir map pack command. It preserves blam.forge_packs in the archived level JSON and adds a ^0.2.0 dependency on each listed pack (see updating a pack). Installing the map through the launcher resolves those dependencies, selecting a compatible published release rather than blindly installing each dependency's latest version. The launcher validates the enabled profile's dependencies before mounting content. A first live map installation can mount new Forge pack dependencies before the map; replacing an already installed pack requires a restart. Installing a pack does not add slots to an already baked map. Such a map must be rebaked and repackaged with blam.forge_packs before those pieces can be placed. There is no automatic rebake or arbitrary runtime palette injection in this implementation. Keep pack/block ordering stable when updating a map if its existing layouts should continue to load.

The launcher writes generated catalog files beneath ue4ss/MJOLNIRForgePacks/: installed.json for the editor's display metadata and installed.txt for the native identity check. These represent enabled, verified releases and include exact archive SHA-256 values. Forge labels match full tag paths, so two packs may use the same block ID without ambiguity. At most 4,096 catalog blocks may be enabled across a profile, matching the native inventory reader's bound; each map still has its smaller palette limit. Saving a layout writes both <MAP>.mvar and <MAP>.mvar.packs beneath ue4ss/Mods/MJOLNIRForge/layouts/. Keep the pair together when copying or sharing a layout. The sidecar starts with forge-packs 1; each following tab-separated row contains: flat-palette-index full-tag-path pack-slug saved-version archive-sha256 The archive SHA-256 records which bytes the layout was saved with, for diagnosing a report; it is not a load condition. Only custom pieces actually used by the layout produce rows. Every new .mvar contains an fpk1 marker, including saves with no custom pieces, so removing its sidecar cannot make it appear to be a legacy layout. Old layouts without the marker remain usable when they do not reference custom pack tags.

Before launch, the launcher reads saved-layout pack requirements. A pack installed at the saved version or a later one in its line serves the layout as it is; otherwise the launcher downloads the newest release of that line through the normal verified Hub install flow and enables the dependency closure. Layouts saved with different releases of one line need the later one. Layouts or enabled maps that need different lines of one pack are written to the launcher log, and the launcher still restores everything else; move the affected layout pair aside or use compatible map/pack versions. Orphan sidecars without a matching .mvar and files in layout history do not trigger downloads. Before the engine recreates saved objects, native Forge checks each recorded flat palette index against the current full tag path and the installed pack's version. Missing inventory, a different palette binding, a missing sidecar on a new save, or an installed release outside the saved one's line (or older than it) refuse the layout. These checks prevent a saved custom index from becoming an unrelated object after a profile or map change. They do not migrate a layout to a different palette.

Downloads happen at launcher installation/launch time. Opening an incompatible layout while the game is already running reports the dependency problem and requires a launcher restart; the native DLL does not access the network. Standalone Hub publishing of .mvar layout pairs and automatic map rebaking remain follow-up work.

The repository tests cover manifest/catalog rejection and Hub release visibility, exact dependency selection and a local HTTP download fixture, signature/archive round trips, IoStore bounds, and native identity mismatches. Useful focused commands are: cargo test -p blam-cli forge cargo test --manifest-path apps/launcher/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib & native/forge/test-pack-bindings.ps1 python forge-packs/foundry/validate.py python forge-packs/foundry-wide/validate.py python forge-packs/roadworks/validate.py Run the Hub's npm test and npm run typecheck from hub/ when changing that component. Geometry validation and the collision builder's ray checks verify authored shapes offline. Before publishing a playable pack, verify in game that each piece renders at its declared size, ramps and platforms support players, apertures stay open, placement/duplication and save/reload work, and a clean launcher profile fetches the exact dependencies.

The first pack, Foundry, began as an original 18-piece industrial construction kit in 0.1.0; 0.2.0 adds six portal and lighting pieces for a total of 24. It provides a repeatable vocabulary for floors, elevation changes, enclosure, cover and trim. The models use no extracted Halo assets. Construction shape families are inspired by the usefulness of Halo's Forge palettes, not by copied mesh geometry or textures.

Reach's structure palette groups building blocks, bridges/platforms, buildings, decorative objects, walls/openings, inclines and natural objects. Its block family spans several footprints and thicknesses; bridge lengths, corners and ramps let players connect those footprints. The Reach structure catalog and Bungie's original palette screenshots mirrored on ForgeHub provide concrete examples of the categories. The original catalogue is an Xbox 360 reference, so it is not an exhaustive list of later MCC additions. In a 2010 developer Q&A, Bungie systems designer Tyson Green explained that pieces were intended to abut, which avoids overlapping-surface flicker. He also described inventory limits shared by object families. Both details support investing in compatible dimensions and useful reusable pieces before large one-off decorative prefabs. The official MCC July 2020 announcement documents Halo 3's rotation snap, coordinate snap, precision edits and world/local rotation axes. Reach received axis toggling plus expanded Forge World and Tempest palettes. These are useful editing expectations for our kit; exact MCC world dimensions have not been assumed or copied.

The Reach manual published by Microsoft says Bungie's own Forge World variants use the same tools and objects as players. Community examples such as Tension Span use multilevel bridgework; Pinnacle illustrates towers, ramps, landing platforms and a central structure. Our demonstration level should similarly show the kit assembled into traversable play space.

The following dimensions are this project's design choices, not measurements claimed for MCC objects. One module is 2 m; placement snap is 0.5 m. All assets use metre coordinates, Z-up and a bottom-centre origin. Keep 90-degree turns and cardinal docking planes predictable; do not place decoration outside the nominal bounds. Small bevels soften the image while collision remains simple and exact. The material system uses warm concrete, dark gunmetal frames, inset deck panels and amber markers. Colour is carried by four reusable PBR materials, avoiding a texture dependency for the first release. Markers on ramps are separate adjacent surface strips, not coplanar decals. Door/window openings remain empty in both the visual geometry and the compound collision geometry. Source scripts, portable JSON geometry and the rebuild instructions live in forge-packs/foundry. Blender 5.2.3 LTS was verified locally and against the official release page. Direct background Python automation is sufficient; no MCP update is needed for the generator. Generated .blend, GLBs, collision exports and the actual rendered contact sheet are kept in that folder's ignored build/ directory.

The first Crossline playtest found the 24 × 40 m arena cramped. Crossline 0.2 expands its footprint to 48 × 80 m using a separate eighteen-piece Foundry Wide structural kit. Each piece doubles X/Y while preserving Z: floor tiles reach 8 × 8 m, bridges are 4 m wide, and 8/16 m ramps retain a 2 m rise. This also keeps cover at 1 m, stair rises at 0.25 m, deck surfaces at 4.5 m and perimeter walls at 9 m. Portal frames, landing pads, light fixtures, player shapes and weapon models retain their original dimensions. The larger arena spreads out their positions without enlarging the native teleporter trigger. Separate pack and tag names avoid reinterpreting existing Foundry placements in Roadworks or saved maps. Original Foundry 0.2 remains available alongside Foundry Wide 0.1.

The separate Roadworks pack provides vehicle-scale straights, connecting curves and eased ramps. Forge racing remains an active design genre: official features include race courses in February 2026 and Death Race in April 2026. These are references for the type of play; the Roadworks geometry is original. The installed Warthog's assembled visual envelope is approximately 6.13 × 3.25 × 2.43 m; the Spartan's standing collision height is 1.981 m. The scale audit distinguishes visible bounds, physics bounds and wheel contact measurements. Foundry's 2 m-wide bridges and ramps suit infantry. Roadworks 0.2.0 uses a 16 m clear deck, 0.8 m shoulders, 24/48 m straights and 40 m centreline-radius curves. Its 48 m ramp rises 4 m, with 4 m flat noses, 8 m slope transitions and a maximum 12.5% grade. Each piece has an optional guarded variant with 1.5 m barriers outside the lane. Deck thickness remains 0.5 m. Curves use separate convex slices so their inner space remains open. The stock vehicle and player dimensions are unchanged.

Historical 0.1.0 dimensions: 8 m clear width, 0.4 m shoulders, 12/24 m straights, R20 curves, 24 m ramps rising 4 m at a maximum 25% grade, and 1 m rails. Vehicle playtesting found that footprint too tight. Version 0.2.0 doubles the XY footprint and raises the rails by 0.5 m, preserving deck/ramp Z heights and the convex topology. Earlier game photos and driving checks document 0.1.0; they are not evidence of driving the enlarged release. The Roadworks Circuit connects those pieces into a roughly 731 m driving fixture on a 320 m recovery deck, including a raised section and a pit pad. Three stock Warthogs provide a scale reference: one beside a Spartan and a true 2 m scale bar, and two facing opposite directions in the track lanes. Normal road surfaces remain 3 m high and the raised section 7 m high, so driving exercises the pieces' collision above the recovery floor. Connector positions and tangents drive the assembly and are checked for closed loops, matching edges and reversed ramp joins. This source metadata does not add automatic connector snapping to the current Forge editor.

Offline checks cover the enlarged geometry, exact joins, two-car static footprint clearance and native collision rays. Updated in-game steering, suspension, passing and rail-contact checks remain pending. The prior 0.1.0 fixture was roughly 366 m long on a 160 m recovery deck with two Warthogs. The user reported the enlarged Roadworks scale was much better. Crossline's subsequent enlargement uses Foundry Wide as described above; Forge Canvas retains its original 64 × 64 m deck and Foundry dependency.

These are design directions, not delivered model packs: Set Visual direction Suitable spaces Relay Pale alloy, dark inset panels, narrow cyan channels and angular cuts Elevated platforms, clean sci-fi arenas Frontier Weathered basalt, oxidized braces and muted ochre panels Outdoor ruins, excavation sites, rugged outposts Reuse the same module, origins and docking planes across sets so creators can mix them. A second set should change silhouettes and material treatment while keeping the same traversal clearances and connector heights.

The delivered Crosswalk assembly fixture places 54 instances of all 18 types inside 16 × 16 m. Its actual Blender render shows two facing upper platforms, a bridge, lower routes, ramps, stairs, cover and rails. Main walking surfaces are 4 m apart, with 3.5 m clear beneath the bridge. This portable metre/Z-up authoring layout still needs a runtime adapter or bake; it is not a native save or proof of playability. Verify floor seams by walking and driving over them; walk through the doorway and fire through the window; test ramp endpoints and stairs; duplicate, rotate, save, reload and delete parts. Finally load the variant on a client without the pack, confirm the pinned pack downloads before loading, and confirm missing/corrupt dependencies produce an actionable failure instead of silently dropping placed pieces. The source validator proves the mesh/collision construction invariants. The render proves the exported geometry and authored material appearance. The game build currently uses stock material references. Separate CU4 validation evidence records all 18 types placed, representative rendering, movement, collision, ramp climbing and save/restart checks, with the remaining traversal, visual and multiplayer work explicitly listed.

A Forge block is an object tag the simulation can place from a map's palette and players stand on. Four things, all checked in CU4: Need Why Where A collision model (coll), ideally a physics model (phmo) The simulation does all collision. Unreal geometry is visual only. the tag's model A multiplayer object block The placement check (0x3049e0) refuses a tag without one (root +0x124) the object definition An Unreal actor Each object tag's wrapper package holds an AssetReference to an actor Blueprint, and the game binds a pooled actor of that class to the object. Without one the object is invisible, like MJOLNIR's flag stands and spawn points. /Game/Tags/<path>-<group>, BlamCrateTagDataAsset and the like Phased physics in forge (multiplayer flags bit 1) Otherwise placing looks for room at the cursor and refuses anything resting on the ground MJOLNIRForge sets it in memory on palette tags

CU4 ships no Forge blocks. Nothing of Reach's Forge World palette survives: a search of all 12,508 tags and 144,482 Unreal packages for forge, block, wall, ramp, bridge, platform or column names found campaign geometry only. What comes closest (surveyed 2026-11-01; every row has a collision model, a physics model and a Blueprint with a mesh): Tag Use Size (m) MP block On B40 objects\props\covenant\crate_space_a\crate_space_a (crate) crate, cover 1.4 × 1.6 × 2.25 yes yes objects\props\covenant\cov_portable_shield\cov_portable_shield (scenery) barrier (the panel can be shot down and recharges) 2.4 × 1.2 × 2.9 yes yes crate_comm_a, crate_comm_b (crate) wall, column 2.9 × 2.6 × 4.2; 1.8 × 2.5 × 4.2 no yes objects\levels\halo1\solo\b40\bridge_glass\bridge_glass (scenery) bridge (breaks at once: vitality 1) 14.7 × 2.6 × 0.25 no yes light_bridge_b40 (machine) bridge 27 × 3.7 × 0.5 no yes elevator_a/b/c_b40 (machine) platform 6.5 × 6.6 × 0.5 no yes Forerunner doors (acr_big_angle_door, for_door_a, acr_control_room_door, chasm_door) walls various no yes More is shipped but not loaded by B40: C20's light bridges (4 × 22 m and 4 × 28 m), E30 wreckage, small UNSC crates and doors. A palette entry that names one loads it by name. Machines follow their device animation, so where a door or a light bridge rests once placed on its own has to be seen in game.

defs/level/palette-map.json blocks lists the two with a multiplayer block, so every map baked with map_variant gets a blocks palette. The others need a multiplayer block grafted in, which makes new tags (see Making blocks below). VERIFIED in game (BGL, 2026-11-01): with crate_space_a put in a palette entry at run time, it placed from the palette, Unreal drew it, it was saved in the layout, and a Slayer game started with it. Not checked: standing on it (the Monitor flies through everything).

A palette entry's object is the tag index in its first variant (+0x10). The simulation reads it every time it places from the entry (0x32f450 → 0x5ee570). MJOLNIRForge points entries at other tags when it reads the palettes, and again at each new map before a saved layout is applied, from MJOLNIRForge\slots.txt: # palette:entry = tag path (an object tag the map loads) 3:1 = objects\props\covenant\crate_space_a\crate_space_a The tag must be loaded: referenced by the map, or by anything the map loads. The entry changes for the whole game. Objects the map itself placed from it change too: pointing BGL's health-pack entry at a crate turned every health pack into a crate. A saved layout's engine payload names entries. New community-pack layouts also save tag/version bindings and refuse an entry whose tag or pack line changed; see saved-layout checks.

The earlier proposal for 32 global slot tags and Hub-assigned slot ranges is retired. Packs now own objects\mjolnir\forge\<pack-id>\<block-id> tag paths. Each map declares its supported subset and order in blam.forge_packs before a standalone bake. The scenario includes these references and their package preloads; the map archive depends on the corresponding Hub release lines. There is no shared global slot allocation and installing a pack does not automatically add it to an existing map. The Hub's Forge catalog displays validated content releases. The launcher downloads map dependencies and missing releases required by saved layout sidecars. Native Forge checks each saved index against its tag path and pack line before recreating objects. The complete contract and current limits are in forge_packs.md.
The Foundry build uses these tools to produce new namespaced meshes, synchronized actors, tags and exact collision hulls. Cooked artifacts are generated locally from the supported game installation.

The tag: mjolnir new-tag --group crate --from objects\props\covenant\crate_space_a\crate_space_a --to <namespaced block path>; --graft "object.multiplayer object=crate:crate_space_a-crate:object.multiplayer object" for a donor without the block; --asset-reference /Game/.../BP_Thing for the actor; --payload for a model, collision and physics of its own. Collision: forge_collision builds triangle collision BSPs and MOPPs; tools/forge/build_collision.py builds fixed polyhedra from the same hulls. Composite pieces retain separate hulls to preserve openings. The Unreal mesh: rewrite a shipped mesh's LOD in place (mesh_rewrite + package_add, docs on UE mesh writing); or cook in the MJOLNIRMaterials editor and retarget (tools/ue/cook.ps1, ue retarget); or draw it the way the Halo 2 machines are drawn: the level loader's follow attaches a mesh to the donor's actor and hides the donor's own (mods/MJOLNIRLevelLoader/Scripts/main.lua, follow). From Halo Reach (MCC): mjolnir cache info forge_halo.map identifies the map, but no stager reads Reach caches yet. One would be modelled on crates/blam-cache/src/h2. The first check is whether Reach's collision and physics model layouts match CU4's, by comparing mjolnir fields for each group. Forge World's blocks are mostly scenery with a Havok physics model, which CU4's crates use too.
Modelled new: a mesh plus collision hulls (boxes and ramps are their own hulls), through the same pipeline. Each physics hull must be convex; a doorway or other compound piece uses multiple hulls.

crates/blam-sbsp/examples/forge_canvas.rs builds an original rectangular slab and an open build volume. It does not use Blood Gulch or another converted map's geometry. The local shipped BSP_03_1_Chasm_old tag supplies the engine's structure and physics wrappers; extracted and generated game data stays in ignored build folders. cargo run -p blam-sbsp --example forge_canvas -- forge-packs/foundry/build/donors/Levels/Halo1/Solo/B40/_Generated_/BSP_03_1_Chasm_old.scenario_structure_bsp forge-packs/foundry/build/canvas/blank.sbsp cargo run -p blam-sbsp --example forge_canvas -- forge-packs/foundry/build/donors/Levels/Halo1/Solo/B40/_Generated_/BSP_03_1_Chasm_old.scenario_structure_bsp forge-packs/foundry-wide/build/canvas/crossline.sbsp --width-m 96 --depth-m 160 --extent-m 96 The output directory must exist. Options, all in metres: Option Default Meaning --width-m 64 Slab width on X, centred at zero --depth-m 64 Slab depth on Y, centred at zero --thickness-m 1 Slab extends from -thickness to Z=0 --extent-m 64 Playable X/Y range is -extent to +extent --below-m 8 Playable volume extends to -below on Z --height-m 64 Playable volume extends to +height on Z

The output uses Blam world units (metres divided by 3.048) and BSP index zero. The sibling <output>.canvas.json records the exact bounds for the scenario and centimetre dimensions for a matching visible slab. World bounds, cluster bounds and every supernode AABB cover the build volume, independently of the floor's vertex bounds. Two unreferenced vertices at the volume's minimum and maximum extend only the world shell's query bounds; they have no edges or surfaces and are added after building the actual floor's Havok collision. The floor definition stays compact. The volume has no ceiling or boundary walls. This is required for selection above a flat floor: the engine rebuilds its global ray-query box from all shell vertices, unions instance bounds and adds 0.1 world units (CU4 0x2c1aa1..0x2c1e20). It does not use the authored world bounds for that initial rejection. Without the extra vertices, a ray above Z=0.1 was rejected before dynamic objects were tested, although a direct ray against the same Forge block hit. The regression preserves every collision table except the two added vertices and checks that elevated space remains open.

Bot navigation is not provided by these maps. The shell's two extra vertices also prevent the current pathfinding::copy_drops matcher (which requires equal vertex counts) from recognizing the compact floor instance, so the bake does not apply its usual 0.001-wu copy lowering. Future navigation support must account for unreferenced bounds vertices when matching collision copies. For a standalone B40-based level, use active_bsps: [8], single_bsp: 8, the reported bounds at scenario BSP index 8, --bsp 8=<output>, and the bare defs/level/empty_world.umap. The bake renumbers the scenario to the BSP's index zero. Supply original rendering, valid multiplayer spawn scenery, lighting, and a kill floor separately. Decorative meshes do not supply Blam collision. Forge pack palettes require blam.map_variant: true, the pack references, and the pack containers available during the bake. Each build checks the source collision and both emitted collision trees with 13,068 floor, edge and elevated-space probes, then verifies the emitted volume bounds. It fails before writing if geometry or bounds disagree. Pure tests cover square and rectangular slabs, packed collision, and invalid dimensions: cargo test -p blam-sbsp --example forge_canvas These are offline checks; traversal and object placement still need a game test of the final standalone map.

Foundry Wide 0.2 adds two self-contained surface profiles to the existing seven shipped-material mappings. The original eighteen Wide pieces keep their previous mesh/material path. New glass and portal pieces use their own cooked masters, textures and shader library; they do not require the TST map to be installed.

The canonical profile data is material_profiles.json. glass_cyan is an original two-sided, lit translucent material: RGB [0.12, 0.55, 0.65], opacity 0.24, roughness 0.12, specular 0.7. Its pane collision stays solid regardless of opacity. teleporter_green reproduces the Halo CE shader tag levels\test\tutorial\shaders\example_tutorial_teleporter, using the existing shader_transparent_chicago graph. The numeric stage parameters were taken from the local TST conversion's materials.spec.json, produced by ce_material_spec.py. Four stages sample two textures: dust in stages 0/1 and mask in stages 2/3. The profile retains their UV animation functions, periods, phases, scales and color/alpha combiners; TST's map-specific fog parameters are omitted. Animation uses GPU material time, not a Lua timer. The visual field has no collision and does not itself teleport a player; native gameplay markers provide travel. The material cook requires these local CE-conversion DDS files in the directory supplied to --ce-textures. They are the bitmap/mip-chain exports described in CE map conversion, not Blender previews or replacement PNGs:
