Use the project's Unreal 5.5 editor and fork shader/layout plugins. A fresh checkout needs the MeteoriteEditor Win64 Development and Meteorite Win64 Shipping targets built for unreal/MJOLNIRMaterials/Meteorite.uproject before the commandlets run. The mjolnir CLI must be built too: tools/ue/cook.ps1 retargets the cooked material properties into the game's layout and the builder rejects a failed retarget. Blender exports and native collision/physics are separate prerequisites, as described in Forge packs. From the repository root, with local paths substituted:

$ceTextures = 'C:/local/CE-conversion/staging/textures' $basePaks = 'C:/local/base-and-runtime-paks' # Preparation alone writes a reviewable input specification. python tools/forge/build_materials.py forge-packs/foundry-wide --ce-textures $ceTextures --chunk 967 # Import, cook, retarget, and fingerprint the material container. python tools/forge/build_materials.py forge-packs/foundry-wide --ce-textures $ceTextures --chunk 967 --cook python tools/forge/build_pack.py forge-packs/foundry-wide --paks $basePaks target/debug/mjolnir.exe forge pack forge-packs/foundry-wide/build/game/all/mjolnir.json --content forge-packs/foundry-wide/build/game/all/content --readme forge-packs/foundry-wide/README.md --changes forge-packs/foundry-wide/build/game/all/changes.json --out forge-packs/foundry-wide/build/foundry-wide-0.2.0.mjolnir --sign Cook under a shader chunk in 900..999 that your own installed packs do not use (build_materials.py enforces the range). Foundry Wide uses 967, as pakchunk967-MJOLNIRFORGEMAT-foundry-wide_P: Unreal opens the shader library whose number matches the container's. Asset paths are derived from the validated pack slug: /Game/MJOLNIR/Forge/<slug>/Materials/ and .../Textures/.

Launcher 0.24.0 and newer give each installed container its own number and rename its shader library to match, so two packs cooked under the same number install side by side (chunk_numbering.md). The rest of this paragraph is what an older launcher does. An older launcher checks the numeric reservation before installing an enabled surface pack, applying a profile, launching, or copying live dependencies. Different slugs do not make the same shader number safe. A conflicting active pack or unrelated .pak/.utoc/.ucas in Paks is refused without modifying game files. The same pack's existing container triple and updates are allowed. Offline profile application can retire old launcher-managed files, but two conflicting packs in the resulting profile are still refused. This check is specific to MJOLNIRFORGEMAT libraries; ordinary pack load ordering is unchanged.

build/materials/materials.spec.json records profile values, source paths and DDS hashes. receipt.json records the specification/profile hashes and the three cooked sibling-file hashes. build_pack.py requires a matching, complete receipt before including surfaces. A changed profile or specification, modified/missing file, wrong slug, or mismatched shader chunk is rejected. Changes to the graph implementation also require a fresh cook; the receipt does not hash Python source files. Unreal-generated IDs may change across cooks, so receipts identify a particular output, not a promise of identical binary hashes on every machine. Local build output contains .utoc, .ucas and the empty .pak mount sibling. The .mjolnir archive stores the .utoc/.ucas pairs; the launcher creates the mount siblings on installation. Keep the material pair and all visual/tag pairs together. The Forge runtime must also include materials.lua and material_profiles.json beside main.lua; the JSON is runtime data, not an optional authoring file. Pack metadata carries only approved profile IDs and slots, never executable code or arbitrary material paths.

The runtime reads the launcher's actual nested inventory: packs[].forge_pack.blocks[]. It requires catalog schema 1, a matching forge_pack.id/release slug, and the exact namespaced block tag. Profiles are assigned on the existing retained game-thread callback, at the 500 ms surface scan cadence. Both masters already contain their intended defaults, including the portal textures and animation, so newly spawned pieces do not wait for a Lua assignment to acquire their basic appearance. Assignment identity includes world, actor address/name and the salted native object binding. Hidden or unbound pooled actors are skipped. A reactivated actor or changed binding receives a fresh material instance. Polling retains only string keys and booleans for these objects: no Blueprint class, actor, component, material instance or texture wrapper crosses a poll. Native engine classes/CDOs are cached; Blueprint classes use the non-loading soft-reference resolver instead of a global UObject scan. Work is bounded to 64 surface classes and 256 active actors per poll. A failed assignment suppresses that class until inventory or world changes and logs once; this includes a temporarily unavailable component. Existing/baked master materials remain in place. This avoids repeated loading on a broken catalog or missing container, but is not a general background asset-retry mechanism. Portable checks:

python -m unittest discover -s tools/forge -p test_build_materials.py lua tools/tests/test_forge_materials.lua lua tools/tests/test_forge_dispatch.lua cargo test -p ue-asset --lib Foundry Wide contains eight material/texture packages, with all /Game/ imports inside its own pack namespace. The glass and portal masters are two-sided translucent/additive respectively. Each surface mesh declares nine slots in both its reflected StaticMaterials and native arrays, including slots 7/8. mesh_rewrite --asset-imports writes both arrays and uses the old reflected entries as an exact format guard (serialization details). Component overrides alone do not establish translucent renderer relevance. Cold-load tests verified transparency and solid collision from both sides of the glass, plus visible green-field animation and native teleport travel in both directions. Appearance while moving, pooling and restoring surface placements remains a separate live check. See the validation record for the tested artifacts and images.

Pack utilities are bounded catalog data. They do not install scripts from a community archive. The Hub scanner, CLI packer and launcher validate the same fields; the launcher preserves them in MJOLNIRForgePacks/installed.json. Old packs can omit them or use null.

A block can carry this optional specification, in its authored local axes and metres (right-handed, Z up): "lift": { "offset_m": [0, 0, 0.45], "size_m": [4, 4, 3.5], "direction": [0, 0, 1], "acceleration_m_s2": 20, "max_speed_m_s": 4.5, "negates_gravity": true } offset_m is the trigger's bottom centre; size_m is its full box size. The trigger follows the piece's live translation and full rotation, independently of its visual mesh normalization. The example overlaps a 0.5 m deck by 5 cm to avoid a floating-point gap. Foundry Wide uses this four-metre-rise preset: its nominal column ends at 3.95 m, with an additional ballistic rise after exiting. Verify the trajectory and landing in your own layout; the speed is not a guaranteed landing height. Horizontal steering is preserved. Offsets are limited to ±100 m per axis; sizes to 0.1–100 m. Direction must be a unit vector (squared-length tolerance 0.001). Acceleration is 0.1–100 m/s², speed 0.1–30 m/s, and negates_gravity must be a boolean. Unknown fields are rejected. Runtime discovery uses at most 16 class definitions, selected by sorted class path, and 64 active lift actors; additional definitions are ignored.

MJOLNIRLevelLoader/Scripts/pack_lifts.lua converts these boxes to the existing Halo 2 phantom format, and lifts.lua hands them to MJOLNIRLobby's DLL with the level's own phantoms. The DLL pushes with the same acceleration, gravity compensation and object_set_velocity as Lockout's lifts, once per simulation tick (native/lobby/lifts_runtime.h). Each peer pushes only its own players, on foot, in Forge and Slayer. Saved-layout actors and later duplicates are discovered from their current Blam bindings; hidden or pooled actors without a binding do nothing. Discovery uses Unreal's native actor-class lists and nonloading soft-class resolution, every 500 ms while an installed pack has a lift block, and the DLL is sent the set again only when a lift moves, appears or goes. It never performs a periodic UE4SS global object scan or retains a Blueprint class/actor wrapper between calls. Travel sends an empty set, and the DLL drops each player's carried velocity on a new game.

Panels may declare: "door": { "travel_m": 4, "speed_m_s": 4, "trigger_size_m": [8, 16, 6], "hold_open_s": 2 } Travel is along local +Z. Travel must be positive and at most 16 m, speed positive and at most 8 m/s, trigger dimensions positive and at most 32 m, and hold time 0–10 seconds. Door panel dimensions_m may not exceed 64 m on any axis. Unknown fields are rejected. The infantry preset above travels 4 m; the vehicle preset travels 6 m with a [12,20,8] trigger, the same 4 m/s speed and two-second hold.

Use MJOLNIRForge 0.4.0, MJOLNIRLobby 0.19.2 and MJOLNIRLevelLoader 0.9.8 or newer together; doors outside Forge need MJOLNIRLobby 0.19.3. Lobby checks the Forge native utility API marker and waits for a compatible native Forge module before animating. It refuses door automation with an older loaded Forge DLL, whose save path would otherwise serialize the animated position. native/lobby/forge_doors_runtime.h runs on the authoritative simulation thread in Forge and ordinary multiplayer modes, including Slayer. It operates on the native crate and its collision body through the engine's transform setter, rather than moving only its Unreal visual. Players approaching the rotated local trigger request opening along the panel's local +Z. After they leave, the panel waits for hold_open_s and closes. Fixed and Phased enable automation; Normal disables it and leaves ordinary physics in control. Fresh scenario construction and Revert seed installed door panels to Fixed, because scenario placements do not encode this physics choice. This happens before the objects are created. Loading a saved layout replaces those defaults with its saved properties, including an explicit Normal choice; other pieces and existing Fixed/Phased choices are unchanged.

Forge mode keeps a panel inside the map variant's bounds. Other modes leave those bounds empty, so no box applies there; travel is still limited by the pack's travel_m. The runtime checks a conservative sphere against the panel's swept box before closing. Bipeds, vehicles and movable Normal crates can keep a door open or reopen it. Opening also stops beneath a dynamic obstacle. Entering Monitor mode, or requesting an edit, attempts to close the panel only if its entire closing path is clear. A parked vehicle can therefore leave the panel raised while editing. Grabbing, duplicating, rotating or changing the physics of that raised panel is deferred with a message to clear the doorway; unrelated objects remain editable. These checks do not test the static world, Fixed/Phased construction pieces, or unparented crates whose native physics model contains only fixed bodies. The last classification is cached per world and salted tag; keyframed, mixed and unknown bodies remain obstacles. Authors must leave space above and beside the panel for its full travel.

Motion advances once per changed simulation tick, using the native tick rate; paused redraws do not consume hold time. Catch-up frames advance at most one tick. There are at most 128 active automated panels and 256 installed door definitions. The adapter scans native object arrays once per tick, with no Unreal global-object polling. It accepts only supported CU4 builds and rejects parented panels, invalid transforms, stale object handles and unmatched pack identities. Unsupported builds or invalid inventory disable automation.
Automatic doors › Editing, saves and multiplayer limits

Forge's native update reapplies each map-variant pose every tick. The adapter therefore publishes the animated position in the live map variant and keeps the authored closed pose in a private cache, keyed by world instance, full object handle and entry identity. Deletion, travel and replaced objects discard stale cache entries; an external authored pose change establishes a new baseline. F5 projects verified closed poses into Forge's temporary serialization copy. Saving does not close the live door or modify the active animation. If a panel has no verified closed baseline, saving is deferred rather than recording its raised pose. This includes enabled door panels on fireteam clients. Ordinary layouts without those panels retain the existing client-save behavior.
Automatic doors › Editing, saves and multiplayer limits

A client that becomes host cannot reconstruct the closed origin of a door it joined while open. Automation and saves requiring that missing baseline remain disabled until the game is rehosted. Closed-origin state is not separately replicated. The engine's object-transform updates are used in Slayer; map-variant dirty updates apply in Forge. Client visual/collision replication, host migration and driving a vehicle beneath an operating gate still require in-game verification. The validation record reports the narrower local save/reload, visible opening/closing and nearby-vehicle obstruction results. The implementation and portable tests are not live evidence.

The launcher emits a companion MJOLNIRForgePacks/doors.txt for the native reader. Its header is forge-doors 1; each row has ten tab-separated fields: tag, travel, speed, trigger X/Y/Z, hold time, panel width/depth/height. All measurements are metres or seconds, using decimal dots. There are at most 256 definitions across enabled packs. The native reader must match each tag against current installed.txt bindings. Panel dimensions come from the validated catalog, not a guessed donor bound. The trigger is centred on the panel in X/Y, with its vertical interval from −0.5 m to trigger Z above the authored bottom origin. The launcher prepares all inventory files before replacing each atomically, publishing the identity bindings last. Disabling/uninstalling packs also rewrites the companion; no door entries leaves a header-only file.

surfaces is an optional list of up to 16 strict {slot, profile} objects. Slots are unique integers 0–15. Profiles are the fixed names glass_cyan and teleporter_green; arbitrary material paths or code are not accepted. The material implementation supplies the approved textures, animation and shader parameters. The green visual does not replace native teleporter sender/receiver/two-way markers and their channel settings. The CLI packer and Hub scanner require these cooked packages inside the archive's installed content/ containers, under /Game/MJOLNIR/Forge/<pack-id>: Profile Required package paths below the pack root glass_cyan Materials/M_ForgeGlassCyan teleporter_green Materials/M_ForgePortalGreen, Textures/T_PortalDust, Textures/T_PortalMask, Materials/T_CE_BlackCube The check uses Unreal package IDs and requires export-bundle chunks; bulk-only chunks, another pack's copies and containers outside content/ do not satisfy it. Packs without surface profiles do not need these assets. The Hub's bounded package-ID hash and the Rust implementation share 15 test vectors spanning minimum, ordinary and maximum pack slug lengths.

This is a presence check, not proof of valid material exports, complete shader code, matching mesh slots or gameplay collision. Door/lift metadata validators check their bounded data shapes; they do not decode tag payloads to prove a compatible native crate and Blueprint binding. The authored cook checks and live runtime checks remain necessary, as does testing the installed pack.

Portable tests cover transformed trigger planes, source-to-Unreal coordinates, the standing-deck overlap, player ownership, actor pooling, class lookup cost boundaries, world travel and use of the shared script writer. Existing Halo 2 math tests remain unchanged. Hub/CLI/launcher tests cover schema limits, unknown keys, normalized inventory round trips, companion fields and stale-row removal. Live gameplay coverage is recorded separately in the validation record. native/lobby/test-forge-doors.ps1 runs the portable door parser and movement tests with MSVC warnings treated as errors. They cover field limits, rejected row isolation, translated/rotated triggers, sphere-versus-swept-panel clearance, opening/closing, hold time and paused or invalid time steps. The same C test also builds with a C11 compiler on other platforms. CI runs it alongside the three lift Lua suites and the launcher Forge inventory tests.

Status: design, 2026-11-03. Nothing here is built unless a line says so. Phase 0 (checking layout files) is built and tested in game on branch work/forge-mvar-bounds. Players build with Forge today, but a build stays on their PC: F5 keeps one layout per map, and the only way to give one to someone is to copy two files by hand. This document plans several named layouts per map, a lobby choice of which one a match starts with, a hub listing that players publish to and download from, and an in-game layouts menu.

A hub hands everyone who downloads a layout a file its author chose, so every reader checks a layout before the game sees it: Forge DLL (built): native/forge/layout_bounds.h checks a layout's labels and label names, and Forge refuses a malformed file with the reason. Hub and launcher (planned): the validator below, on upload and on install.

One Rust function, blam_megalo::layout::validate(bytes) -> Result<Summary>, used by the hub (built to WebAssembly), the launcher and the tag editor (native). A second implementation in TypeScript would be a second grammar to keep in step. It accepts a file when: The envelope is the one Forge writes: _blf 1.2, one mvar 31.1 with a payload of at most 0x7000 bytes (the DLL's buffer), an optional fpk1 1.0, _eof, then only zero padding. The payload decodes completely with crates/blam-megalo/grammar/megalo_cu4.json, with fewer than 8 bits left over. Content type 5 (map variant) and encoding version 31. At most 256 labels, at most 0x1000 bytes of label names (the declared size, the compressed stream's prefix and the inflated bytes), and at most 256 quotas. It encodes back to the same bytes, so nothing the grammar does not name travels in it. Every placed object's palette index is inside the palette (to confirm against the decoder before relying on it). Summary carries what the hub and launcher store: title, description, map id, object count, labels, and the palette entries used. The sidecar is parsed by the parser the launcher already has (forge_packs::layout_pins).

WebAssembly on the hub works. A spike on 2026-11-03 built blam-megalo for wasm32-unknown-unknown (382 KB, grammar included) and imported the .wasm from a route. OpenNext bundled it, wrangler dev ran it on workerd, and the route returned the right label counts for a MJOLNIR save (0) and Reach's Asylum (13), about 2 ms a file. A local Cloudflare build on Windows needs pnpm install --config.node-linker=hoisted, because OpenNext's file copy cannot create pnpm's symlinks without Developer Mode. CI builds on Linux and is unaffected.

Mods\MJOLNIRForge\layouts\ FRB.mvar, FRB.mvar.packs active: what every match on FRB starts with (unchanged) FRB.active the library entry the active pair came from, if any history... unchanged library\FRB\ layout.mvar layout.mvar.packs layout.json title, description, created, updated, map version, source (local, or hub slug + version + release id) preview.png optional The active pair keeps its name, so everything that reads it today (match start, F6, the launcher's pins, history) is unchanged. The launcher scans layouts\ without recursing, so library entries never take part in the launch-time pins. A downloaded layout built against a newer pack line cannot block a launch. An entry whose packs are missing or on another line is refused when it is loaded, by the same caret check, with "restart through the launcher".

Action What happens Save (F5) as today; if FRB.active names an entry, the entry is updated too Save as F5, then the active pair is copied into a new entry; the id comes from the title plus a number, and the title can be changed later without moving files Use the active pair goes to history, the entry's pair becomes active, FRB.active names it; in a FORGE game the objects are replaced as F6 does Original (F2) as today; FRB.active is cleared Rename, delete layout.json only, or the entry's folder The DLL does the file work, because layout_files.h already commits two files safely and never overwrites. Its exports take no arguments, so the menu writes a request (layouts\request.txt: an operation, map code, entry id and title, one per line) and calls a new library export. The DLL answers in layouts\library.txt: one line per entry, with id, title, objects, packs and when it was saved. Library requests run from pump rather than the sandbox tick, so the lobby can use them outside a FORGE game. Use, F5 and F6 still need the sandbox.
Phase 1: named layouts › The lobby choice

The map select shows Layout: Original and the map's library entries when the chosen map has any. START GAME makes the choice active before startGame writes pending_variant.txt, so the existing match-start path does the rest. The lobby broadcast gains a seventh field, the layout's title. Older clients read six fields by position and ignore it. The vote after a match keeps each option's layout.
Phase 2: the hub and the launcher › Archive

mjolnir.json type "layout", a layout block, deps layout/layout.mvar layout/layout.mvar.packs layout/preview.png (or .jpg / .webp, at most 1 MiB) docs/README.md optional signature.json mjolnir.json: { "schema_version": 1, "type": "layout", "name": "Crossline Towers", "version": "1.0.0", "summary": "Two towers over the vehicle lane.", "layout": { "map": "FRB", "objects": 312 }, "deps": [ { "slug": "crossline", "range": "^0.3.0" }, { "slug": "foundry-wide", "range": "^0.2.0" } ] } The base map is the dependency whose map listing has the code in layout.map. Every pack in the sidecar must be a dependency at the caret line it names.
Phase 2: the hub and the launcher › Hub

Change Where Manifest type gains "layout"; the layout block is required for it alone (manifest.ts 28, 74) Scanner for a layout only: allow the four layout/ files and skip the container rule (scan.ts 39, 344, 424); run the validator; compare the manifest's map and object count with the file's; check the sidecar against deps; cap the archive at 2 MiB Validator blam-megalo built to .wasm, imported by scan.ts Complete category forced to layouts; deps into release_deps; a layout_listings row (publish.ts 693-738) Schema migration 0025_forge_layouts.sql, additive: layout_listings (mod_id PK, map_code, base_slug, title, objects, packs JSON, updated_at) and an index on map_code. Apply it before the merge API GET /maps/{code}/layouts and GET /layouts?map=&sort=, for the website, the launcher and the game Website a Layouts section on a map's page (hub/src/app/mods/[slug]/page.tsx), Community layouts on /forge, and layouts in /mods/new's categories. The manage page's single PUT already fits Review hold: a decision for the owner. A layout carries bytes that the engine decodes, which is a map's risk rather than a texture's.
Phase 2: the hub and the launcher › Hub

Hold new authors (as maps do: trust level below 2 waits for a moderator). Safe whatever the validator misses. Moderators would see the scanner's summary. The catch: trust_level has no writer in the hub today, so every new author waits on a person. Publish on a pass (as content does). Faster for players. It rests entirely on the validator: the full decode, the caps and the re-encode. Reports and yanking stay available. The validator design favours publishing on a pass. Holding new authors for the first releases is the cautious start.
Phase 2: the hub and the launcher › Launcher

install_one_as (hub.rs 1085) learns the manifest type layout. A layout's hub mod is a content mod, so the trust-tier check (1112) already passes. For a layout it skips the container rule (1320) and runs the same validator natively before writing anything. It writes library\<CODE>\hub-<slug>\ with layout.json naming the release, and installs the map and packs through the usual deps. Uninstalling removes the entry. If that entry is active, the active pair stays and FRB.active is cleared, so a match is never left without its layout. Library entries get a best-effort pin pass. Their packs are installed when they don't conflict with the active layouts. A conflict is noted on the Updates screen rather than failing the launch. --install-layout <slug> [--release <id>] --progress <file>, gated by layouts in launcher_features.txt, as --install-map is. Nothing needs mounting. A pack the game has not loaded still needs a restart, which the menu says. mjolnir://layout/<slug> opens the layout's page in Browse Hub, as mod/ and map/ links do (links.rs 79).

WBP_MJOLNIRForgeLayouts is a cooked widget in the Forge UI container (pakchunk980-MJOLNIRFORGEUI, build_forge_hud in unreal/MJOLNIRMaterials/Scripts/build_mjolnir_ui.py), so it ships in a CE runtime release. Opening it: in a FORGE game, from a FORGE LAYOUTS item in the pause menu (the HOST MENU pattern, MJOLNIRLobby/Scripts/main.lua 3969) and from a key still to be chosen. F7-F9 belong to MJOLNIRFlyCam. The list: this map's entries in ten authored rows that slide over the list, the palette's pattern. Each row shows title, objects, packs and date, and the active one is marked. Buttons: Load, Save as, Rename, Delete, Use for matches, Publish, Get more. Names: an EditableTextBox, focused the way chat focuses its input (MJOLNIRHud/Scripts/chat.lua 433). Forge ignores its own keys while it has focus (typingInChat). Get more: lists the hub's layouts for the map (GET /maps/{code}/layouts through Games.call) with their covers (the existing FILE download into _covers), and installs through --install-layout.

The game can't publish on its own. It holds no key that can write, and the lobby DLL sends only JSON. Publish in the menu writes layouts\publish_request.json (map, entry) and starts the launcher through the lobby DLL's existing launcher action, with --publish-layout <CODE>/<id>, window shown. The launcher shows a publish form: title, summary, version (the next patch for an update), the preview, and what the layout depends on. Nothing is sent until the player confirms. It builds the archive and signs it with a launcher signing key. That key is DPAPI-protected Ed25519, as the tag editor's keystore.rs, and registered once through POST /account/signing-keys. Then it uploads with the existing four calls. A new scope, layouts:write, offered when the launcher pairs and shown on the device approval page. requireScoped accepts it only for a mod whose category is layouts, and /complete refuses anything but a layout manifest for a key that has only this scope. Giving the launcher mods:write instead would let every paired launcher publish any mod. Two existing gaps this depends on:

POST /account/signing-keys only authenticates (account.ts 224), despite its comment. It should require mods:write or layouts:write. Nothing checks that a joiner has the packs the host's layout uses. The lobby broadcast should carry the active layout's pins, and a client missing a pack should be told before the match, as for a missing map. The tag editor can already publish with mods:write. A Publish layout button there is the quickest working path, and it belongs with the editor's Forge mode.

Status: design, 2026-11-03. Nothing here is built unless a line says so. It builds on forge_layout_sharing.md: the layout library, the validator and the publishing flow. Forge in the game is one player with a cursor. The tag editor can show the whole map at once. Forge mode lets a builder place, move, turn and delete a layout's objects in the editor's 3D view, with real meshes and grid snapping. While the game runs a FORGE game on the same map, each edit appears in the game on the next tick, and objects moved in the game move in the editor. With the two windows side by side, the editor is the floor plan and the game is the walk-through.

The parts › 1. A layout model in blam-megalo

A layout module over the existing tree: pub struct Layout { pub header: Header, pub bounds: Bounds, pub objects: Vec, /* the rest kept as tree */ } pub struct Placement { pub entry: u16, // 0..651, stable across edits pub palette: u8, // flat index across map variant palettes pub variant: Option, pub position: [f32; 3], // world units pub yaw: f32, // radians pub up: Option, // packed, carried as read (see below) pub flags: u8, pub properties: Properties, // physics, team, spawn order, label... carried exactly } impl Layout { fn decode(mvar: &[u8]) -> Result; fn encode(&self) -> Result>; }
The parts › 1. A layout model in blam-megalo

Positions: decode with the widths position_widths already computes, lo + span / 2^bits × (raw + 0.5). Encoding is the inverse, rounded, so a position moves by at most half a step. That is under a millimetre on a Forge map, as in the game. Turning: yaw is 14 bits (radians = raw × 0.000383495 − 3.141401). The 20-bit up vector (0x3f57d0) is not modelled, so an edited object keeps its up as read. The game turns about the vertical only, so nothing is lost. File writer: the envelope the DLL writes (_blf 1.2, mvar 31.1 with a zero hash, fpk1, _eof). The sidecar writer uses the launcher's format. Every save passes the validator in the layout sharing design, so the editor can never write a file the game refuses. Tests: decode → encode is byte-identical on every MJOLNIR save and every MCC map variant. Moving one object changes only that entry. The DLL's own reader (test_layout_bounds.c) accepts what the writer produces.

Open a map by code. The editor reads the installed maps the way the game does (ue4ss\MJOLNIRMaps\maps.json, then the loader's maps.json). It finds the map's scenario in the catalog and shows its world as the World view does. MJOLNIR's own Forge maps also have floors that MJOLNIRLevelLoader spawns at runtime from map/level.json (decor: Crossline's slab, Forge Canvas's deck). Forge mode draws those as plain shapes, so the map isn't floating in space. Palette. The scenario's map variant palettes block, read in geometry.rs, gives each flat index a tag. Pack pieces are named from MJOLNIRForgePacks\installed.json and grouped by pack and category, as in the game's palette. Each piece's mesh comes from loadRenderGroup. If a pack mesh doesn't resolve, its catalog box (dimensions_m) stands in, so a missing mesh never hides a piece. Open a layout. Choose a library entry, the active layout, or the map's own. Objects are drawn at their decoded transforms and selected by click or from a list, with a box select. Edit. Move with the gizmo, on a grid of 0.25 to 4 m (the game's steps), and turn by the game's angle steps. Duplicate, delete, and place from the palette. Physics mode, team, spawn order and label use the same values as the game's property keys. Undo goes through the editor's existing journal. Budgets.

The palette shows placed and maximum counts and the price, as the game's HUD does, and refuses a placement over the maximum. Save. Saving goes to a library entry (Save, or Save as), never straight over the active layout. In the game, Use or F6 puts it on the map.

Reading needs no game change. While the game runs a FORGE game on the same map: The editor reads the live entry table about ten times a second, through blam-live as mapvar_probe does. It moves its copies of anything that changed, so an object the player carries in the game moves in the editor. It marks the object the player is holding (forge_state.txt names it) and locks it against editing while it's held. Writing needs the game thread. Writing the entry table from outside would not move the objects, because the engine moves them through object_set_pose and its dirty marks. It would also race the simulation. So the Forge DLL gains a small command server:

Piece Design Transport a named pipe, \\.\pipe\mjolnir-forge-<pid>, created by the DLL with an ACL for the current user only. One client at a time Operations snapshot (entries with palette, transform, flags, and a generation number); move <entry> <pos> <yaw>; place <palette> <pos> <yaw>; delete <entry>; highlight <entry> Execution a reader thread queues operations, and the sandbox tick runs them (the slot 113 hook, as Lua's commands do), at most a few per tick Reuse place uses place_entry. move uses the pose sequence of finish_grid_drop: 0x5ec880 pre-move, 0x59f600 set pose, 0x59f470 modified, the entry's position, forward and up, then mv_entry_dirty(entry, 2). delete is engine request 1 Answers each operation replies with the entry's pose as the engine left it. Fixed and Phased objects take the pose exactly, while Normal physics may settle Guards host only, FORGE games only, refused on a fireteam client. An operation names the layout generation it was made against, and the DLL bumps the generation when a layout is replaced (F6, F2, Use), so stale edits are refused. Nothing runs while the player holds that object Why not MJOLNIRBridge: players don't have it enabled, and it runs any Lua it's sent. A pipe with five typed operations, local to the user, is much narrower.

Conflicts. The last writer wins for each entry. The editor shows the game's version whenever its snapshot disagrees with an edit that hasn't been answered yet. Camera. "Follow the game" moves the editor's camera to the player's view (the player unit's position and aim, read through blam-live). It's optional and comes later.

The editor already pairs with mods:write and signs releases (src-tauri/src/hub.rs, keystore.rs). Publish layout builds the archive described in the layout sharing design from a library entry. That makes the editor the first working path for publishing.

Is a named pipe from the Forge DLL acceptable as the live channel, or should it be files beside forge_state.txt, as the Forge HUD's are? Should Forge mode be a mode of the existing World view, or a separate Forge tab that starts from a map code?

The interchange format of the level authoring pipeline: what the Blender exporter writes, what mjolnir level bake turns into a scenario override, and what the MJOLNIRLevelLoader UE4SS mod reads at runtime. One file describes one custom level. A level is baked one of two ways. Every published map is a standalone scenario with its own BSP and world (map_distribution.md). The older lane, still used for authoring and tests, is the map variant: a shipped campaign scenario's world and BSP stay as the canvas, and the level is everything placed on top. That split exists because the Blam simulation collides only with its own world — BSP plus Blam objects — and ignores Unreal geometry entirely (verified 2026-08-19, multiplayer_investigation_notes.md). The format therefore carries two kinds of content: Lane Section Spawned by Solid? Blam objects blam.* the sim, from the baked scnr override yes — pawns, vehicles, projectiles all collide Unreal decor decor MJOLNIRLevelLoader at runtime no — visuals only Anything the player must stand on, drive over, hide behind, or shoot goes in blam.*. Anything that only needs to look right can go in decor.

A standalone bake (mjolnir level bake --standalone CODE) ships the result as a new launchable scenario instead of an override of the canvas, and can give it a structure BSP (--bsp) and an Unreal world (--world) of its own; the converted CE maps are built that way (ce_map_conversion.md).

The file stores UE-native values: centimeters, Unreal's left-handed Z-up axes, rotations in degrees as [pitch, yaw, roll]. The Lua loader consumes them conversion-free; the two converters live at the edges: Edge Conversion Blender → file (exporter) meters → cm (×100); negate Y; Blender Z-up right-handed → UE Z-up left-handed file → Blam (level bake) cm → world units (÷304.8); negate Y; rotation mapping is verified against live spawns during bake development Worked example: a Blender object at (2.0 m, 3.0 m, 0.5 m) exports as [200, -300, 50] UE cm. Baked to Blam (with origin [0,0,0]): (0.656, 0.984, 0.164) wu — the double Y-negation means Blam Y equals Blender Y. Sign bugs live here; when in doubt, spawn something and read the engine position back (the proven check: a weapon placed at Blam (8.0, 47.0, 65.5) appears at engine (800, -4700, 6551) relative cm — see tag_data_pipeline.md). All positions in the file are relative to canvas.origin (a UE-space point on the canvas map). Author around your own origin in Blender; move the whole level by editing one value.

{ "schema_version": 1, "name": "proving_ground", // slug: [a-z0-9_]+, used in filenames "title": "Proving Ground", // display name "canvas": { "scenario": "B40", // one of the 13 shipped scenario names "origin": [76200, -30480, 1800] // UE cm, absolute; all positions below are relative to it }, "environment": { // spawned by the loader; the bake ignores it "sun": { "pitch": -50, "yaw": 30, "intensity": 8.0 }, "skylight": { "intensity": 3.0 }, "atmosphere": true }, "blam": { // consumed by mjolnir level bake, ignored by the Lua loader "clear": { // neutralize the host mission "squads": true, // zero AI squads "bipeds": true, // remove placed bipeds "weapons": true, // remove the mission's own weapon placements "vehicles": true, // remove the mission's own vehicle placements "equipment": true, // remove the mission's own equipment placements "scripts": true // stub the mission's HSC scripts }, "player_representations": [ { "third person unit": "bipd:..." } ], // this map's players: every row, as --set values "player_starts": [ // >= 2 for co-op { "pos": [0, 0, 0], "yaw": 0 }, { "pos": [4000, 0, 0], "yaw": 180 } ], "vehicles": [ { "type": "warthog", "pos": [800, 600, 0], "yaw": 90 } ], "weapons": [ { "type": "assault_rifle", "pos": [200, 0, 50], "yaw": 0 } ], "equipment": [ // pickups: grenades, powerups, ammo { "type": "active_camouflage", "pos": [2000, 0, 0] } ], "objects": [

// the structures lane — these are SOLID { "tag": "objects\props\covenant\cov_portable_shield\cov_portable_shield", "group": "scenery", "pos": [1000, 0, 0], "rot": [0, 45, 0] } ] }, "decor": [ // consumed by MJOLNIRLevelLoader, ignored by bake — NOT solid { "id": "banner_l", "mesh": "/Engine/BasicShapes/Cube.Cube", "pos": [0, -2000, 300], "rot": [0, 0, 0], "scale": [0.2, 6, 4], "tint": [0.8, 0.2, 0.2, 1.0], "materials": ["", "/Game/.../MI_Ground.MI_Ground"] } // slot 0, slot 1, ... ], "markers": [ // named points; ce_objectives.py turns some into objectives { "name": "flag_red", "pos": [0, 0, 0] } ] } defs/level/level.schema.json is a JSON Schema for the format, but it has fallen behind the keys below and nothing in the repository reads it. mjolnir level validate <file> checks a file the way the bake reads it (LevelFile in crates/blam-cli/src/level.rs): no unknown keys, one of the 13 canvas scenarios, a slug name, known palette types, and scenery, crates, machines or controls objects. The keys a remastered map adds for the loader alone are unknown to it (see Keys a converted map adds).

scenario must be one of the 13 launchable names (A15 A30 A50 B30 B40 C10 C20 C45 D20 D40 E10 E20 E30) — the canvas has to be a shipped scenario; a new launchable name comes from a standalone bake, which registers its codename (pakchunk996-MJOLNIRREG_P). The default canvas for the pipeline is B40 (fullest vehicle palette, large flat canyon floors). origin should sit on walkable BSP: the level's playable area must lie on the canvas map's Blam collision, because that is the only floor the sim knows.

Sun, skylight and atmosphere, spawned by MJOLNIRLevelLoader when the world arrives. It exists because blam.clear is now the default for an exported level: once the host mission's own placements are gone, so is anything that was lighting them, and an unlit canvas reads as a black void rather than a level. All three keys are optional and each falls back to the shown default. sun becomes a DirectionalLight, skylight a real-time-capture SkyLight, and atmosphere: false suppresses the SkyAtmosphere. The bake never reads this section, so lighting changes are a mjolnir_level_reload away — no re-bake, no restart. A converted CE map also carries post (a fixed exposure, docs/re/fork_renderer.md) and may carry light_scale (default 256). With a fixed exposure, the loader multiplies the sun and skylight by the scale and lowers the exposure by log2 of it. The CE materials divide the exposure back out, so the level looks the same, while the game's own physical lights (headlights, muzzle flashes, effects) come down to their designed strength next to it. At scale 1 a Warthog headlight was 160 times the sun and turned whatever it reached white. mjolnir_light_scale <k> tries a value live; default hands it back to the file.

post.max_traced_roughness caps which surfaces get ray-traced Lumen reflections: anything rougher reflects from Lumen's radiance cache instead. Use it only where the surfaces are actually rough. The cache is too coarse for near-mirror metal: on the Forge pieces' first material, the game's layered +MIP_FR_Gen_Metal at roughness 0.15, a cap of 0.1 turned the metal blotchy. With the UNSC painted and rough metal the packs use now, the Forge maps' 0.1 looks the same as tracing and took a floor-heavy 4K view on Crossline from 7.61 to 5.86 ms of GPU time (RTX 5090, 2026-11-02). Turning Lumen reflections off instead leaves metal black. post.sky_leak (0 to about 0.3) lets that fraction of the sky light into enclosed spaces (Lumen's skylight leaking). Lit by Lumen alone, Zanzibar's rooms (lumen_cells) took their light from the sunlit sand and walls outside and went yellow; 0.2 brings back neutral concrete and keeps the stairwells' shade. Two more keys come from a CE map's sky and BSP:

sky_fog: { color, start, density, height }. A CE sky with no model, such as Coldsnap's, draws as its outdoor fog colour. The loader spawns an ExponentialHeightFog that starts at start (cm, CE's opaque distance), so everything farther away turns color, the empty sky included. color is linear and is raised by the light scale like a light. density defaults to 0.5. height (default 400,000 cm) is how far above the canvas origin the fog sits. weather: { system, copies, params, follow }. A Niagara system the game ships, copies of it (1 to 16), each given params (user parameters by name, floats). The PNW snow fills a box around its component, not around the view, so the copies are spawned in the world at the camera and follow it (checked ten times a second, moved once the camera has gone half a metre) unless follow is false. Attaching them to the camera draws nothing, because the camera manager is a hidden actor. roofs ({ cell, reach, cells }, written by gen_ce_level.py) lists the ceilings over the level by cell; while one is within reach above the camera the copies are hidden, as CE's weather polygons kept snow out from under Coldsnap's roofs. MJOLNIRWorldBuilder stands down for any world that has a level file, so its auto-built sun and floor pad cannot land on top of an authored environment.
Section notes › blam.vehicles / blam.weapons / blam.equipment — type values

Friendly names resolve through defs/level/palette-map.json to tag paths. A type the canvas palette lacks gets a palette entry of its own, cloned from entry 0 and re-pointed (B40 has no shotgun or fuel rod, for example); the canvas needs at least one placement and one palette entry of that kind to clone from. The palette map records what each of the 13 canvases already carries (B40: warthog, ghost, scorpion, banshee, wraith, shade, pelican). The added object's assets may still not be streamed for that map; treat cross-map placements as experimental. A placement can also name a tag of its own with tag, a path built with mjolnir new-tag; type then only labels it. The tag's container must be installed beside the map. A clone of the Warthog placed this way loads, boards and drives, also when bound to a cloned Blueprint.
Section notes › blam.objects — the structures lane

Each entry becomes a scenery, crates or machines placement in the scnr (palette entry appended as needed, element cloned from a donor and re-pointed). Object tags bring their own collision and render models, so this is how ramps, walls, bases, and cover are built. Block capacity is generous (scenery 2000, crates 1536, palettes 256 each). A machine is cut loose from the donor's device groups (power and position group none), so it runs on its own: a gear turns from the map's start. Controls need device-group wiring and are not supported. Tag paths must exist in the shipped tag set (mjolnir list --paks ... --group scenery, or --group crate for crates) or in a container installed beside the map (Halo 2's machines, tools/level/h2_machines.py).

The host mission keeps running under the variant — its AI, objectives, and scripting are noise for an arena level. The bake runs its placement passes first and the clears afterwards, so each clone still has a shipped donor to copy from; the clear then keeps only the elements this bake appended (Op::KeepLast) and drops the mission's prefix. clear empties the relevant placement blocks (counts set to zero or elements disabled; equipment covers the mission's equipment placements, and blocks names any other root block to empty, e.g. ["machines", "scenario kill triggers"]) and scripts: true swaps the scenario's HSC source for one startup script (mechanism proven — script sections already resize through blam-tag::write::Edits). Expect per-mission iteration on how much clearing a mission tolerates before something native asserts.

That startup script is not optional dressing. A Blam map boots faded to black with the HUD hidden and every player input faded out; the mission's own script hands them back, and this engine's missions do it through f_insertion_fade_to_gameplay (decompile any shipped scenario with mjolnir script --tag B40 --decompile): wait for (game_all_players_active), then (player_control_fade_in_all_input 1.0), (chud_cinematic_fade 1.0 30), (fade_in 0 0 0 30) and (unit_raise_weapon player0 30). A stub that only fades the screen in and calls player_enable_input leaves the player able to look around but not move, shoot or switch weapons — a cutscene lock with no cutscene. The stub the bake writes does the full handoff. Until 2026-11-02 that stub never actually loaded, in any bake: the bake dropped the script source (since the first stub), and from 2026-09-10 the stub also carried an unregistered string id. Either one makes the engine load the scenario with no scripts at all (re/ce_map_scripts.md). The bake now keeps the source and refuses any string_id literal missing from defs/hce/string-ids.json.
Section notes › Names, volumes and flags for a script

blam.object_names lists names a script can use; a placement claims one with name. A name no placement claims stays in the block, and the engine drops any script that uses it. placed: false leaves a placement for object_create. blam.trigger_volumes are box volumes (name, pos their corner, forward, up, extents in wu). blam.cutscene_flags are pos, yaw, optional pitch and name, and go past the canvas's count by cloning. blam.device_groups are name, initial_value, flags, for a placement's power_group and position_group; a device with neither gets private groups, which is all a script watching a control needs. objects[].group takes controls. Machines and controls stay out of the map variant's palettes: a tag listed there is not created from its placement. tools/level/add_devices.py writes all of this for a converted CE map (re/ce_map_scripts.md), and the runtime level's devices list, which MJOLNIRLevelLoader/Scripts/devices.lua rides the map's meshes on.
Section notes › blam.script — the level's own scripts

"script": "my_level.hsc" (a path relative to the level file) is compiled into the scenario beside the startup stub, so it needs clear.scripts. Object, device-group, trigger-volume and flag names resolve against the scenario as the bake leaves it, so don't clear the blocks the script names (for example, keep machines, controls and object names for a script that drives doors). Startup, dormant and continuous scripts all run in a multiplayer match. Script names need not be registered string ids, but string_id arguments must be. Names compile to block indices when the clears run, before map_variant, single_bsp, bots and set. A later pass that adds or removes elements of object names, trigger volumes, cutscene flags or device groups would silently point the script at the wrong element. None does today. Keep it that way, or move the compile after them. examples/levels/device_test/ is a worked example: a switch that opens a door, on B40's elevator room.
Section notes › blam.world_bounds, blam.set, blam.active_bsps, blam.single_bsp, blam.map_variant, blam.forge, blam.cutscene_flags

world_bounds: [{ "bsp": 8, "min": [x, y, z], "max": [x, y, z] }], Halo wu. Sets a structure BSP's box in the scenario; the boxes decide which BSP a point belongs to, and a point outside every box is outside the world. set: { "field path": "value" } for any other scenario field, in the form the inspector prints ("type": "multiplayer"). Applied last. active_bsps: [8] makes the starting zone set (zone set 0) load only these BSPs, and trims its PVS to match. A map on its own BSP needs this: every other canvas BSP left active claims its own space. Each kept BSP's PVS clusters keep their bit vectors and seam cluster references for the kept BSPs only. single_bsp: 8 (the BSP active_bsps lists) makes that BSP the scenario's only one, at index 0. The bake applies it after --bsp, so --bsp and world_bounds still name the canvas index. The per-BSP tables keep its element; only zone set 0 and its PVS and audibility entries stay; the designs, soft ceilings, seams, other insertion points and their player starts go; and every placement's origin BSP becomes 0. The BSP tag must be built for index 0 (level collision --own-bsp --bsp-index 0).
Section notes › blam.world_bounds, blam.set, blam.active_bsps, blam.single_bsp, blam.map_variant, blam.forge, blam.cutscene_flags

map_variant: true adds the map variant palettes: one per category (weapons, vehicles, equipment, scenery), listing every tag the level places and every kind defs/level/palette-map.json knows (not the pelican, space banshee, seraph or battle rifle, unless the level places one), with no quota. Under a multiplayer (Megalo) engine, objects whose tags carry multiplayer data exist only through the map variant, which the simulation builds from the palette-listed placements; in Forge the palettes are what the Monitor places from (forge.md). forge: Forge's limits, with map_variant. { "budget": 500, "price": { "scorpion": 150 }, "maximum": { "scorpion": 2 } }. budget is the scenario's sandbox budget; price (price per instance, counted against the budget) and maximum (maximum allowed, 0 for no quota) are per palette-map kind, or tag path for scenery. Each value replaces the default in defs/level/palette-map.json's forge section, which sets none. The simulation enforces them when placing; with no budget, only free objects can be placed, so set a budget whenever you set prices. cutscene_flags: [{ "pos": [x, y, z], "yaw": 0 }] moves the canvas's first cutscene flags to these points, so their names stay valid for player_teleport / object_teleport from the Blam console.
Section notes › blam.world_bounds, blam.set, blam.active_bsps, blam.single_bsp, blam.map_variant, blam.forge, blam.cutscene_flags
A blam.objects, vehicles, weapons or equipment element also takes set: fields of the placement, relative to its element ("multiplayer data.owner team": "neutral").

Both add palette entries without placing objects in the starting layout and require blam.map_variant: true and level bake --standalone. The baker also adds their tag packages to the scenario's cooked preloads. Missing references fail the bake; their runtime/pack containers must be in its input Paks view. forge_packs declares exact community pack versions and an ordered subset of their block IDs/tags. The map packer keeps these declarations and emits exact Hub dependencies. See the Forge pack contract for the complete shape. There are at most 63 packs and 200 custom references. forge_objects lists up to 64 existing runtime tags, for example: "forge_objects": [ { "group": "scenery", "tag": "objects\multi\spawning\player_spawn" }, { "group": "scenery", "tag": "objects\multi\teleporters\teleporter_sender" }, { "group": "scenery", "tag": "objects\multi\teleporters\teleporter_receiver" }, { "group": "scenery", "tag": "objects\multi\teleporters\teleporter_2way" } ]

Groups are scenery or crates; tag path segments contain lowercase letters, digits, underscores or hyphens. Duplicate group/tag pairs are rejected. Paths under objects\mjolnir\forge\ must use forge_packs so a model cannot lose its versioned dependency. Preplaced objects that also appear in either list retain the declared palette order instead of gaining a second scenery entry. The combined palette, including standard weapons/vehicles/equipment, must fit the engine's 255-entry limit.

Top-level "kill_floor": -600 kills players below absolute Unreal Z −600 cm. The value must be finite. This is a runtime host check in MJOLNIRLevelLoader; the bake does not create a collision plane or kill volume. The original level JSON is retained in the map archive, so the value reaches the loader. Omit it or use null to leave the loader's per-map default in effect.

"bots": { "squad": "insertion_cov_elites", // the canvas squad each bot is cloned from "count": 15, // squads bot_0 .. bot_14 (default: one per spawn) "spawns": [{ "pos": [x, y, z], "yaw": 0 }], // default: player_starts; those on the // main ground, cycled farthest first "weapon": "plasma_rifle", // a weapon palette entry's path, by substring "spacing": 2.5, // firing position grid, wu (widened to fit 2048, // narrowed to 1 wu for 8 per area) "areas": 16, // the firing positions' grid of areas "types": [ // kinds of bot, count squads each: _ { "name": "spartan", "character": "objects\characters\spartans\ai\mjolnir_bot_spartan", "weapon": "assault_rifle", "team": "covenant" }, { "name": "elite", "character": "elite\ai\elite", "weapon": "plasma_rifle" } ] } A type's character is a substring of a character palette entry, or a full character tag path, which the bake adds to the palette; weapon falls back to bots.weapon, weapons (a list) hands its entries out in turn across the kind's squads, and team sets the squads' team. Without types there is one kind, bot_<k>, from the donor squad.

The bake clones, before the clears (which keep them): one single-actor squad per bot, one zone (mjolnir_bots) whose firing positions cover the walkable ground the spawns stand on (a spacing grid, finer down to 1 wu where narrow ground leaves fewer than eight per area), one objective (mjolnir_bots: task hunt over every area, then area_0 .. area_15 sharing the areas out, all with magic player sight; MJOLNIRHud orders bots to those sixteen whatever the map has), and one ai user hint data element with every hint list emptied: the AI reads element 0 without checking the block has one, and a map that cleared it crashed. After single_bsp it writes the kept BSP's ai pathfinding data, generated from the --bsp payload's collision shell (blam_sbsp::pathfinding), and clears that BSP's no default structure pathfinding flag. So bots needs the level's BSP named by single_bsp (or active_bsps) and given with --bsp.

Beside its output the bake writes <CODE>.bots.json (--install-test: in the loader's levels/, beside the level file): {"schema_version": 1, "starts": [[x, y, z], ...], "areas": [[x0, y0, x1, y1], ...], "tasks": [[area, ...], ...]}, in absolute Unreal cm: where squad k of every kind stands, each zone area's extent (the grid cell its firing positions came from), and the areas each task area_<k> covers. mjolnir map pack ships it as map/bots.json. MJOLNIRHud picks each bot's squad from starts as the bot comes in, and from areas and tasks sends a bot that stays put somewhere else and places it again if it does not go (bots.md "Bots frozen in place").
Top-level "multiplayer": true asks MJOLNIRLevelLoader to start the level under the simulation's Megalo engine rather than the campaign (re/megalo_engine.md). The bake ignores it.
Section notes › Keys a converted map adds

A converted CE map's level file carries more. All but modes are read by MJOLNIRLevelLoader, and the loader's comments beside each are the reference. Accepted by level bake and passed over: variant (the Megalo game type the map starts with), modes (the game types the multiplayer menu offers, listed in the maps.json an install writes), vehicle_sets (CE's vehicle sets, from which the loader picks the labels a game type requires), spawn_sets (the hidden spawn points' labels, spawn_set_<k>, each with the families it serves: [{"label": "spawn_set_0", "families": ["king", "oddball", "slayer"]}]; the loader adds a filter for each set the game type's family is in, see ce_map_conversion.md, "Spawn sets"), ctf (Capture the Flag's look: the flag mesh, its materials, the stands), health_pack (the CE health pack's look), koth_hills (King's hills in rotation order, for the HUD's hill line: x, y, z and radius in cm, from tools/level/ce_objectives.py), race_flags (Race's checkpoints by rank, in the same form) and foliage (the game's grass, tufts and stones, from a file beside the level). Also game (halo1 or halo2: the map select's game filter), warfare ({protocol, layout_revision}, Pelican Warfare's layout contract), lifts, doors and gears (Halo 2's lifts, part-moving machines and turning parts, from gen_ce_level.py), author and description.
Section notes › Keys a converted map adds

Written by tools/level/upgrade_ce_map.py for a remastered map, and unknown to level validate and level bake: landscape (an Unreal Landscape for the ground), flux (Fluid Flux over rivers and the sea), decals (the game's decal materials), lights (CE's placed lights as shadowed point lights), effects (the game's Niagara ambient life), slot_meshes (translucent terrain slots as meshes of their own), shadow_shell, lumen_cells (the terrain as a grid of editor-built meshes Lumen can light, drawn in its place: { item, cells: [{ mesh, slots }] }; the structures' fill goes to zero) and waterfalls. Under environment, beside the keys above: haze (Unreal's height fog as distance haze), clouds (volumetric clouds), water (CE water drawn as rolling, reflecting water), sun_mask (a cooked mask of where the sun reaches the terrain), sounds (CE's or Halo 2's background sound and sound scenery; an entry's optional pitch is a playback rate multiplier) and fade_in (false opts out of the fade-in the loader asks the Blam console for).

mesh is a full UE object path: /Engine/BasicShapes/*, any shipped SM_ package (catalog via mjolnir mesh list), or one of our own packages under /Game/MJOLNIR/. The loader spawns StaticMeshActors with Mobility=Movable (the SetStaticMesh-refuses-when-Static edge is handled) and applies tint through a dynamic material instance when the base material exposes a color parameter (BasicShapeMaterial does; WorldGridMaterial does not). Decor never blocks anything — do not fake floors or walls with it. materials assigns a material per slot, in order, an empty entry leaving a slot alone. An entry is a material path (a shipped instance, or one of our own cooked materials) or a runtime material, { "parent", "textures", "scalars", "vectors", "linear" }, which the loader makes into a dynamic instance of parent. They go on the component, not the mesh: a mesh whose geometry was written into a donor package (see ue_mesh_write.md) still reports the donor's single slot however many the package declares, while SetMaterial grows the component's override list to as many sections as the render data names. That is what makes a transplanted mesh come out textured rather than default grey — Blood Gulch's terrain is one decor entry with three. mesh_rewrite --material prints the list to paste here.

A converted map's decor also uses cast_shadow (false on level geometry whose shadows are baked), sort_priority (translucent sort order, for the sky), pulse (one runtime-material scalar driven by a CE periodic function), scalars (values on the mesh's own materials), static (no world-position offset), capture_only (seen by the Fluid Flux ground capture, then hidden) and motion (a Halo 2 gear that turns: pivot_cm from the actor, period in seconds, keys as [seconds, yaw degrees], linear between them; with axis, a unit vector, the keys are degrees about it instead of yaw; events, {t, wave, gain, inner, falloff}, are one-shots played at the pivot as the turn passes t; follow, {class, pos}, names a machine of the simulation's own (its Unreal Blueprint class and position, from the canvas origin) whose collision turns with the part: the loader attaches the mesh to that actor's turning part once it finds it, and fits the turn's phase, for the sounds, to what the part does; meshes with the same entry (a part's opaque and translucent ones) share that actor, and each other part claims its own; until then, and without follow, the loader turns the actor about the pivot on the world's clock); see the loader's spawnDecorItem.

Named points the bake does not place. An authored level names them, following the MapKit convention (flag_red, hill_1, ...); a converted CE map lists its netgame flags as { "type", "team", "pos", "yaw" } (ctf_flag, hill, oddball, ..., from defs/level/ce-tag-map.json). tools/level/ce_objectives.py turns hill, oddball and race_track markers into labelled objects (koth_hill, oddball_spawn, race_flag) and the map's koth, oddball and race modes; the bake and the game read nothing else from them. A CE hill keeps CE's first 12 flags in marker order, which is tag order, and a one-flag hill is CE's 2 by 2 wu square. A Halo 2 hill keeps every corner. Race flags take spawn order 0 to n-1 from their sorted team index, and share one radius: 6 m, less where two flags in a row, the closing leg included, are closer than two radii, and never under 2.5 m. modes lists engines only: slayer, ctf, koth, oddball, race. The lobby derives the rest (Team Slayer, Crazy King, Rally and so on), which keeps a hub manifest within its 8. tools/level/add_objectives.py does this for a published map: it rebakes the pack's scenario and writes the next release.

A rebake does not always give back a shipped scenario byte for byte, even with the level unchanged. Until 2026-11-08 the bots' pathfinding seams came out of a hash map (blam-sbsp pathfinding.rs, the crack search), so seams that tied on score were numbered, and could be chosen, differently from run to run: of 28 maps rebaked on 2026-11-07, 16 came back exact. Ties now go by segment index, so a bake gives the same bytes every run (Damnation and Chill Out, each baked twice). A map without tied seams bakes as before; one baked before with ties keeps its shipped numbering until it is rebaked, which then numbers its seams the new way. A map baked before a bake change also picks that change up (Crossline's equipment palette, which saved Forge layouts index). For an edit to a few fields, tools/level/fix_teleporter_teams.py shows the other way: set the fields in the shipped scenario with mjolnir tag-file, rebuild the map container around it with ue-iostore's replace_chunk example (the writer level bake uses; unchanged, it rebuilds a container byte for byte), and check with mjolnir tagdiff that only those fields moved.

Status: 2026-10-21. The 19 stock maps and the Custom Edition maps Yoyorast Island and Coldsnap convert with the one command below. A converted map is hosted from the main menu's MULTIPLAYER entry (MJOLNIRLobby, "Playing it"), and kills score and are recorded (two PCs, 2026-10-03). Update 2026-11-21: the same script also converts MCC's Halo 2 maps, staged by mjolnir cache stage instead of halo2ue (h2_map_conversion.md). tools/level/upgrade_ce_map.py takes a converted map further ("Upgraded maps"). First verified in game on 2026-09-30, on Blood Gulch and Sidewinder, started from the menu with nothing done by hand: own collision at CE coordinates, terrain mesh, spawns, vehicles and weapons, the Megalo engine and the Slayer script. A classic Halo CE .map becomes a standalone multiplayer mission in Halo: Campaign Evolved: its own scenario, its own collision, its players, vehicles and weapons placed where CE put them, running under the simulation's Megalo multiplayer engine. export HCE_PAKS=".../Halo Campaign Evolved/Meteorite/Content/Paks" tools/level/convert_ce_map.sh maps/bloodgulch.map BGL out/bgl --install

CODE is the new scenario's three-character codename. --install writes the containers into the game and the level file into MJOLNIRLevelLoader; without it everything lands in the output folder. Those containers are loose files: if the same map is also installed from the hub, the hub's copy wins (launcher 0.24.0 and newer). Disable the hub map while testing, or install the build with mjolnir dev install (chunk_numbering.md). Step 1 needs halo2ue-export, from the separate HalcyonRing project; it is not part of this repository. The script finds it through HALO2UE_EXPORT.

Community maps convert the same way (TITLE="Yoyorast Island" tools/level/convert_ce_map.sh "maps/Yoyorast Island V2.map" YOY out/yoy). Their file name becomes [a-z0-9_] for file and asset names; TITLE is the menu name. Three things differ from the stock maps:

Protected maps (Yoyorast Island V2): a protection tool replaced every primary tag class with ztpt and every tag path with <zteam>. halo2ue repairs the index in memory (HalcyonRing map-core/src/parsers/deprotect.rs) before anything reads it. Every tag reference inside the tag data (and the BSP's own region) still carries the real class, so each tag's class is the majority of the references to it; the scenario comes from the header. The names come back by fingerprinting each tag (its data with pointers masked and references replaced by the referenced tag's fingerprint, a few rounds) against the unprotected maps in the same folder (--reference-maps). Yoyorast: all 3,091 classes and 1,261 of 1,838 names, every stock weapon, power-up and item collection among them. The rest get protected\<class>\<index>, and a second copy of a stock tag <stock path>__p<index> (placed as the stock tag). halo2ue writes the repaired index to staging/tags.json for ce_sounds.py. Custom vehicles the tag map does not list are placed by the CE vehicle type halo2ue stages (vehicle_type): jeep as warthog, tank as scorpion, scout as ghost, fighter as banshee, turret as shade (vehicle_types in defs/level/ce-tag-map.json). A custom vehicle can also run as itself, cloned from a shipped one: see custom_vehicles.md. Big BSPs.

Coldsnap's BSP is 35,173 surfaces once its polygons are split into triangles, past a definition's 32,767. Where triangles do not fit, the split makes quads instead (32,257); see ce_terrain_collision.md. Its second BSP is a copy of the first. Sounds a custom map keeps inside the .map (not in sounds.map) are not extracted. Archiving halomaps.org. tools/halomaps/halomaps.py mirrors the site's multiplayer sections (the listings, each map's page, screenshots and file), keeps a JSON record per map with everything the site shows plus what tools/halomaps/cemap.py reads from the .map itself (type, build, BSP count, protection, the tags no stock map carries), and converts the best-rated unconverted map through this command (convert --next, with --pack for the map pack). Its report lists the custom weapons, vehicles, scenery and bipeds across the archive and what every conversion dropped, so the edge cases are worked in order of how many maps they touch. The exporter's resources and reference maps come from HALO2UE_RESOURCES and HALO2UE_REFERENCE_MAPS when the map is kept away from the stock folder.

Step Tool Result 1 halo2ue-export (HalcyonRing) the .map staged: collision BSP, placements, netgame flags 2 merge_ce_collision.py, mjolnir level collision --own-bsp the structure BSP, scenery collision included 3 merge_ce_scene.py, ce_material_spec.py, build_terrain_meshes.py (mesh_rewrite + package_add), scatter_foliage.py, unreal/MJOLNIRMaterials the terrain, scenery, transparent sections, sky and (where CE has it) water as meshes of the map's own (pakchunk986-MJOLNIRMESH-<CODE>_P, see "The terrain, scenery and sky"), their CE materials and bitmaps (the map's bitmaps in pakchunk985-MJOLNIRCOOK-<CODE>_P), and the game's grass, tufts and shore stones on the ground (<name>.foliage.bin beside the level file; FOLIAGE=0 leaves it out) 4 tools/level/gen_ce_level.py the level file 5 mjolnir level bake --standalone CODE --bsp 8=… scenario and registration containers, on the map's own empty Unreal world 6 tools/level/build_spawn_point.sh the spawn-point and teleporter scenery every converted map places

The script's other settings: LIGHTMAP_ARGS (extra solver flags, e.g. --cpu), BAKE_ARGS (extra lightmap_bake flags: --max-size 1024 took Coldsnap's pack from 58.6 MB to 41.8 MB), CE_START_LIFT (the player starts' lift, 1 wu by default, lower for low ceilings), WORLD (another world .umap, or none for the canvas mission's), DELTA (moves the whole map, in wu), SOUNDS_MAP (a sounds.map other than the one beside the map) and SCORE (Slayer's score to win, 25). A failed cook stops the conversion: copying the last good cook's chunk had shipped the wrong textures without a word (Coldsnap, 2026-10-10). The world must be a Blam world. Step 5 gives the bare MapKit world BlamWorldSettings with a DefaultScenario path (blam_world_settings in crates/blam-cli/src/level.rs). Four world subsystems are created only when the glue engine subsystem accepts the world (CU4 +0x7b93a50: the settings are a BlamWorldSettings whose DefaultScenario soft path is set): HaloMaterialResponseWorldSubsystem BlamMapGlueOuterSubsystem BlamSynchronizationPrecreateObjectActorWorldSubsystem BlamBreakableSurfaceSaveGameSubsystem

On plain WorldSettings none of them existed, and bullet impacts, tracers and surface footsteps were missing. A shipped level points DefaultScenario at its BlamScenario actor. Ours names PersistentLevel.BlamScenario, which the gate does not resolve, and with it the world has the same 35 subsystems as B40. Build the tools first: cargo build --release -p blam-cli -p ue-asset --example mesh_rewrite -p blam-pack --example package_add --example package_override -p ue-texture --example lightmap_bake (package_override only for the CE_COOK=0 fallback). Without lightmap_bake the map converts without its baked corners and sun.

Step 3 also re-solves the map's lightmaps (mjolnir level lightmaps, crates/blam-radiosity: tool.exe's own radiosity, the sun and sky fill evaluated per texel, its rays cast on the GPU by default since 2026-10-10 and on the CPU, the reference path, with LIGHTMAP_ARGS=--cpu) at LIGHTMAP_SCALE times the shipped pages' size (auto by default: the power of two that brings the lit surfaces' median texel density to 4 per metre, no page over 2048 and 48 million texels in all; Blood Gulch comes out at 8x, Danger Canyon at 8x, Hang 'Em High at 4x); the shipped pages are 1x and blur every shadow edge, and at 2x a pillar's shadow on a base roof was still a soft blob beside the traced shadow's hard edge. LIGHTMAP_SCALE=0 keeps the shipped pages. A map's interior light is its emitting shaders' (Death Island's red and blue strips, the door glyphs): they shoot before the progressive loop, which would otherwise starve them on a large map, and their bounce fills the bases as CE's pages have them. The light tags placed objects carry go to scene_lights.json (merge_ce_scene.py --lights) but light nothing unless --placed-lights: tool.exe's own pages show no pool beside Death Island's twenty fixtures. Surfaces whose collision material is water take tool.exe's constant (230 230 255), and a rendered surface with no collision (water, strips) never blocks a ray, so the sea floor is lit through the water.

The solved pages replace the shipped ones in the material spec (ce_material_spec.py --lightmaps), the bake's pages take their size, and the bake's sun channel (where CE's sun reaches) comes from the solver's <page>_sunvis.png. The solver's <page>_sunshare.png (each texel's light without the sun) goes to the materials as SunShare: the masters run CE's texture pass over it for the emissive, so CE's ambient, fill and bounce are drawn, rebuild the sunlit lightmap per channel from it and the sky's sun (environment.sun.ce_light) for the sun's albedo (at N.L no lower than 0.3, so a face turned from the sun keeps a colour for headlights and flashes: at its own N.L it had none, and Death Island's headlights stopped at a hard line where a cliff turned away), and Unreal's sun, shadowed by the terrain copy, draws every sun shadow; the lightmap's own texel-stepped shadow edge never shows inside the crisp one. Such a level has no sun mask (gen_ce_level.py --no-sun-mask): the copy's shadows are the sun's shadows, and the mask's metre-wide transition would soften them. Placed scenery stays as CE lights it: the light sampled under each object from the lightmap, shaded by its incident direction, with no Unreal sun on it. CE never shadowed scenery dynamically, and under the copy's shadows a boulder beneath a tree drew half bright and half black, and boughs shadowed each other black.
What the command does › The structure BSP (step 2)

Built on BSP_03_1_Chasm_old, a small shipped BSP with one kd supernode, one cluster and one instance, of which only the file format is kept (blam_sbsp::convert::convert_own, ce_terrain_collision.md): the CE collision tree goes into the world shell, which decides what is inside the world; and into definition 0 behind instance 0, which the collision queries test (the instance is listed at the collision kd hierarchy's root). The two meet at one height to within f32 rounding, and an AI that the simulation found on the copy was on no sector, so level bake lowers the instance 0.001 wu under the shell (re/ai_in_multiplayer.md); the BSP's static Havok body, structure_physics, is recompiled with one key per CE surface (one whole-instance key on the biggest maps, see "Limits"), and since 2026-10-12 one whole-instance key for each scenery piece behind an instance of its own. This is what players, vehicles and items stand on; nothing rebuilds it at load. The map keeps its CE coordinates. It is built for index 0 (level collision --bsp-index 0): every kd hierarchy header and instance shape names the BSP's index, and the donor's own say 7. A scenario of its own. The scenario is still cloned from B40's, but the bake leaves none of B40 in it (blam.single_bsp, applied after --bsp 8= has pointed slot 8 at the map's BSP):
What the command does › The structure BSP (step 2)

structure bsps, ai pathfinding data, scenario cluster data and each PVS's and audibility's per-BSP mappings keep slot 8's element, now index 0. The cluster data's BSP reference names the map's own BSP. Only zone set 0 stays, with its PVS and audibility entries. Its masks, each PVS cluster's bit vectors and its seam cluster references name BSP 0 alone. The designs (B40's soft ceilings), the soft ceilings and both seams references are cleared, as are B40's other insertion points and their 36 player starts. Every placement's origin BSP is 0 and it may attach to BSP 0. B40's mission content goes with the rest of the clears: crates (on BSP 0 they would spawn in the map), device groups, object names, cutscene flags, cinematics, AI objectives, reference frames, UI objectives, AI hints and the script point sets (the last two name B40's BSPs by index). The baked scenario shrinks from 7.1 MB to about 0.27 MB. CANVAS_BSPS=1 convert_ce_map.sh keeps the canvas's BSPs (index 8, blam.active_bsps only). Scenery collision. The game ships no Blam rocks or trees whose collision a placement could borrow, so tools/level/merge_ce_collision.py adds the scenery's own collision models to the BSP's collision first:
What the command does › The structure BSP (step 2)

the exporter stages each scenery tag's collision triangles (collision/*.json); every placement's triangles go in as standalone two-sided surfaces; the compiled MOPP reaches every surface, through a key of its own or, for scenery behind an instance of its own, through the instance's key, which Havok descends into the instance's own MOPP (since 2026-10-12: as surface keys, Death Island's ~96k piece surfaces shared the structure tree's coarse quantisation and players fell through the terrain), so players and vehicles stand on and run into rocks and trees as in CE; mjolnir level collision puts them into the BSP tree as well (blam_sbsp::scenery), so queries that walk the tree, projectiles among them, meet them too: every leaf a scenery triangle passes through is split on the triangle's plane into two flagged copies of itself that name the triangle, the rule the simulation's line test uses for two-sided surfaces between open leaves (its polygon test takes one winding, so such a surface stops a ray only from the side its plane faces; see "Limits"). Where the scenery does not fit the BSP's 16-bit tables it goes to instances of its own, each with such a tree (until 2026-10-03 no leaf named a scenery surface, and bullets went through the Covenant shields).
What the command does › The structure BSP (step 2)

Surface materials. The game picks footstep sounds, tire dust and bullet impacts from each collision surface's material. Each surface keeps its CE collision material (convert::Options::keep_materials), and mjolnir level collision writes the BSP's collision materials block with one entry per CE material. Each entry's render method is the game's own shaders\<material>, and its runtime global material index is that shader's material name looked up in globals. CE shader material type (header +34) game material dirt, sand, stone, snow tough_terrain_dirt, _sand, hard_terrain_stone, soft_terrain_snow wood, leaves tough_organic_wood, soft_organic_plant metal hollow / thin, metal thick hard_metal_thin, hard_metal_thick rubber, glass, force field, water, ice tough_inorganic_rubber, brittle_glass, energy_hologram, liquid_thin_water, hard_terrain_ice anything else default_material merge_ce_collision.py adds two corrections before the conversion:
What the command does › The structure BSP (step 2)

Grass. CE has no grass type. Blood Gulch's ground is one "sand" shader, blended, whose secondary detail map is grass. Each of its surfaces is sampled through the render geometry: the base map's alpha at the surface's points (low alpha shows the secondary detail). Surfaces that are mostly grass get tough_terrain_grass, 1,178 of 2,423 on Blood Gulch. Scenery carries no shader, so its material comes from its name: rock, wood or plant, and the Covenant shield (c_field_generator) takes the Jackal shield's energy_shield_thick_cov_jackal, an energy material made to stop small-arms fire (energy_hologram is the hologram decoy's). Whether every projectile stops on it is still to be seen in game. Gephyrophobia has more than 8,191 surfaces, so its structure_physics uses one whole-instance key (see above). Havok contacts there may report one material even though the surfaces carry theirs. Untested.
What the command does › The terrain, scenery and sky (step 3)
