Tags. new-tag clones the donor's skeleton, model and vehicle. Model variant none drops the Warthog's turret. Blueprint. crates/ue-asset/examples/vehicle_actor.rs clones the donor's actor under /Game/MJOLNIR/Vehicles/, so stock vehicles stay stock. Parts. Every donor part leaves the actor's RuntimeRegions, and the CE parts go in. Each rides a bone by name with its own Transform. Tyres ride the wheel bones, yawed a quarter turn because a wheel bone spins about its X axis. Parts that do not turn ride b_chassis. Size. The rig is scaled (0.589 for the Mongoose on the Warthog), which lands the donor's wheel bones on the CE tyres. Parts divide by that scale. Look. CE's shaders become cooked material instances on the M_CE_* masters, named by the mesh slots, so nothing happens at spawn and joiners get the same parts. The masters come from the CE runtime, which must be installed. Collision. level machine-collision --plan writes CE's hull and tyre BSPs into the donor's collision model, in the regions the plan names. The physics model keeps the donor's bodies with its shapes shrunk to the CE vehicle. Wheel boxes. A wheel only pushes back while its marker is above the ground. The driven body's shape list is a box by each wheel and the polyhedron, and on the Warthog each box's foot sits 2.8 cm under its marker, so the body lands before a marker can pass the surface.

The biggest box belongs to the second, proxy body, which does not touch the level, so it stops nothing. Stretching the boxes with the hull left the Mongoose's feet 24 cm over its markers, and rear boxes 43 cm ahead of the rear wheels: a hard landing put the wheels under the ground for good, with the vehicle riding on its boxes. wheel_boxes keeps each one by its wheel at the tyre's scale, and mass distributions stay, so handling does not change. Handling. Each number is the shipped Warthog's times CE Mongoose over CE Warthog: mass 1650, steering two thirds. Lights. The donor's lights ride VFX sockets of its rig, so they keep the Warthog's shape at the rig's scale and float off a CE body. Niagara components can't be edited in the cooked Blueprint (NiagaraVariable is refused), so ce_vehicle_lights.py adds a lights entry to vehicle_sounds.json, and vehicle_sounds.lua moves them onto CE's headlight and taillight markers at spawn and hides the Warthog's roof pair. That file sits in each level's folder. CE's markers can sit inside the model: the Mongoose's taillights are 3.4 cm behind their lamp faces, so a glow on the marker is buried and only the light on the ground shows. Pass --bones with ce_vehicle_skin.py's bones.json, whose lights it moved clear of the body: 4.5 cm for the taillights, 10.7 cm for the outer headlights. Name.

Status: 2026-10-21. Closed. What every converted map ships is "A BSP of our own" below: mjolnir level collision --own-bsp (blam_sbsp::convert::convert_own), with scenery in the BSP tree or behind instances of its own (2026-10-03), each such piece one whole-instance key in structure_physics since 2026-10-12. ce_map_conversion.md has the pipeline. The sections before "A BSP of our own" are the investigation, superseded turns included; the in-game test the next paragraph awaits has long since passed. How a classic bloodgulch.map collision BSP becomes something the Meteorite simulation walks on, what was proven offline, and what the single remaining in-game test is. Tooling lives in crates/blam-sbsp (unpack16, pack16, transplant, examples). No claim below needed the game running unless it says so.

The world shell (raw_items.collision bsp) is not what the pawn stands on. Every walkable surface is an instanced-geometry definition, referenced by an instance (transform, bounds, a physics block with the Havok shape) and reached through a two-level Havok broadphase: cluster to instance group spheres / mopps -> instance group to instance spheres / mopps -> instance A definition's collision info carries the same eight 16-bit tables as the shell (nodes 8 B, planes 16, leaves 8, 2D refs 4, 2D nodes 16, surfaces 14, edges 12, vertices 16) plus bsp3d supernodes. Nine shipped definitions have no supernode; one ships 3,205 surfaces, so size is not a limit. Raising the definitions under the spawn by 3 wu (examples/shift_defs.rs) changed what the pawn stood on (it fell through), so these tables are the source. Confirmed in game, one launch. An instance without a physics block (the navmesh instance) is never collidable. An instance moved away from its group's sphere is culled before its shape is tested: relocating instance 105 to the origin gave no collision even with valid tables. instance group to instance spheres[g] has center, radius, and an instance indices block; examples/groups.rs <payload> <instance> finds the group. Instance 763 (a spawn-floor platform) sits in group 58, radius 17.87.

examples/roundtrip16.rs decodes a shipped block into the CE structs (unpack16), re-packs it with pack16, and compares. Definitions 10, 159 and 178 and the world shell of BSP_01_1_Start all come back identical, every table. Our leaf flags, 2D sign bits, plane-negated flag and edge order match the engine's.
The 2D projection convention, and the translation bug

Each 2D BSP lives in the projection of its parent 3D plane. Scoring every candidate against the surfaces the shipped 2D trees actually sort: convention def 10 def 159 def 178 shell drop the largest-normal axis; keep the other two in cyclic order when that component is positive, swapped when negative; right child = positive side 100% 100% 100% 99.5% every other candidate 0–72% 28–72% 39–65% 19–81% pack16::translate used to move vertices and 3D planes and leave the 2D split lines alone. After any sideways move every point-in-leaf lookup then chose the wrong surface, which is why transplanted shells and definitions let the pawn through. It now shifts each 2D line by i·t[u] + j·t[v] in its parent plane's projection (pack16::projection_axes, pack16::node_planes); the probe stays at 100% after a (-35.4, 151.17, 50) move of a shipped definition. On the Halo data the probe reads 98.3% both before and after translation, so that residual is the data or the probe, not the move. examples/probe_residual.rs narrows it to 14 of 5,098 surfaces (flat floors among them), with no 2D subtree shared between references. Scored in each reference's own frame (below) that is 12 surfaces, and clipped to the 2D cell above each node it is none: the rest is outlines that reach past their cell, not bad trees.

Launch log, 2026-09-03 evening › The fault address is zero

The pass-through-supernode build crashed at the same instruction, and the exception records of the last two dumps both read address 0x0. At that instruction the address is arena_base + (block_ref_offset + node*2)*4, so the definition's runtime block reference for bsp3d nodes was still zero: the block header was never relocated at load. The rewrite leaves the layout sections byte-identical and only grows the data section; the wrapping .uasset is 769 bytes with no offset table; the block fields and tgbl headers are shaped exactly like the shipped ones (examples/block_headers.rs, tag_sections.rs, uasset_offsets.rs). So whatever the loader uses to decide which nested block headers to relocate is not in the layout, not in the package, and not in the header shape — and the world shell's silent "no collision" is most likely the same unrelocated reference read by a walker that tolerates null. This is where the definition route stops without reversing the loader; C:\tools\ghidra_12.1.2_PUBLIC is available for that pass, starting from the caller chain into HaloSimulation_tag_release.dll +0x2eb130 and the relocation of raw_items blocks at BSP mount.
Launch log, 2026-09-03 evening › Ghidra: the relocation, found (2026-09-04)

Full write-up in docs/re/collision_bsp/. The sim resolves collision data through 16 memory arenas: a reference is (arena<<28) (dword offset), resolved as arena_base_table[arena] + offset*4 (base table at .data 0x1802c2ccc0). On-disk block fields are {count, 0, 0}; the two zeros are the data and struct-def refs, filled at load into a resident structure-BSP record at DAT_1813d45a8 + bsp_index*0x490. The crash (+0x2eb450, the kd supernode walk) reads arena_base[ref>>28] and gets null: the collision block's ref was never correctly relocated. The trigger is changing a nested collision block's element count — the same-size shift_defs edit loads and the pawn stands, while every count change (transplant grow, shipped-copy, all-clear shrink) crashes, regardless of byte validity or total size. The exact writer populates the 0x490 record through a passed pointer, so the cheapest next step is a live memory diff of that record between a shipped and a resized load to name the block whose relocation breaks.
The MOPP compiler, and the supernode bug (2026-09-08)

Two real blockers were found and fixed; the pawn now lands on transplanted Blood Gulch terrain, though it does not yet stay there. The broadphase is three trees deep. Collision reaches an instance through cluster -> instance group -> instance before the definition's own tree is consulted, and each level is a Havok MOPP. A transplant that moves or grows an instance leaves all of the upper trees describing where it used to be, and widening the group sphere does not help: the sphere and the tree are separate tests. examples/group_mopp.rs recompiles the instance-group and cluster trees; examples/def_mopp.rs recompiles the definition's own. Terminal conventions, read off the shipped data: an instance-group tree names absolute instance indices (group 58 ships Reindex nodes so its terminals come out as its member list, 165..779), and the cluster tree names absolute group indices (0..91).
The MOPP compiler, and the supernode bug (2026-09-08)

The pass-through supernode was writing the wrong slots. A bsp3d supernode is thirty-two dwords: fifteen split planes at 0..14, sixteen child cells at 15..30, and the packed axis word at 31. passthrough_from was setting cells at 16..30 and leaving slot 15 alone — and the walk (FUN_1802eb130) descends exactly four levels, so the cell it lands on is 15..=30, slot 15 included. Definition 159 ships 0x80000000 there, which the walk reads as "no hit, stop", so every query whose descent went left four times found nothing. Shipped supernode 1 carries 0x400000b9 in that same slot, which is plainly a child, so the old comment claiming slot 15 is never a child was simply wrong. passthrough_supernode had the matching error: it put the axis word after the planes instead of last. That is why the earlier note here said a pass-through supernode "hung the simulation" and why def_transplant defaulted to emitting none. Emitting none leaves the definition with zero supernodes, and the walk then has nothing to traverse, which is the fall-through that survived every other fix.

A BSP of our own: Blood Gulch without B40's geometry (2026-09-30, late)

mjolnir level collision <collision_N.json> --out <bsp> --own-bsp [--delta dx dy dz] builds the structure BSP from BSP_03_1_Chasm_old — a small shipped BSP with one kd supernode, one cluster and one instance — instead of B40's start BSP (convert::convert_own): the CE tree goes into its world shell (the inside test, with its own kd companion tables widened) and into definition 0 behind instance 0 (seeded with a MOPP element cloned from the static body's, since it ships none), and structure_physics is rebuilt with one surface key per CE surface. Only the package wrapper is still a shipped tag's (a rebuilt BSP wrapper does not start); none of the canvas mission's geometry remains, and there is no region or size limit. Two things learned on the way: A static body of shell keys alone (type 1, one per CE shell surface) did not hold anything. The instance-surface keys (type 3) are what work. The map must stay inside the level's overall extent. Lifted 800 wu above B40, objects fell and vehicles were flung hundreds of wu (Havok's world extent, presumably). What also matters is that no active canvas BSP's world box covers the map (B40's start zone set activates BSPs 4, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16); Blood Gulch was moved by (334.1, -509.8, 0) into a corner only inactive BSPs cover.

Result, under Megalo on the canvas's Unreal world: the player spawns at a CE start and stands at (377.15, -600.41, 0.17); all 28 vehicles rest on Blood Gulch at the CE bases' heights (z 0..4). 1.18 MB payload, 5,305 surfaces. Next: trim the standalone scenario to this one BSP and zone set (then the coordinates can stay CE's own), the terrain mesh, and the bare world. Update 2026-10-21: done on 2026-10-01. The bake trims the scenario to the map's BSP alone (blam.single_bsp, the BSP built for index 0 with --bsp-index 0), the map keeps CE's coordinates (--lift 0 by default), its terrain meshes ship with it, and it bakes onto the bare MapKit world (defs/level/empty_world.umap); see ce_map_conversion.md.
Scenery behind instances of its own (2026-10-01)

A definition's tables are 16-bit (surfaces 32,767, planes 65,535, edges and vertices 65,534), and merge_ce_collision.py adds every scenery triangle as a standalone surface with its own plane, three edges and three vertices. The forested maps overflow one definition on scenery alone: Timberland 31,950 scenery surfaces, Danger Canyon 43,646, Infinity 58,464 (planes first). When the merged collision does not fit, mjolnir level collision --own-bsp splits the scenery tail off (split::split_standalone, using the manifest's scenery_surfaces count) into pieces of 8,192 surfaces, so every surface keeps a type-3 key of its own. Each piece gets a copy of definition 0 and instance 0 (convert::add_scenery_instances): its tables behind an identity frame at the host's position, a one-node tree with the same empty leaf on both sides (every point open space; Blam queries never reached scenery surfaces anyway), its MOPP and the instance's copies of it, the instance's own index in its collision shape, a place in group 0, and a collidable header at every kd root. The group, cluster and structure trees are then rebuilt over all of the instances. The BSP itself stays in the shell and definition 0. Maps that fit are built exactly as before. Timberland (4 scenery instances), Danger Canyon (6), Death Island (3) and Infinity (8) build this way.
Scenery behind instances of its own (2026-10-01)

Since 2026-10-03 each piece has a real tree instead (below), and a piece holds as many surfaces as its tables allow, at most 8,192. Update 2026-10-21: since 2026-10-12, each piece is one whole-instance key (type 2) in structure_physics, and Havok descends through the piece's own MOPP. As type-3 keys, Death Island's ~96k piece surfaces shared the structure tree's quantisation, about 10 wu a step, so a pawn's query came back with 10,000-20,000 candidates and players fell through the terrain. Verified in game on Death Island and Blood Gulch. A child of "none" in a bsp3d node is solid, not empty. The first version gave each piece a node with "none" on both sides, so every point of the map was inside solid scenery: a player was killed by the guardians (guardian_kill) the moment they moved, and teleporters refused to exit into it (teleporter_blocked). Danger Canyon, 2026-10-01; one empty leaf fixed both. Coldsnap did not: its BSP alone has 35,173 surfaces as triangles.

The fan split (split::fan_split_into) cuts a CE polygon past four vertices into a fan around its first vertex; shipped definitions carry triangles and quads, so the pieces may be either. fan_split_fit keeps triangles when they fit the 16-bit tables, so every map that converted before converts byte for byte the same, and makes quads when they do not: Coldsnap's BSP (9,662 triangles, 18,707 quads, 1,860 polygons of five to eight vertices) becomes 32,257 surfaces instead of 35,173. level collision decides whether the scenery moves to instances of its own after this split, not before (Coldsnap fits before it and not after). ray_probe packed on Coldsnap gives the same result as on the unsplit CE tables (no misses).
Scenery in the tree, for projectiles (2026-10-03)

Bullets went through the Covenant shields on Danger Canyon, Gephyrophobia and Rat Race (playtest_2026-10-03.md, issue 5): Havok stands on every surface through the MOPP, but a line test walks the bsp3d tree, and no leaf named a scenery surface. blam_sbsp::scenery puts them in the tree, by the rule of the simulation's own leaf handler (fn_2eb3d0, docs/re/collision_bsp/). Between two open leaves it looks for a surface only when both carry leaf flag bit 0 (two-sided); it takes a 2D reference on the crossed plane from the leaf the ray left, only if the reference's sign matches the direction of travel (no sign: against the plane's normal), and tests the point against the surface's polygon. CE's own two-sided surfaces are stored that way: positive reference in the front leaf, negated in the back one.
Scenery in the tree, for projectiles (2026-10-03)

Every leaf a scenery triangle passes through is split on its plane into two copies of itself, both flagged, both keeping the leaf's own references, front naming the triangle positive and back negated. Nothing becomes "none", so the inside test is unchanged. A triangle on a plane the tree already splits on gets references on that plane, not a coincident node. A leaf more than 12 triangle parts reach is first cut along the axes between them, so tree meshes do not slice each other to pieces. Leaves cut from one leaf share its references in pairs: [scenery A, own, scenery B]. split_standalone gives each scenery piece the same tree (root on the first triangle's plane between two open leaves) and fills each piece as far as its 2D references (65,535) allow. raytest now walks by the same rule; on Damnation's staged BSP its displaced hits went from 35 to 0 and phantoms from 81 to 0 (ray_probe ce, step 2). examples/scenery_probe.rs casts rays through every scenery triangle and the BSP's floors before and after: every miss left has an end in solid (a triangle buried in the ground), and no floor ray is lost.
Scenery in the tree, for projectiles (2026-10-03)

Update 2026-10-21: the simulation's polygon test for that crossing is one-winding (FUN_1802f0170, CU4): the point, projected on the crossed plane (negated for a signed reference), must lie left of every edge of the surface's loop, so a two-sided surface stops a ray only from the side its plane faces. Hulls wound inward stopped bullets on their far wall, from inside (Death Island, in game, 2026-10-18). raytest::tree_game walks by this rule; tree, which ray_probe and scenery_probe use, takes either winding. map scenery where nodes 2D references Rat Race 280 BSP 2,646 -> 3,526 3,251 -> 9,291 Gephyrophobia 1,120 BSP 15,771 -> 18,888 18,084 -> 36,263 Blood Gulch 1,794 BSP 12,159 -> 18,483 13,221 -> 55,634 Boarding Action 5,670 BSP 5,154 -> 12,545 5,879 -> 58,539 Danger Canyon 43,646 17 instances (was 6) ~23,000 each ~64,000 each Scenery that no longer fits the BSP's tables once linked moves to instances of its own, so two maps change route: Sidewinder (3,190 triangles, 105,065 references in the tree) to 1 instance and Ice Fields (11,718) to 3. The maps that already split take more instances: Timberland 11 (was 4), Death Island 7 (was 3), Infinity 25 (was 8). All of them hit every scenery ray in open space offline (2026-10-03); none has been loaded with its scenery linked.
Scenery in the tree, for projectiles (2026-10-03)

Both judgements (in the tree, or in instances) are made after the transplant's fan split (fan_split_fit), as for the quads above. Coldsnap and Yoyorast Island have not been run with their scenery linked. Update 2026-10-21: Death Island and Blood Gulch have since been played in game with their scenery linked (2026-10-12; on Death Island against a B30 rock's hull too). level collision links a staging's scenery whenever it lists any, so every conversion since 2026-10-03 has it, Yoyorast Island's and Coldsnap's of 2026-10-10 included.

translate and the fan split both worked in the plane's unsigned frame, so anything under a negated reference came out wrong. Every converted map has some, and two steps reached them: translate runs on every conversion, not only under --delta: the shell keeps the map's coordinates, but definition 0 is moved by minus its instance's position. Split lines under a negated reference moved along the swapped axes. The fan split built one chain of diagonals, in the unsigned frame, for every reference to a polygon. A negated reference then landed on the wrong piece of its own polygon, the polygon test failed, and a ray went through. CE's two-sided polygons are always reached this way from one side. Now the frame comes from the reference (pack16::node_frames), and the fan split builds a chain per sign the polygon is reached under (split::fan_chain). A polygon reached under both signs costs a second chain, so a map's 2D nodes can grow; of the 50 maps below only two scenery pieces on SFN do (1,260 nodes). Nothing else in the tag moves, the breakable bit below aside: surfaces, planes, edges, vertices, the tree and both MOPPs are as they were, so nothing about standing on a map changes. What changes is which surface a line test finds.

Run over the newest staging of 50 maps with level collision --own-bsp, in the shell and definition 0 of the finished tag (a check takes a surface's centroid down each reference that reaches it; a ray crosses each surface's centroid in both directions, by raytest::tree_game): before after shell: checks that land off the polygon, of 558,285 17,539 0 definition 0: the same 43,901 2 shell: rays that newly hit, of 894,466 3,667 definition 0: the same 7,842 rays that stopped hitting 0 Scenery pieces with 2D trees of their own go from 1,887 to 16. The two left in definition 0 (Containment) and the 16 (one piece of SFN, eight polygons under each sign) sit under plain references too and were there before. The fan split leaves a map's route alone: every map stays in the 16-bit tables, the largest at 27,905 of 32,767 2D nodes (District), and takes the same triangles or quads and the same scenery placement as before.

pack16 no longer carries the breakable bit. It writes no breakable set, so the bit named nothing, and the game never ships it that way: of the 34,189,419 surfaces in the 122 shipped BSPs, 8,968 have the bit and all of them name a set (B40's BSP_01_1_Start has none, A15's BSP_Cryo 392). Ten of the 50 maps had it without one (BVR, CSN, DST, HDL, IVT, PRS, TBS, TRF, TRM, ZAN; 4,230 surfaces). What the simulation did with such a surface has not been measured in game. Surfaces that really break would need a breakable set written for them. validate::two_sided_leaves_unflagged lists leaves that reach a two-sided surface without leaf flag bit 0, which a ray would never look in. It is in the validate example; conversions do not run it.

Status: solved. A brand-new scenario starts from a cooked DT_Scenarios row and ScenarioList handle (2026-09-11), on its own Unreal world through mjolnir_map_registry.dll (the same night), and since 2026-10-09 a map installed while the game runs is registered in memory (PR #165, docs/live_map_install.md). The 2026-09-03 sections are the turns that led there. How Halo: Campaign Evolved decides whether a scenario name can launch, what a new scenario package needs, and how far a new one (PG1) gets today. Every claim below was checked in the running game (CU4, host exe PE timestamp 0x8a03f777) or read out of the shipping binary; the probe tooling is in native/scenario_probe/ and the raw run log is probe_log_2026-09-02.md.

The standalone container that mjolnir level bake --standalone <CODE> builds is mounted into the UE package store. A vtable-slot hook on FFilePackageStoreBackend (vtable RVA 0xB446618; slot 2 BeginRead, slot 4 GetPackageStoreEntry) listed it among the mounted containers with one package registered (FMountedContainer::NumMountedPackages == 1). Every piece of that container format — FPackageId, ContainerHeader, BLAKE3 metas, directory index — was already right. What proved nothing was the probe: UE4SS's Lua LoadAsset never reaches the package store for a package it does not know (a made-up name and the new package both produced zero GetPackageStoreEntry calls), so "LoadAsset returns invalid" measured UE4SS's own gatekeeping, not the loader.

Read from the exe (RVAs image-relative) and confirmed live: UBlamCampaignFlowGameSubsystem::SetAndBeginCampaign — exec thunk 0x7B433C0, implementation 0x7B446E0 — does a linear scan of the active campaign asset's ScenarioList (TArray<FDataTableRowHandle> at UBlamCampaignDataAsset + 0x40, 16-byte elements {UDataTable*, FName}) comparing the 64-bit FName. No match → CurrentScenarioIndex stays −1 → false in under a millisecond with no Blam error. Nothing here touches tags, the IoDispatcher or the package store. StartScenario (0x7B44CB0) fetches the row from /Game/Blueprints/Campaign/DT_Scenarios (a UDataTable, 13 rows, row struct BlamScenarioDataTableRow), fails if the row is missing, if UnrealLevel is unset or if ScenarioName is shorter than two characters, then derives the scenario tag's package path from the row and opens it via 0x7B9F240: FPackageId::FromName → FIoDispatcher::GetSizeForChunk (chunk existence, not the package store). Tag reads go through the TagIoHandler (0x7B9EBB0), which consults BlamCookedTagReferencesEngineSubsystem when the cvar Blam.TagIoHandler.IoStore.UseCookedTagReferences.Enabled (backing byte .data 0xD0A94DC, default 1) is set.
What gates a scenario name › BlamScenarioDataTableRow (176 bytes per row)

offset field notes +0 vtable (FTableRowBase) +8 UnrealLevel TSoftObjectPtr<UWorld> weak ptr @8, FTopLevelAssetPath @16 (package FName, asset FName), sub-path FString @32 +48 ScenarioName FString "B40" — the codename the tag path is derived from +64 MapGuid +80 / +96 MissionTitle / MissionDescription FText +112 MissionPreviewImage soft ptr +152 InsertionPointsDataAsset UObject* drives RALLY POINT SELECT +160 ProgressionUnlockTag FName UDataTable::RowMap is a TMap<FName, uint8*> at +0x30 (UE 5.5 TSet layout: elements {ptr,num,max} @0x30, inline allocation bits @0x40, NumBits @0x58, hash buckets pointer @0x70, HashSize @0x78; 24-byte elements {FName, uint8*, HashNext, HashIndex}). Bucket = GetTypeHash(FName) & (HashSize-1) with the 5.5 FNameEntryHandle hash (block<<19)+block+(offset<<16)+offset+(offset>>4) (block = id>>16, offset = id&0xffff), verified against all 13 shipped rows.
What gates a scenario name › BlamCookedTagReferencesEngineSubsystem

+0x30 TArray<FString> of 10,201 cooked tag package paths — element index is the runtime tag index; searched by TArray<FString>::Find (linear, case-insensitive). +0x40 TMap<int32 tag index, TArray<int32>> with 13 entries (one per shipped scenario), each the list of tag indices that scenario references — the preload set. 0x1fff at +0x50 is the sparse array's inline allocation bits (13 live elements), not a hash mask.

Its package in its own folder: /Game/Tags/Levels/Halo1/Solo/<CODE>/_Generated_/<CODE>-scenario. The flow derives that path from the row, so a package left in the donor's folder is never found. mjolnir level bake --standalone now renames the folder segment as well as the leaf (still same-length surgery; codenames are three characters like every shipped one). A DT_Scenarios row — clone B40's 176 bytes, replace ScenarioName. A ScenarioList handle {DT_Scenarios, FName(<CODE>)} on the campaign asset (DA_FirstPlayableCampaign). Optionally its path appended to the cooked-references path table and a per-scenario reference entry (borrowing B40's list); the spare capacity in both arrays is enough without reallocation. With 1–3 in place, SetAndBeginCampaign(DA_FirstPlayableCampaign, "PG1") returns true, the row's world loads, and the only BlamScenarioTagDataAsset in memory is /Game/Tags/Levels/Halo1/Solo/PG1/_Generated_/PG1-scenario — served from the mod container. The real CAMPAIGN → NEW GAME → MISSION SELECT screen shows PG1 as an eleventh mission (with the cloned row's title) and launches it through the game's own flow.

Superseded by "2026-09-11: the door is open" below: PG1 started once its row was registered at boot, with no change to the loading pipeline. The simulation does not start for PG1: the pawn stays at the origin and the frame is black, while shipped missions started through the same menu run. The stall has a precise signature (measured 2026-09-03 on CU4, host pid 13828): signal shipped mission (B40) new scenario (PG1) SetAndBeginCampaign returns true true scenario tag asset in memory B40-scenario PG1-scenario (mod container) ServerMarkFinishedBlamMapLoad fires ~4 s after launch never fires bWaitingForBlamGameplayStart clears stays true So the blocker sits in the Blam simulation's own map load, upstream of every UE-side gate. Three candidates were ruled out by experiment:

The world's scenario actor is not the binding. BlamScenario is an Actor subclass (ScenarioName, CampaignId, MapId, MAPNAME, StructureBsps, ZoneSets...) and the cooked B40 world package does contain an export named BlamScenario_UAID_F02F74DC4569B31902. But in the loaded, stalled world FindAllOf("BlamScenario") returns zero actors and no actor's name contains "BlamScenario" (28 actors; the only Blam-named one is BP_BlamCameraManager_C). The actor is spawned after the sim's map load succeeds, so it cannot be what refuses PG1. The B40 world also does not import B40-scenario. The UE map-load handshake is downstream. Calling ServerMarkFinishedBlamMapLoad, ServerMarkHasFinishedHaloActorPooling and ServerMarkHasFinishedProcessingPsoCache by hand flips all three flags, brings BlamNetworkGameStateComponent::bSessionRunning to true and spawns a BP_MeteoritePawn_C — but bWaitingForBlamGameplayStart stays true and the pawn stays at the origin. Forcing the handshake does not start the sim. The cooked-reference table is not the gate. With Blam.TagIoHandler.IoStore.UseCookedTagReferences.Enabled 0 (set through KismetSystemLibrary::ExecuteConsoleCommand; the backing byte at .data 0xD0A94DC reads 0 afterwards) a shipped mission still loads and plays normally, and PG1 still stalls identically.

Adding PG1 to the path table and cloning B40's per-scenario reference list (earlier run) also changed nothing. Remaining hypotheses, cheapest first: The sim keys campaign maps by name through its own registry. The Blam console carries levels_add_campaign_map and levels_add_campaign_map_with_id, but both are stubs in this release build, so the registry (if it exists) cannot be extended from the console. Something in the scenario's own root fields (map id, campaign id, map name string id) is matched against a sim-side table. The scnr field documentation in the sim binary describes map name as "Used to associate external resources with" the scenario. The loading pipeline itself: a tick state machine at RVA 0x7B48160 (registered by 0x7B47FE0, which sets a state byte at +0xD9 and a repeating timer) dispatches five states, one of which consults the cooked-reference lookup (0x6720650, the same helper BuildTagIoRequest uses) and one of which is a float-timeout wait at +0x1F0/+0x1F4. Instrumenting that state byte during a PG1 load is the next concrete step.
The name is fine; the package is not (2026-09-03, second session)

A clean discriminator settles what the simulation actually rejects. Inject a data-table row keyed PG2 — a name the game has never seen — but leave its ScenarioName field reading B40, so the flow derives the shipped tag path from it. Launched from MISSION SELECT as an eleventh mission, that row starts normally: ServerMarkFinishedBlamMapLoad fires 1.8 s later and the mission plays. So new names, new DT_Scenarios rows and new ScenarioList entries are all accepted. What the simulation refuses is a new scenario tag package, even one whose .uasset and .ubulk are byte-identical to a shipped scenario's (verified: both chunks ship in the mod container at the same sizes, and a byte search for the donor codename finds the same 46 and 413 hits at the same offsets as the shipped tag). Until the tag registry the simulation builds at startup can be extended, a custom map has to ride on a shipped scenario tag, with a new menu row pointing at that shipped codename. Also worth keeping: a bare SetAndBeginCampaign from script does not cold-start the simulation even for a shipped mission — it returns true, the world loads, and no map-load mark ever arrives. Only the menu flow brings the session up, so it is not a shortcut for automation and not evidence about a new scenario.
Making a blank map out of a shipped mission

mjolnir level bake now strips a mission to bare geometry. blam.clear takes the placement flags it always had plus a blocks list naming any other root block to empty, and clear.scripts no longer just empties the script block: "clear": { "squads": true, "vehicles": true, "scripts": true, "blocks": ["scenery", "machines", "trigger volumes", "scenario kill triggers"] } A map with no script at all boots black and frozen. Blam hands a level to the player from the mission's own script: the screen starts faded out, the camera is under script control and player input is off. B40 in particular opens with the player belted into a Pelican for the intro cinematic, so a script-less bake leaves a live simulation the player cannot see or move in — the simulation is fine (a console player_teleport moves the unit), only the handover never happens. clear.scripts therefore compiles a replacement section holding one script: (script startup mjolnir_level_startup (begin (fade_in 0 0 0 15) (camera_control false) (player_enable_input true)))
Making a blank map out of a shipped mission

That is enough: the map fades in, the player owns the camera and walks. Update 2026-10-21: it was not. That script left the player able to look around but not move, shoot or switch weapons, a cutscene lock with no cutscene. This engine's missions enter gameplay through f_insertion_fade_to_gameplay, so clear.scripts now writes what it does: a bounded wait for game_all_players_active, player_control_fade_in_all_input, the HUD and screen faded back, player_disable_movement false, the gaze unlocked and the weapon raised (stub_scripts in crates/blam-cli/src/level.rs, commit 54ccee93, 2026-09-10). examples/levels/blank_b40.level.json is the worked example — B40 with every placement, every AI, every trigger and the whole mission script gone, plus a sky and four landmark shapes spawned by the runtime loader.

native/scenario_probe/tagrefs_probe.c exports, loaded from the UE4SS Lua sandbox with package.loadlib(path, "<export>")() and driven through small request files next to the DLL: export request file effect dump_bytes dump_req.txt = <hex addr> <len> hexdump to tagrefs.log dt_addrow dt_req.txt = <table> <template row> <fname idx> <row size> <name> clone a row, replace ScenarioName, insert into RowMap scenlist_append scenlist_req.txt = <TArray addr> <fname idx> <number> grow ScenarioList by one handle tagrefs_append tagrefs_addr.txt, tagrefs_append.txt append a path to the cooked path table refs_addentry refs_req.txt = <subsystem> <key> <template key> add a per-scenario reference entry store_probe.c hooks the package-store backend (probe_open, probe_logall, probe_close) and writes store_probe.log. Hazards learned the hard way: an FString is {ptr, Num @+8, Max @+12} (a count written at +4 corrupted the pointer's high dword and crashed StartScenario); assigning an FText from UE4SS Lua to a menu item crashes in the HaloUIViewItemData destructor at the next garbage collection (set only StartingScenarioName/CampaignData on a shipped BP_DebugMapItemData_C); buffers the probe allocates with HeapAlloc are freed by FMemory::Free at shutdown (exit crash) — a shipping mod must allocate through the engine or only grow into existing capacity.
Two exe details worth keeping: mjolnir_mission <CODE> cannot cold-start the sim on CU4 (the UI performs a session bring-up the bare call does not), and UE4SS LoadAsset is not a loader probe.
2026-09-11: the door is open — the row has to be cooked

The "new package is refused" conclusion above was one step short. The simulation does not resolve campaign maps from DT_Scenarios on demand; it builds its own levels registry once, at boot, from the tables the BlamBuiltInMapInfoDataAsset names — /Game/Blueprints/Campaign/BuiltInMapInfoData, CampaignMapInfoTables = [DT_Scenarios, DT_Test_Scenarios] (mjolnir ue get --package BuiltInMapInfoData). The sim side is Reach's levels system (HaloSimulation_tag_release.dll CU4 FUN_180322aa0 allocates the "campaigns", "campaign levels" (64 × 0x274 bytes), "campaign insertions", "multiplayer levels"… arrays; the console's levels_add_campaign_map* are stubs pointing at the same no-op handlers). So a row injected at runtime satisfied StartScenario, which reads the table then, but the registry the simulation had already built did not know the codename — and a shipped codename in a new row worked because the registry knew that one. Update 2026-10-21: the gate was one layer up. The simulation's own levels arrays are empty on CU4; what boot builds and a late row lacked is the exe's frontend levels cache: UBlamFrontendLevelsEngineGlueSubsystem::BuildRuntimeCachesFromBuiltInMapInfoDataAsset (0x7B7D180) passes each DT_Scenarios row to a per-map insert (0x7BAC140).
2026-09-11: the door is open — the row has to be cooked

Called for a row added at runtime, that insert lets a new codename start without a restart: mjolnir_scenario_add in native/map_registry does it for maps installed while the game runs (commit a404f288, 2026-10-09, PR #165, mods-v0.20.0; docs/live_map_install.md). A map present at boot still gets the cooked row. blam-pack --example scenario_register <CODE> cooks the row: it clones the donor's DT_Scenarios row under the new name with ScenarioName = CODE (ue_asset::datatable — the table's native tail is the u32 object trailer, a u32 count, then FName + unversioned row struct per row, rebuilt byte for byte before anything changes), appends a ScenarioList handle to DA_FirstPlayableCampaign, and packs both into pakchunk996-MJOLNIRREG-<CODE>_P. Verified live (CU4): with that container beside the standalone PG1 package from mjolnir level bake --standalone PG1, MISSION SELECT lists an eleventh mission, and launching it starts the simulation — PG1-scenario is the only scenario asset in memory, the pawn is placed, ServerMarkFinishedBlamMapLoad fires, and B40's intro cinematic and mission play on the new tag package. A brand-new scenario tag package loads.
2026-09-11: the door is open — the row has to be cooked

What that opens: the scenario, its BSPs and its other tags can all live under the new codename's folder (ordinary new tags were already proven to load by name), so a map no longer has to override a shipped mission. What is still shared is the UE side: the row's UnrealLevel points at B40's world, and a brand-new world package has not been tried natively yet — LoadAsset was never a valid probe for it either.

mjolnir level bake <file> --standalone BGL --bsp 8=<collision payload> gives the map its own structure BSP: the canvas scenario's structure bsps[8] pair — bsp_01_1_start (sbsp) and its scenario_structure_lighting_info — is cloned under /Solo/BGL/_Generated_/, the BSP with the given body, the lighting info as shipped, and the baked scenario's two references are repointed (sbsp:levels\halo1\solo gl sp_01_1_start). The clones are the shipped wrappers with the codename swapped into the package path — the same same-length surgery as the scenario package — packed into the map container beside it. Verified live: with no override of B40's BSP installed, BGL starts and the pawn stands on the Blood Gulch collision at its start. One negative result worth keeping: a BSP wrapper rebuilt from scratch by blam_pack::newtag::build (the route that works for collision models and projectiles) registers and the scenario loads, but the simulation never starts the map — pawn at the origin, loader waiting. Whatever the structure BSP's cooked wrapper carries beyond what tagwrap models, the map load needs it, so BSPs are cloned, not rebuilt.

tools/level/build_landscape.py --heightfield <manifest> reads the verified pwr-heightfield-v1 contract through tools/level/heightfield.py. This is an offline input builder; it does not launch Unreal or alter an installed map. The regular scene glTF and materials spec remain required for material UVs, texture bakes and identification of ground mesh slots that the Landscape hides. The manifest fixes the physical terrain, independent of image dimensions: { "schema": "pwr-heightfield-v1", "coordinates": "authoring_metres_z_up", "origin_m": [-1000, -1000], "spacing_m": [1.9550342130987293, 1.9550342130987293], "dimensions": [1024, 1024], "row_order": "+y", "height": { "path": "master.r32", "encoding": "float32_raw_le", "offset_m": 0, "scale_m": 1, "sha256": "" } } This example spans exactly 2,000 metres. Values decode as offset_m + stored * scale_m; normalized exports need an explicit physical vertical scale. Origin always means minimum X/Y, even when row_order is -y. The reader canonicalizes rows to increasing Y. It validates dimensions, finite heights and file hashes; it also supports the other encodings documented by its module and tests. Do not infer height from reference-image brightness or silently normalize each export's minimum and maximum. The approved visual references guide authored geography; the exported physical field is the numerical source of truth.

The current editor builder uses a square grid of components, each with 63 quads. Direct import requires square physical bounds. --components 16 makes 1009² vertices. Spacing is derived from the manifest's complete extent: a 2,000-metre field uses approximately 198.4126984 cm quads; a 2,016-metre field uses 200 cm. An explicitly supplied --quad must agree, otherwise the builder fails rather than cropping or stretching the terrain. With no component count, it chooses the nearest whole component count to the source resolution (1–64 per side). Authoring coordinates become Unreal [100*x, -100*y, 100*z], then --offset adds centimetres. Consequently the output height image reverses canonical authoring Y. Lift defaults to zero for direct fields and remains 8 cm for the legacy mesh path. Use zero lift for shared terrain alignment. Direct heights bypass the mesh workflow's settling, steep-step holes, overlap holes and synthetic seabed. Large erosion features therefore survive even when the CE mesh is coarser. --sea, --zone and --min-z cannot be combined with --heightfield; changes to the physical ground belong in a revised master. This path represents one continuous heightfield, not caves or overhangs. Separate meshes can supply those structures. Lip/foot material masks use the master, while the colour/lightmap material bakes still come from the CE scene.

Height encoding sets the actor's Z near the middle of the field and expands Landscape Z scale when relief exceeds the usual approximately 512-metre range. It reports the resulting vertical quantization and rejects clipping. It does not replace an out-of-range sample with a clamped height.

From the worktree root, add a manifest to an upgrade map entry: { "heightfield": "levels/warfare/pwr/terrain/master.heightfield.json", "components": 16, "landscape_lift": 0 } Remove a previous quad setting unless it exactly matches the new field extent. The map's other upgrade options remain necessary. stage_land resolves the manifest relative to the repository and fails before process launch if missing. It forwards the file to the normal Landscape input build. Alternatively: python tools/level/build_landscape.py --shader --name LPW --heightfield --components 16 The output remains compatible with the existing editor/cook path: landscape.json, heights.r16, holes.r8, material bakes and edge masks. No runtime heightfield reader or PCG plugin is required by these outputs.

Both landscape.json.heightfield and heightfield.receipt.json record the manifest/height/output hashes, source/output dimensions, physical bounds, axis transform, offset/lift, vertical quantization and clipped sample count. They also record: Master-versus-CE-mesh disagreement at Landscape vertices: coverage, maximum, 95th percentile and RMS vertical error. This is diagnostic; the converted render mesh is not proof of the installed native collision mesh. Reconstruction error at every source grid vertex after resampling and R16 encoding. Bilinear error and the larger error of both possible triangle diagonals are reported. This measures sampled detail loss, not a continuous surface bound or inspection of the cooked Landscape triangles. Native collision parity remains explicitly unmeasured in this receipt. An accepted map still needs the separate adaptive collision error report, surface/budget validation, and live player/vehicle checks. Reproject trees, grass, roads and bases against the accepted final master before rerunning PCG. The previous flat-map PCG receipts do not validate a revised terrain field.

The offline regression suite covers axis/row orientation, offsets, exact bounds, rejection of mismatched spacing, tall-relief quantization, detection of detail lost between output vertices, retention of detailed ground over a flat proxy, legacy mesh behaviour and upgrade config forwarding: python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_build_landscape.py -v python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_upgrade_ce_map.py -v
Water depths and shores on the runtime field

For PWR's river and lake at different elevations, the coarse CE core is not a valid source of water depth. Set FROZEN_HEIGHTFIELD to the decoded runtime Landscape field, not the original Gaea source, before convert_ce_map.sh: $env:FROZEN_HEIGHTFIELD = (Resolve-Path 'levels/warfare/pwr/terrain/runtime-v3/runtime-master.json').Path The converter passes this through build_terrain_meshes.py --heightfield to refine_water_gltf.bake_shore. Other maps without the option retain the existing coastal bake. For a standalone refinement: python tools/level/refine_water_gltf.py --heightfield --shore-cell 2 Every water vertex receives TEXCOORD_1 = [shore_distance_m, depth_m]. Depth is its own surface elevation minus field.sample(x, -gltf_z), clamped to 0–50 m; the runtime manifest selects the verified Landscape triangle interpolation. There is no common sea elevation. The shoreline raster is the union of the authored water triangles where the local water surface is above the terrain. Dry island cells and the outside of the water footprint are both shore. An exact Euclidean distance transform of those raster cells supplies distance, bilinearly sampled at vertices and limited to 200 m. The default 2 m raster is a discretized shoreline, not an exact vector contour or continuous error bound. A dry/occluded water vertex has zero shore distance and depth.
Water depths and shores on the runtime field

glTF input must contain applied node transforms in pre-offset authoring metres (x, z, -y); nonidentity node transforms, out-of-bounds vertices, changed heightfield hashes, and malformed UV buffers fail before publishing. Later mesh normalization/actor placement is unchanged. A .shore.json beside the water glTF records source/output hashes, field hash, interpolation, grid size, depth/shore ranges, and float32 depth precision. The isolated actual PWR proof is in out/pwr/water-heightfield-proof/. All 54,950 vertices agree with the frozen runtime triangles to 0.000000477 m; all nonshore attributes remain unchanged. Of 9,563 vertices over less than 1 m of water, none now incorrectly reports depth above 3 m (previously 9,252) or shore distance above 50 m (previously 8,202). Water elevations remain 55–150 m, and measured local depths are 0–9.396 m. The proof does not certify live transparency, water collision, or swimming behavior. The explicit PWR Shelf=[0,40,5,0] and ShoreParams=[0,14,0.12,0] keep the ocean material's synthetic shelf and incoming beach waves off for this freshwater layout.

It does not install files. Future conversions should use the environment hook instead of this one-off receipt-bound script. python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_refine_water_heightfield.py -v

tools/level/heightfield.py is shared by terrain rendering and collision research. A pwr-heightfield-v1 manifest explicitly states metre-space origin, spacing, dimensions, axis order, encoded-height scale/offset and SHA-256 hashes. It never normalizes a terrain to its observed minimum/maximum. The origin is always minimum X/Y; row_order: "-y" means the stored image starts at maximum Y and is flipped when loaded. Decoded arrays always increase in authoring Y. { "schema": "pwr-heightfield-v1", "coordinates": "authoring_metres_z_up", "origin_m": [-1000, -1000], "spacing_m": [1.9550342130987293, 1.9550342130987293], "dimensions": [1024, 1024], "row_order": "+y", "height": { "path": "terrain.r32", "encoding": "float32_raw_le", "offset_m": 0, "scale_m": 400, "sha256": "replace-with-the-export-file-sha256" } } That example assumes a calibrated normalized R32 export. If the export stores actual metres, use scale 1. Supported heights include 16-bit PNG/TIFF/raw LE and float32 NPY/TIFF/raw LE. Eight-bit concept images cannot masquerade as 16-bit terrain. Optional same-grid masks decode to [0,1]; road, shore, flat or bases supply collision priorities. Metadata such as water_level_m, generator settings and source receipts is preserved.

load_heightfield(path) returns Heightfield: heights_m, origin_m, spacing_m, dimensions, bounds_m, masks, metadata, manifest_sha256, sample(x,y), sample_mask(...) and resample_grid(dimensions). Sampling is bilinear unless surface_interpolation: "triangle_nw_se" explicitly selects the actual Unreal Landscape triangles in canonical +Y authoring space. Masks remain bilinear. Sampling rejects out-of-bounds coordinates by default. Input hashes, dimensions, finite values and explicit height calibration are checked.

python tools/level/adaptive_heightfield.py --out out/pwr/terrain-collision --terrain-budget 26000 --reserve-surfaces 4000 --reserve-edges 10000 --refinement-iterations 5 The NumPy-only RTIN hierarchy pads edge samples to a 2^k+1 working grid at the original spacing, then clips the mesh back to the original domain. It does not stretch1024 samples into1025: that shifts sharp features before collision approximation even begins. It uses shared edge decisions, then independently rasterizes the resulting mesh at every original master vertex and cell centre. Measured failures guide subsequent priority adjustments under the same triangle budget. This follows the right-triangulated hierarchy concept described in Mapbox Martini; the implementation and measurement code live in this repository. Outputs are collision-surface.npz (vertices_m, triangles) and collision-report.json. The latter includes region maxima/RMS/percentiles, signed offsets, topology, reserved architectural surfaces, estimated closure surfaces/edges, and native table headroom. Default measured targets are 0.50 m ground, 0.15 m roads, 0.25 m shore and 0.10 m flat foundations. Budget changes must preserve the native 32,767-surface and 65,534-edge limits after architecture and the world enclosure. Reported reserves are estimates, not compiler counts.

accuracy_and_mesh_budget_pass is an explicit acceptance gate. A completed research command can exit successfully while truthfully reporting a failed accuracy target; consumers must inspect that gate. runtime_ready is always false: this output is an open height surface, not a native collision package. World closure, architecture intersections, packed BSP table validation, native ray probes, vehicle handling and multiplayer remain separate requirements. For bilinear source fields, sampled measurements do not establish a mathematical continuous error bound. They include full original source resolution and cell centres, not only retained mesh vertices. Rendering must use the same finalized master. Any road cut/fill or proposed local visual adjustment creates a new master and must regenerate dependent masks, placements and error reports.

--chunked --hierarchy-threshold 0.2 --cliff-error 2 measures dense terrain for the existing standalone-static collision path. This requires an explicit walkable mask. --terrain-budget is a total triangle cap, not a claim that the whole terrain fits one 16-bit definition. The native compiler must validate each actual piece and report its real surface ranges. Uniform runtime NW–SE triangles require special care: RTIN alternates diagonal directions, and a saddle may have zero midpoint residual while differing at its cell centre. The builder forces implicated cells to leaves, then changes paired unit-cell diagonals to match Unreal. The independent source-grid/centre audit then covers the complete overlay of the axis/45-degree triangle meshes. export_terrain_collision.py checks the accuracy and hash receipt and exports Morton-ordered CE-world-unit triangles. It also writes an ordered NPZ and a candidate seam receipt. Native splitting can take fewer than 8,192 surfaces when tree tables grow, so candidate seams must not be presented as verified compiled boundaries. upgrade_ce_map.py validates the exported master hash before appending these surfaces to the foliage/architecture collision tail.

python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_heightfield.py -v python tools/level/probe_adaptive_heightfield.py --out out/pwr/terrain-prototype The synthetic 2 km fixture is explicitly not PWR geography. It exercises curved graded roads, a lake shore, rolling relief and a flat foundation. Its reports demonstrate both attainable precision and insufficient-budget failures. A flat plane remains two triangles with exact sampled height. The test suite also checks Gaea-style raw calibration, axis direction, content tampering, source format rejection and non-power-of-two source coverage.

The new opt-in path is flux.schema = "mjolnir-flux-v2" with domains. Existing single-domain/coast maps retain their previous loader behavior. Authoring uses playback: "simulate"; release assembly requires playback: "baked" and a matching saved state. Baked playback spawns a native surface (River by default), imports the state textures, and calls the installed SetSimulationState(State) function. No simulation domain or source modifiers are created by that path. Cooked Blueprint inspection matters here: SetSimulationState assigns the state and invokes InitializeStates. This game's StopSimulation talks only to its editor helper, so calling it is not evidence of stopped runtime simulation. The author documents direct surface playback from a saved state, and recommends bounded simulation resolution and capture-only slopes for difficult cascades: Fluid Flux documentation.

Upgrade config flux.heightfield names the decoded runtime master, with surface_interpolation: "triangle_nw_se"; flux.water_geometry names the 3D water/profile geometry. Each entry in flux.domains contains id, domain, sources, and optionally playback, prime_ms, surface, color_preset, and surface_vectors, surface_scalars, and native simulation foam parameters. Domain positions, cell size and height use Unreal centimetres; the master uses authoring metres with Y reflected into Unreal. tools/level/flux_heightfield.py retains original grid vertices and the same diagonal as Landscape, without resampling. It writes a double-sided, capture-only mesh plus a receipt. Domain rectangles outside actual terrain coverage fail rather than inventing a floor. The helper rejects resolutions above 1024 or non-power-of-two dimensions and capture height above 32,000 cm. This is a capture mesh, not an additional Blam collision mesh.

The current fork's Flux capture does not reliably capture Landscape. The older CE-based flux_bed path therefore cannot be reused for PWR's buried coarse core. The new bed is built from actual rendered terrain. Bridges, foliage and other overhead decor are excluded from capture; the capture bed is hidden afterward. The new path sets the native SceneCapture to UseShowOnlyList and populates ShowOnlyActorComponents from the explicit bed IDs. A tag exclusion list is insufficient: streamed terrain can exist outside the loader's actor dictionary. This was caught by comparing every captured pixel with the final field while authoring v5 water inside the older v3 visual world. Before the allowlist, old mountains entered capture; afterward every pixel matched within the exported half-float depth precision. Do not replace this with a broader scene capture.

Five SHA-256 values bind a bake to its terrain manifest, decoded terrain data, 3D water geometry, capture mesh, and domain/source/simulation settings. The settings hash also binds the explicit-bed capture policy. Domain geometry and canvas origin must match as well. Assembly validates EXR headers/dimensions and seals the texture hashes. A new terrain with unchanged domain bounds still invalidates the old bake. All named states live under flux_state/<id>/ and contain state.json, height.exr, velocity.exr, and ground.exr. Ground is required by the native surface material, even without a solver. UE5.5's Kismet exporter writes EXR only for RGBA16F targets, so the height and ground maps are copied through RGBA16F before export. The source capture mesh retains exact terrain vertices; the exported depth has half-float quantization. All-baked assembly omits the capture bed actor entirely. Its mesh and receipt remain offline inputs for provenance validation; they are not runtime surfaces.

Authoring commands are mjolnir_flux_status and mjolnir_flux_bake <id all>. Baking records current GPU state; removal of primers does not certify settled or visually correct flow. Review shoreline depth, cascade continuity and bridge clearance first, then export, assemble with playback: "baked", reload and confirm simulation_domain:false. Release packaging rejects authoring modes or any missing named state. Fluid Flux remains presentation here. Native player and vehicle support stays with the Blam bed, ford and bridge collision. This change does not implement swimming, drowning, buoyancy, or replicated fluid forces.

levels/warfare/pwr/terrain/prepare_flux_probe.py --heightfield <runtime-master> --geometry <terrain.geometry.json> --out <proof-directory> --package builds an isolated 512 m upper-cascade capture tile. It does not install or call the game. tools/level/flux_probe_install.py install restore --proof <proof-directory> requires a closed game, snapshots exact installed metadata/helper hashes, and touches only narrow loader hooks plus temporary chunk 962. No DLL or main map container is replaced. tools/level/flux_probe_readback.lua reads actual surface, solver and capture-bed transforms through the existing bridge. Offline checks: lua tools/tests/test_flux_runtime.lua python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_flux_heightfield.py python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_upgrade_ce_map.py python -m unittest discover -s tools/level -p test_pack_local_map.py Tests cover exact source vertices/diagonal, stale terrain/water/settings, modified capture/EXR files, missing bakes, two independent baked surfaces with zero solver/modifier allocation, invalid paths, failure cleanup and stale callbacks and the explicit capture-component allowlist.
