MJOLNIR's screens (the lobby, map select, FIND GAMES, game settings, post-game and map download screens, and the HUD's chat, kill feed and scoreboard) are real Widget Blueprints, cooked in our Unreal project and loaded by the game from a container of ours (unreal/MJOLNIRMaterials/Scripts/build_mjolnir_ui.py). They don't have to be buttons injected into the shipped screens; mods/MJOLNIRLobby falls back to those only when our UI container is missing. Proven 2026-10-01 with WBP_MJOLNIRHello: The game loaded the cooked class from pakchunk984-MJOLNIRUI-Windows. Lua created it, added it to the viewport and called its Blueprint function SetMessage. A real mouse click on its button ran the widget's own OnClicked graph, which called MJ_Event("hello_clicked"). A Lua RegisterHook on MJ_Event received the call. No native delegate binding was needed for any of it.
Why widgets cook when meshes and components don't

The game runs 343's fork of UE 5.5.4. Our project (unreal/MJOLNIRMaterials) is stock UE 5.5. Cooked packages store properties unversioned, by position, so a class whose property layout differs in the fork reads garbage. That is why a stock cook of scene components, static meshes or materials is misread (ue_mesh_write.md, re/fork_renderer.md). tools/ue/cook.ps1 now re-encodes each staged container's materials (and, with -Classes, other classes such as StaticMesh) in the game's layout by property name (mjolnir ue retarget --rewrite, crates/ue-asset/src/retarget.rs). The widget classes listed as identical below need none of it. Comparing the fork's layouts (defs/ue/Meteorite-2607-CU3.usmap) with stock headers, 2026-10-01: Identical to stock: Widget, UserWidget, WidgetTree, WidgetAnimation, WidgetBlueprintGeneratedClass TextBlock, Button, EditableText, EditableTextBox, Image, Border ScrollBox, ListView, the box slots, CanvasPanelSlot CommonActivatableWidget, CommonUserWidget Different, so never cook them: CommonButtonBase (adds bSetIsSelectedWhenClicked) CommonTextBlock (adds TextScalingCategory) SceneComponent and PrimitiveComponent, so no components in a widget
Why widgets cook when meshes and components don't

Re-checked 2026-10-17 against defs/ue/UE-5.5-stock.usmap, also identical: Overlay/OverlaySlot, SizeBox/SizeBoxSlot, ScaleBox, Spacer, SlateBrush with SlateBrushOutlineSettings (so rounded-box brushes cook), SlateFontInfo, WidgetTransform, Texture/Texture2D (so our own UI textures cook; the kill feed's glyphs are in chunk 984). Re-check after a game update: re-dump the .usmap with UE4SS and compare again.

Our widgets can use the game's own pictures and fonts at runtime, without copying them: A texture or material: KismetSystemLibrary:LoadAsset_Blocking on Conv_SoftObjPathToSoftObjRef(MakeSoftObjectPath(path)), then Image:SetBrushFromTexture or SetBrushFromMaterial. The HUD's weapon silhouettes are channel-packed masks, drawn through the game's own icon material: SetBrushFromMaterial(MI_HUDCradleIcon_FragGrenade), GetDynamicMaterial(), SetTextureParameterValue("InputTexture", tex). The image's colour multiplies the material's cyan; it cannot recolour it. A font: /Game/Fonts/Font_Oxanium (the menus' face) and Font_NormativePro, through TextBlock:SetFont({ FontObject = font, TypefaceFontName = FName("Bold"), Size = block.Font.Size, ... }). Oxanium has Light ... ExtraBold; Normative Pro Light, Regular, Medium, Bold and their italics. Keep what you find. StaticFindObject by path costs ~2 ms in UE4SS (19 ms the first call), so a lookup per use adds up: the kill feed's first build did half a dozen per line and held the game thread 50-80 ms on every kill (two PCs, 2026-10-17). Keep the handle, check it with IsValid() before each use (an object no engine object holds may be collected), and find it again only when that fails.

The UI Builder plugin (Plugins/MjolnirUIBuilder, editor only) does what Python can't: create_widget_blueprint add_widget: a tree widget made a variable, returned so Python can set its properties and slot. add_string_function: a function taking one String. It is empty (an event for Lua to hook) or sets a text block. bind_event_to_function: a widget's delegate, such as a Button's OnClicked, calls a function with a fixed argument. compile_widget The graphs it places use only engine functions (Conv_StringToText, TextBlock.SetText), so the cooked widget never references the plugin. # once, and after changing the plugin (a short -Package path: the default # scratch path is past MAX_PATH) & "C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.5\Engine\Build\BatchFiles\RunUAT.bat" BuildPlugin -Plugin="$PWD\unreal\MJOLNIRMaterials\Plugins\MjolnirUIBuilder\MjolnirUIBuilder.uplugin" -Package="C:\mjb\MjolnirUIBuilderBuild" -TargetPlatforms=Win64 -Rocket Copy-Item C:\mjb\MjolnirUIBuilderBuild\Binaries unreal\MJOLNIRMaterials\Plugins\MjolnirUIBuilder -Recurse -Force powershell -File tools/ue/editor_cmd.ps1 -Script Scripts/build_mjolnir_ui.py powershell -File tools/ue/cook.ps1 # also writes pakchunk984-Windows PAL_MJOLNIR_UI puts /Game/MJOLNIR/UI in chunk 984. Install the staged pakchunk984-Windows.{utoc,ucas,pak} as pakchunk984-MJOLNIRUI-Windows.*.

The MJOLNIR CORE emblem at the top right of every menu screen (screen_header) is Art/Brand/Logo.png, made from the hub's own logo by python tools/ue/brand_logo.py (cropped, centred, 256 pixels). It is imported with mips, since 720p draws it at about a third of that. It sits in LogoButton, whose click finish_screen binds to MJ_Event("logo") on every menu screen. The Forge HUD (WBP_MJOLNIRForge, forge.md) is built by the same script but lives in /Game/MJOLNIR/ForgeUI with its own glyphs (Art/ForgeIcons, T_MJForge_*) and its own label, PAL_MJOLNIR_ForgeUI, which puts it in chunk 980. It ships as pakchunk980-MJOLNIRFORGEUI-Windows beside the CE runtime's monitor fix, without touching chunk 984. Before installing, list the container: find_files <StagedBuilds Paks dir> MJOLNIR/UI EngineFonts. It must hold our widgets only. The engine assets a widget imports (Roboto) cook into chunk 0, which we don't ship, so the import resolves to the game's own copy.
Driving it from Lua › Class lifetime during map travel

UE4SS build c838a8ac can retain a reflected-property pointer after a UI Blueprint class is collected. A 2026-11-01 crash while loading Forge Canvas after Crossline and the lobby failed in FFieldClassVariant::GetFName: the Lua lookup key was Watermark, and the cached field's class pointer was invalid. The HUD had already created a new kill-feed widget; checking that widget with IsValid() does not repair stale reflection metadata. HUD, Lobby, Forge and the Level Loader (its sound mixer) therefore run their loaded classes through Scripts/class_lifetime.lua before creating a visible widget. An explicit allowlist permits one named, inactive instance per UI class in /Engine/Transient, constructed with RF_Transient and internal RootSet. These instances retain the classes for the process lifetime without a world, player controller or viewport. They are reused across script reloads; failed retention delays UI creation and logs the reason. Start a fresh game process when installing this mitigation, because it cannot repair an already stale UE4SS cache. The four self-contained helper copies must remain identical.
Driving it from Lua › Class lifetime during map travel

The reserved MJOLNIR_UI_ClassPin_ instances are not screens: UI.liveWidget and Forge's chat lookup exclude them. Any new widget enumeration must also exclude class defaults and pins, and require the appropriate active or in-viewport state. tools/tests/test_ui_class_lifetime.lua covers class retention, map-widget release, reload reuse, failures and discovery filtering. UE4SS's LoadAsset only finds what the game's asset registry lists. Load through a soft class path instead: local ksl = StaticFindObject("/Script/Engine.Default__KismetSystemLibrary") local cls = ksl:LoadClassAsset_Blocking(ksl:Conv_SoftClassPathToSoftClassRef( ksl:MakeSoftClassPath("/Game/MJOLNIR/UI/WBP_MJOLNIRHello.WBP_MJOLNIRHello_C"))) local wbl = StaticFindObject("/Script/UMG.Default__WidgetBlueprintLibrary") local w = wbl:Create(pc, cls, pc) w:AddToViewport(50) w:SetMessage("hello") -- a Blueprint function, called with a Lua string RegisterHook("/Game/MJOLNIR/UI/WBP_MJOLNIRHello.WBP_MJOLNIRHello_C:MJ_Event", function(self, name) print(name:get():ToString()) end) w:SetVisibility(1) -- Collapsed; never RemoveFromParent (it hung the game once)
Driving it from Lua › Class lifetime during map travel

Widgets are variables, so Lua reaches them by name (w.Ok, w.Message). PlayerController:SetMouseLocation places the cursor in viewport pixels (3840×2160 here), which is how the click was tested. Text input: chat's ChatInput is an EditableTextBox that Lua focuses (SetKeyboardFocus); a UE4SS RegisterKeyBind on ENTER reads it with GetText(), so no delegate binding is needed. Keys the box does not use bubble up to the game viewport, which feeds the simulation, so while the box is open the game is in UI-only input (SetInputMode_UIOnlyEx; mods/MJOLNIRHud/Scripts/chat.lua). A delegate with parameters binds like OnClicked: the map select's search box sends MJ_Event("search") from OnTextChanged and MJ_Event("searched") from OnTextCommitted (bind_event_to_function drops the parameters), and Lua reads GetText(). On a menu screen the frontend has no simulation to feed, so the box needs no input mode of its own; Escape still pops the screen while it has focus.
Screens on the game's menu stack

A widget whose parent is CommonActivatableWidget (the project enables CommonUI for it) can be pushed onto the game's own menu stack with WBP_MeteoriteUILayout_C.ContentStack:BP_AddWidget(cls). That gives it everything a shipped screen has: the screen beneath is hidden; Back (Escape, the gamepad's B) pops it, with bIsBackHandler set on the class defaults (finish_screen); DeactivateWidget() pops it from Lua. WBP_MJOLNIRLobby, WBP_MJOLNIRMapSelect, WBP_MJOLNIRFindGames, WBP_MJOLNIRGameSettings, WBP_MJOLNIRPostGame and WBP_MJOLNIRMapDownload work this way (multiplayer_menu.md). Their buttons use stock Button styling (tinted brushes): the game's own CommonUI buttons can't be cooked. The main menu's MULTIPLAYER button is not one of ours: it is the shipped WBP_MainMenu with a button added, rewritten into chunk 985 (pakchunk985-MJOLNIRMENU_P, mjolnir ue menu-button). MJOLNIRLobby injects a button only when that container is missing.

Status: 2026-10-21, Steam build 19905945. Every layout below was read off the installed files (halo2/h2_maps_win64_dx11): the container on lockout.map, coagulation.map, shared.map and mainmenu.map, the tag layouts on Lockout and shared.map, the scenario layout on all 24 multiplayer maps. The reader is crates/blam-cache (h2::cache, h2::collision, h2::geometry, h2::bitmap); public tools (Assembly's Halo2MCC plugins, TagTool's Gen2 definitions, Reclaimer) agree except where noted. How a map is converted is in h2_map_conversion.md.

Every MCC title writes cache version 13 at offset 4. The game is the low byte of the u32 at 0x0C, and the header ends with foot four bytes before its own size (blam_cache::detect, mjolnir cache info): game 0x0C header name scenario path Halo 1 0 0x800 0x20 (none) Halo 2 0x201 0x380 0xB0 0xD0 Halo 3 0x202 0x4000 0xC0 0xE0 Halo 4 0x203 0x1E000 0xB8 0xD8 Halo 2 Anniversary MP (groundhog) 0x204 0x1E000 0xB8 0xD8 Halo: Reach 0x206 0xA000 0xC0 0xE0 The classic builds keep their versions: Halo 1 Xbox 5, PC 7, Custom Edition 609 (what the stock-map conversions read, through halo2ue), Halo 2 Xbox and Vista 8. MCC's Halo 1 maps (version 13, tag memory at 0x50000000) are not read by halo2ue yet.

The file is the 0x380-byte header, then zlib chunks of at most 0x40000 bytes each (zlib header 28 15, a 1 KiB window). The chunk table is at the offset the header gives at 0x310, with the count at 0x314: per chunk, u32 compressed size and u32 file offset. The decompressed image is the header followed by the chunks back to back; its length is the header's u32 at 0x08, and every offset below is into it. offset field 0x10 tag index offset 0x14 tag buffer size (index + tag data) 0x20 / 0x24 / 0x2C tag name count / name buffer / name offset table (u32, -1 none) 0x30 / 0x34 / 0x38 / 0x3C string id count / buffer / size / offset table 0xB0 map name (32) 0xD0 scenario path (256) 0x2D0 virtual base: 0x3200000 for a scenario map, 0 for shared.map and mainmenu.map 0x2D4 / 0x2D8 index size / tag data size 0x2F0 header size (0x380), where the chunks start 0x308 / 0x310 / 0x314 chunk size / chunk table offset / chunk count 0x37C foot Addresses. A tag address a is at image offset a - base(0x2D0) + index offset(0x10); tag data starts at the index offset plus the index size. The sbsp and ltmp are ordinary tags (the scenario's structure BSP entries keep offset/size/address 0, unlike Xbox and Vista).

Tag index at 0x10: u32 group table offset (relative, 0x20), group count, tag table offset (relative), scenario datum, globals datum, checksum, tag count, tags. Group entries are 12 bytes (fourcc, parent, grandparent); tag entries 16 (fourcc, datum, address, size). datum & 0xFFFF is the index. A scenario map holds only its own tags (Lockout: 224 of 23,131 index entries); an entry with address 0 or -1 is in shared.map, found there by name (the same index holds the same tag in both, but mainmenu.map's address range overlaps shared.map's, so addresses never decide the file). Fields. A tag block is {u32 count, u32 address}, a tag reference {u32 fourcc, u32 datum}, a data reference {u32 size, u32 address}, a string id 4 bytes: index in the low 24 bits, length in the top 8.

Geometry lives outside the tags. A geometry block info is u32 offset, u32 size, u32 section struct size, u32 resource size, then a resources block. The offset's top two bits pick the file (0 the tag's own, 1 mainmenu.map, 2 shared.map, 3 single_player_shared.map); the low 30 are an offset into that file's decompressed image. The block is blkh, u32 resource size, the section struct, rsrc, the resources, blkf. A resource entry (16 bytes) is u8 type (0 a tag block, 1 tag data, 2 a vertex buffer), u8, u16 the section field it fills, u16, i16 element size or vertex buffer index, u32 size, u32 offset from the rsrc marker. The section struct (0x48 for BSP sections, 0x78 for render models): parts at 0x00 (72 bytes: i16 type, u16 flags (bit 3 triangle list), i16 material, i16 first index, i16 index count, ...), subparts 0x08, u16 indices 0x20, vertex buffer descriptors 0x38 (32 bytes: vertex type, stride). MCC's vertex types, all floats: 0x01 position (12), 0x17 texture coordinate (8), 0x19 normal, binormal, tangent (36), 0x1D lightmap coordinate (8), 0x2F incident light direction (12). BSP sections are triangle lists winding counter-clockwise about their normals (7,048 of Lockout's 7,049); render models are strips.

Bitmaps are all in textures.dat. A bitm element (168 bytes on MCC, 116 on Xbox and Vista) has i16 width and height at 0x04, type at 0x0A (0 2D, 1 3D, 2 cube), format at 0x0C (0 A8, 1 Y8, 2 AY8, 3 A8Y8, 6 R5G6B5, 8 A1R5G5B5, 9 A4R4G4B4, 10 X8R8G8B8, 11 A8R8G8B8, 14 DXT1, 15 DXT3, 16 DXT5, 22 V8U8, 23 G8B8), mipmap count at 0x14, the entry's offset in textures.dat at 0x38 and its size at 0x50. An entry is i32 n, i32 sizes[n], then the chunks: positive sizes are zlib, negative ones stored. They concatenate to every level from the largest down, unswizzled: Lockout's 512 x 256 X8R8G8B8 sky with nine mipmaps is 699,052 bytes, the levels down to 1 x 1.

scnr (base 0x3E0): skies 0x08, scenery 0x50 / palette 0x58, vehicles 0x70, weapons 0x90, player starts 0x100 (0x34: position, facing, i16 team, i16 BSP, four i16 game types), netgame flags 0x118 (0x20: position, facing, i16 type, i16 team, i16 identifier, flags), netgame equipment 0x120 (0x90: flags (bit 0 levitate), four game types, i16 team, i16 spawn time at 0x0E, classification 0x14, position 0x40, yaw/pitch/roll 0x4C, item or vehicle collection reference 0x58), structure BSPs 0x210 (0x44: sbsp reference 0x10, ltmp 0x18), crates 0x328 / palette 0x330. Placements share a 0x34-byte header (palette index, name index, flags, position 0x08, yaw/pitch/roll 0x14, scale 0x20, 0 meaning 1). Scenery +0x5A is the multiplayer game types it appears in (bit 1 Slayer; 0 all). Decals 0x138 (0x10: i16 palette index, i8 yaw, i8 pitch, position 0x04) / palette 0x140 (deca references); a deca: u16 flags, u16 type (0 scratch, 1 splatter, 2 burn, 3 painted sign), u16 layer 0x04 (1 lit alpha blend: every decal on Zanzibar), radius 0x10 (world units), bitmap 0x88.

Netgame flag types: 0 CTF flag spawn, 1 CTF flag return, 2 assault bomb spawn, 3 assault bomb return, 4 oddball, 5 unused, 6 race checkpoint, 7 teleporter source, 8 teleporter destination (paired by identifier), 9 headhunter bin, 10 territory, 11-18 King of the Hill hills 0-7 (each hill a ring of about eight flags). Game types: 0 none, 1 CTF, 2 Slayer, 3 Oddball, 4 KotH, 5 Race, 6 Headhunter, 7 Juggernaut, 8 Territories, 12 all, 13 all but CTF, 14 all but CTF and Race. sbsp (base 0x23C): collision materials 0x0C (0x14: old shader ref, i16 global material index, i16 conveyor surface, shader ref at 0x0C), collision BSP 0x14 (0x40), clusters 0x9C (0xB0: vertex count at 0x00, geometry block info at 0x28), materials 0xA4 (0x20: old shader ref, shader ref at 0x08), instanced geometry definitions 0x138 (0xC8: vertex count 0x00, geometry block info 0x28, bounding sphere 0x60, collision BSP 0x70), instances 0x140 (0x58: scale, forward, left, up, position; i16 definition 0x34; name 0x50).

Collision BSP (sbsp, instanced geometry, coll): eight blocks. 3D nodes 8 bytes (u16 plane, u24 back, u24 front; bit 23 leaf, 0xFFFFFF none); planes 16; leaves 4 (u8 flags, u8 2D reference count, u16 first, 0xFFFF none: Zanzibar has such leaves); 2D references 4 (i16 plane, sign = flipped; i16 node, sign = surface); 2D nodes 16 (line, i16 left, i16 right); surfaces 8 (u16 plane, 0x8000 = flipped; u16 first edge; u8 flags; u8 breakable, 255 none; u16 material, 65535 none); edges 12 (six u16); vertices 16. Lockout's 3,162 surfaces are 3- to 8-sided polygons lying within 2e-4 wu of their planes.

ltmp: lightmap groups at 0x80 (0x68): bitmap group reference 0x18, cluster render info 0x28 and instance render info 0x48 (4 bytes: i16 bitmap index, -1 for a vertex-lit instance), geometry buckets 0x40 (0x38: u16 flags, bit 0 incident direction, bit 1 colour; the raw block offset at 0x0C, section struct size 0x14 (8), resources block 0x1C), instance bucket refs 0x50 (12 bytes: i16 flags, i16 bucket, a block of i16 section offsets: the instance's first vertex in the bucket). A bucket's raw block is laid out as a geometry section's, with vertex buffers of type 0x2F (12 bytes: the incident light direction, in world space) and, for vertex-lit geometry, 0x2E (u8 R, G, B, 0: the light's colour, in the pages' units, half intensity). Definition vertex k of instance i is bucket vertex offset + k; every instance has a ref, so every instance's incident directions come from its bucket (no instanced geometry definition carries a 0x2F buffer). Checked on all 24 maps' 2,341 instances. Lockout's 65 pages are A8R8G8B8.

Nodes (mode +0x48, 0x60 bytes): string id name, i16 parent, first child, next sibling, import index; translation in the parent's space at 0x0C; rotation quaternion (i, j, k, w) at 0x18, the node's forward rotation; inverse forward, left, up and position at 0x2C, 0x38, 0x44, 0x50. A node's object transform is its parent's composed with its own (rotate, then translate), parents first. A collision model's BSP vertices are in its node's space (the coll node list matches the mode's by index); a render section's vertices are already in object space, whatever their node (rigid: section +0x2C; rigid boned and skinned: node map indices and weights after each vertex's position), so the node transforms serve animation only. Checked on Zanzibar's crane and hinged lights, where the posed collision lands on the mesh within 1 cm.

shad: template (stem) 0x00, global material name 0x08, runtime properties 0x0C (0x50: diffuse map 0x00), postprocess definition 0x20 (0x7C: bitmaps at 0x04, 12 bytes each (datum, submap, log size); pixel constants at 0x0C, 4 bytes each as D3DCOLOR (B, G, R, A); vertex constants at 0x14, float4: for the opaque templates the maps' u and v scales, for the transparent ones a 2 x 4 texture transform per map (u row, v row: scale in .x/.y, offset in .w); overlays at 0x3C (0x14: f32 period at 8, the function at 0xC as {size, address}: byte 0 type, 0 identity, the value at t = 0 at +4 and at t = period at +8); overlay refs at 0x44 (i16 overlay, i16 transform type: 4 translation u, 5 translation v); animated parameters at 0x4C (u16: count in the top 7 bits, first in the low 9, into the overlay refs); animated parameter refs at 0x54 (u16 descriptor, u8, i8 parameter; a descriptor below 0x100 is the bitmap slot)). MCC keeps no parameter names; each template's bitmap slots come in its own order (the table is h2::render::template). The pixel math is in the compiled DXBC pixel shaders inside the spas tags (postprocess definitions 0x1C, implementation +0x132, three data refs);

read back for the glass, plasma and "two plus two" families: glass = base x albedo tint x base.a + cube(reflection) x environment tint x specular mask, both scaled by a facing/glancing tint (pixel constants 0 environment tint, 1 albedo tint; vertex constants 0 facing, 1 glancing), premultiplied blend; "two plus two" = the product of its three maps, colour and alpha, alpha blended, two-sided; plasma = two noise maps banded against each other through the mask's alpha, additive. The opaque templates draw an albedo pass (base x detail x 2, alpha base.a x detail.a; tex_bump_detail_blend blends its two details by the base's alpha, the second where it is high) and a lightmap pass: 2 x light x albedo, the light bent by the bump against the incident direction. The env templates' lightmap pass adds cube(reflection) x lerp(glancing, facing colour, N.V) x lerp(glancing, facing brightness, N.V) x albedo alpha x min(1, 0.753 (r + g + b) of the light); the two colours sit just before the first pair of pixel constants holding only alpha (the brightnesses). The cube's bitmap slot differs by template. tex_bump's lightmap pass has no specular term, and its specular-sphere pass has no implementation.

The alpha-test templates' lightmap_tex_detail_alpha_test pass discards where an alpha rounds to 0: the base map's for tex_bump_alpha_test, the bump map's for the single_pass variants (Zanzibar's foliage, whose colour maps are solid). plasma_one_channel_self_illumination (tex_bump_plasma_one_channel_illum, bitmap 3) adds red x band(alpha) x pixel constant 5 + green x 3 + blue x 4, the band peaking at pixel constant 2's alpha and sharpened twice by (2x - 1)^2. overlay draws 2 x base x detail x pixel constant 0 with D3D blend DESTCOLOR, SRCCOLOR (a double multiply; alpha unused) and a depth bias. water_edge_blend writes bitmap 0's alpha with colour writes masked to alpha (D3DRS_COLORWRITEENABLE 0x8): no colour. water_pool writes opaque lerp(frame copy at the screen position, reflection map (bitmap 1, a cube in water_pool_cube), fresnel), both offset by the ripple map's (bitmap 0) du/dv through vertex constant 0. waves (alpha blend) is min(1, bitmap 0 x (bitmap 1 + bitmap 2)) x bitmap 3 x vertex colour, alpha the same sum's x vertex alpha x pixel constant 0's alpha.

sky: render model 0x00, flags 0x10 (bit 0 fixed in world space, bit 2 casts light from below, bit 5 use clear colour), render model scale 0x14, indoor ambient 0x24, outdoor ambient 0x34, atmospheric fog 0x48 (0x18: colour, maximum density 0x0C, start 0x10, opaque 0x14), lights 0x78 (0x34: yaw 0x0C, pitch 0x10, radians, towards the sun as (cos p cos y, cos p sin y, sin p); radiosity block 0x2C (0x28: flags (bit 0 affects exteriors, bit 1 interiors, bit 2 direct light in the lightmaps, bit 3 indirect), colour 0x04, power 0x10, angular diameter 0x24)), clear colour 0xA0. Every multiplayer map has one light; Lockout's has no radiosity flags and its lightmaps' incident directions (yaw 78, pitch 48 degrees over flat ground) match the sky model's brightness, not the light.

Planar fog: sbsp fog planes at 0x64 (i16 scenario planar fog index, i16 material, plane i, j, k, d; at most one, horizontal, on the 24 maps); the scenario's planar fog palette at 0x348 (0x10: name, fog reference 0x04, i16 material); fog (0x60): flags 0x00 (bit 0 render only submerged geometry, bit 5 do not render unless submerged), priority 0x02, material 0x04 / 0x08, maximum density 0x0C, opaque distance 0x10, opaque depth 0x14 (world units), atmospheric-planar depth 0x18, eye offset scale 0x20, colour 0x24, patchy fog block 0x30 (0x34: colour, density range 0x18, distance range 0x20, minimum depth fraction 0x28, fpch 0x2C; Lockout's clouds, Dune's and Needle's water), background sound 0x38, sound environment 0x40. Eleven maps have a plane; Ascension's big_fog is density 1, distance 0, depth 18, (0.38, 0.41, 0.40) at z = -1.89, no patchy fog. Planar fog is drawn per surface by every opaque template's fog_planar pass (z-test equal over the lit surface); there is no fog-plane mesh or full-screen planar fog pass.

Shader animation (halo2.dll): an overlay's value is lo + (hi - lo) x clamp01(f) with lo and hi at +4 and +8 and x = time / period, wrapped to 0..1 except for periodic functions; f by byte 0: 0 identity (x), 1 constant (0), 2 transition (lerp(+0x14, +0x18, g(x)), g the curve at byte 2, 0 linear), 3 periodic (lerp(+0x1C, +0x20, P(x +0x14 + +0x18)), P the wave at byte 2, 6 slide = frac), 4 linear (x +0x24 + +0x28). Value records per texture slot hold uniform scale, scale u/v/w, translation u/v/w and rotation (turns); the constant writer (0x959380) builds the 2D affine rows as row 1 = (su cos, -su sin, 0, tu + 0.5 su ((1 - cos) + sin)), row 2 = (sv sin, sv cos, 0, tv + 0.5 sv ((1 - cos) - sin)): the translation is added. A constant descriptor: register bits 0-3, bank bit 4, mask bits 5-9 (14 and 15 the affine rows), texture slot bits 10-12; the template's remapping table names each slot's bitmap.

Machines (scnr +0xA8, 0x48 bytes: palette index 0x00, position 0x08, rotation 0x14, scale 0x20; power and position groups i16 0x34 / 0x36, device and machine flags 0x38 / 0x3C; palette +0xB0). The mach tag's device part: position transition at +0xC8 stored as a rate (1 / seconds; a time of 0 is stored as 900), machine type u16 +0x11C (0 door, 1 platform, 2 gear). A gear's position runs 0 to 1 over its transition time and starts again, from the map's load (Ascension's scenario has no scripts or device groups). The model's animation graph (jmad, hlmt +0x10): nodes 0x0C (0x20), sound refs 0x14 (0xC), animations 0x2C (0x60: name 0x00, type u8 0x10, node count u8 0x13, frame count i16 0x14, frame data dataref 0x28, static data size i16 0x36, sound events 0x48 (8 bytes: sound ref, frame, marker)). The frame data sits in the tag: the static codec block, then the animated one. Keyframe codecs 4-7 (byte, word, reverse byte, reverse word frame indices): u8 codec, u8 rotating / sliding / scaling node counts, error and rate floats, eight u32 offsets from 0x0C (translation and scale frame info, rotation / translation / scale keyframe indices, rotation / translation / scale data), the rotating nodes' frame info from 0x30 (count in the low 12 bits, first key in the high 20); a rotation key is i16 (i, j, k, w) / 32767, the node's turn from its default pose;

a translation key three floats in world units. Ascension's antenna (codec 6, 21 frames over 40 s) turns about +Z: 0, +20 (held 6-10 s), -30 (22-26 s), +5 (32-36 s), 0. Codec 3 stores every frame (halo2.dll's codec table, 0xe12f60): a 0x20-byte header (u8 codec, u8 rotating / sliding / scaling node counts, error and rate floats, translation and scale data offsets 0x0C / 0x10, per-node strides 0x14 / 0x18 / 0x1C), then each rotating node's frames as i16 (i, j, k, w) / 32767 from 0x20. Zanzibar's big wheel and blades (30 s) and flywheels (5 s) turn a full circle about +Y in five frames, 90 degrees each; Foundation's fans (30 s) about -Z. The engine lerps the four components between frames and renormalizes (81.6 to 94.9 degrees a frame between 90-degree keys). A sound event fires as the animation passes its frame, at frame / (frames - of the transition time: the antenna's 12 (0 slow_move2, 2 antenna1, 3 antenna1_stop, 5 slow_move, 6 antenna2, ...) are 2 s apart.

Sound (samples outside the maps, in sounds_neutral.dat, sounds_remastered.dat and sounds_<language>.dat beside them, headerless). snd! (0x1C): flags u16 0x00 (0x0800 remastered only), class u8 0x02, codec index i8 0x03, playback index i16 0x06, first pitch range i16 0x08, pitch range count i8 0x0A, maximum play time i32 0x10 (ms). Its indices are into the ugh! (sound gestalt) of the cache file holding the snd!: codecs 0x00 (3 bytes: rate 0 22050, 1 44100, 2 32000, 3 48000; encoding 0 mono, 1 stereo, 3 quad; compression 0 big-endian PCM, 1 Xbox ADPCM, 3 little-endian PCM, 4 WMA (the menu music only), 5 Opus), playback 0x08 (0x38: minimum and maximum distance 0x00 / 0x04 in world units, gain dB 0x10, random pitch bounds i16 x 2 in cents 0x18), pitch ranges 0x28 (0x0C: first permutation i16 0x08, count 0x0A), permutations 0x30 (0x10: name, skip, gain, then per language at 0x08 {u32 PCM bytes, i16 first chunk, i16 chunk count}), permutation chunks 0x60 (one block per language; 0x10 each: i32 offset in the .dat, u32 size in the low 24 bits, i32 PCM bytes). A remastered-only sound is in sounds_remastered.dat, one of a class the sound classes tag marks multilingual (sound\sound_classes, 0x78 each, internal flag bit 7 at 0x08: classes 19, 44-48, 53) in sounds_<language>.dat, the rest in sounds_neutral.dat; that held for every chunk of shared, Ascension and Lockout.

An Opus chunk is i16 length repeated, the last length negative; the packets are CELT fullband 5 ms (0xE8 mono, 0xEC stereo), and a permutation's chunks are one stream, its first packet 240 samples of silence the tag counts. Xbox ADPCM is CE's 36-byte block a channel, 65 samples. Every Opus decode of the two maps' 677 looping permutations matched its tag's byte count. lsnd (0x34): distance bounds 0x14, tracks 0x24 (0x58: gain dB 0x08, fade in / out 0x0C / 0x10, in / loop / out / alternate loop / alternate out references 0x14 / 0x1C / 0x24 / 0x2C / 0x34, output effect i16 0x3C, 1 front speakers, 2 rear), detail sounds 0x2C (0x34: sound 0x04, random period 0x0C, yaw / pitch / distance bounds 0x1C / 0x24 / 0x2C). Sound scenery: scnr 0xD8 (0x50: palette index 0x00, position 0x08, rotation 0x14, distance override 0x3C, cone override 0x44), palette 0xE0 (0x28, ssce at 0x00). An object's attachments (+0x94 on every object tag, 0x18: reference 0x00, marker 0x08, primary scale function 0x10) carry its loops. The BSP's background sound: sbsp clusters 0x9C (0xB0: background sound i16 0x72, sound environment i16 0x74) into the palettes at 0xD4 (0x64, lsnd 0x20) and 0xDC (0x48, snde 0x20).

Cube maps (bitm type 2) are stored mip-major, the six faces of each level together in the order +X, +Y, -X, -Y, +Z, -Z on Halo's axes, no face flipped (every seam matched across the Lockout and Forerunner cubes). mode (MCC): compression info 0x14 (0x38: seven ranges, position x, y, z, texture u, v, secondary u, v), regions 0x1C (0x10: name, permutations at 0x08, 16 bytes: name, L1-L6 section indices), sections 0x24 (0x5C: u32, then the section info from 0x04: vertex count 0x04, compression flags 0x1A (bit 0 position, bit 1 texture coordinate), its own compression info 0x1C, geometry block info 0x38), nodes 0x48, materials 0x60 (0x20: shader ref at 0x08). A compressed value is stored in -1..1 across its range (min + (v + 1) / 2 * (max - min)): Lockout's sky spans hundreds of world units from vertices within -1..1. BSP clusters and instanced geometry carry no ranges. hlmt: render model 0x00, collision model 0x08. Objects: model at 0x34. sky: render model 0x00. itmc / vehc: permutations 0x00 (0x10: weight, item reference, variant). coll: regions 0x1C (0x0C: permutations at 0x04, 0x14 each: BSPs at 0x04, 0x44 each: i16 node, then the collision BSP).

Every shader on the Halo 2 multiplayer maps (MCC's h2_maps_win64_dx11, the 25 .map files besides shared and mainmenu), grouped by template. For each template the census compares what Halo 2 draws (the passes its template runs) with what mjolnir cache stage makes of it, and weights it by the triangles that use it in the staged BSPs and placed models. Run on 2026-11-10, with specular read from each template's passes. How to run it again: cargo run --release -p blam-cache --example h2_shader_census -- "" /shader_census.json mjolnir cache stage .map --out /staged/ # each map python tools/level/h2_shader_census.py

141 templates in all; 97 are used by the maps themselves and 44 only by shared.map (weapons, characters, vehicles, effects, which the conversion does not draw from Halo 2). 88 templates reach a converted map, over 692,409 triangles. tex_bump alone is 43% of them; the top ten templates are 79%. Every drawn template but four has a branch of its own in crates/blam-cache/src/h2/render.rs. The four on the default branch (diffuse map, opaque) are 0.3% of triangles: prt_simple, plasma_mask_offset, tex_env_3_channel_illum and roadsign_glass_newmombasa. Specular: 25 templates, 61% of all triangles, shine as in Halo 2 (the base map's alpha as the mask); the env, overlay and no-specular templates draw the specular pass but their lightmap pass leaves no mask, so they never shine in Halo 2 either (below). Twelve templates the maps use are never drawn, among them every decorator (grass, rubble, debris and blast marks on 11 maps) and the open water of Headlong, Dune, Needle and Zanzibar. The census measures coverage, not likeness. "Handled" means a template has a branch that reads its maps and constants as its compiled shaders use them; only Lockout, Ascension, Zanzibar and Turf have been compared in game. Triangle share is not screen share: a sky dome or a sea is few triangles and much of the picture.

Nearly every opaque template draws Halo 2's default_light_combined_tangentspace_specular_sphere pass, but it only shows where the template's lightmap pass wrote a mask into the frame's alpha (docs/h2_map_conversion.md, Specular). The census reads each template's passes from its postprocess definition (the earlier byte scan missed every other pass) and takes a template as specular where the specular pass has its colours (vertex registers 10 and 11) and every lightmap pass writes the base alpha mask: specular (25 templates, 61% of triangles): tex_bump, the detail blends and keeps, two and three detail, tex_bump_illum and its variants, tex_bump_shiny, tex_bump_one_change_color and four_change_color, tex_alpha_test, tex_illum, tex_detail_blend, the tiling and honor guard variants; no specular in Halo 2 (alpha 0): every env lightmap pass (tex_bump_env*, tex_env), tex_bump_detail_overlay and tex_bump_illum_no_specular; not converted: the alpha-tested templates whose cut-out is staged in the base alpha (tex_bump_alpha_test_single_pass and the clamped and env alpha tests). Their lightmap passes write other terms; read as the staged alpha, a frond would shine all over.

A knowledge base on how the game's simulation works: what each subsystem does, which tag fields drive it, where its code lives in the simulation DLL, and how we know. It is written for two readers: a person who wants to understand or change something, and an AI agent that has to get a fact right without rediscovering it. The game is Halo: Campaign Evolved. Its rules run in a Blam simulation (HaloSimulation_tag_release.dll, a descendant of the Reach engine that reads Halo 1 content), and Unreal Engine draws the result. Most "how does the game decide X" questions are questions about the simulation and the tags it reads.

Every article follows the same shape, so a fact is always in the same place: Header table: the subsystem, its tag data, its code, our code and tools, and its status. The idea in one paragraph. The tag data: blocks, fields, sizes, limits, and what shipped maps actually put there. How the simulation uses it: a build pin, a code map (address, role, evidence), and the behaviour as pseudocode in our own words. What a writer must get right: the rules a tool has to follow. Our implementation and how to run it. Open questions, each with why it matters and how to settle it. History. Every claim carries an evidence label: Label Meaning traced Read from the simulation's code in a disassembler. data Measured on shipped tags, with a tool anyone can run again. live Seen in the running game. inferred Fits everything else, but has not been tested on its own. Addresses are RVAs in one named build. Add the image base (0x180000000) for Ghidra. An address without a build is worth nothing, because the game updates; each article's build pin says which file it means, and build_lock.md says which build is current. How to research and verify has the method: the Ghidra setup, how to anchor a function so it can be found again, how to census shipped data, and what may and may not be committed.

Part of the engine reference. This page covers the ground an AI can walk: the tag data that describes it, the simulation code that reads it, and the generator that writes it for maps that ship without any. Subsystem AI navigation over level geometry Tag data scenario > ai pathfinding data[bsp]; scenario_structure_bsp > instanced geometry instances[i].pathfinding policy Simulation code HaloSimulation_tag_release.dll, CU4 (build pin below) Our code crates/blam-sbsp/src/pathfinding.rs, crates/blam-sbsp/src/navmesh.rs Tools pf_stats, pf_objects, pf_roundtrip, pf_generate, pf_dump, pf_where (crates/blam-sbsp/examples/) Status Lookup traced and matched to shipped data. Generator built and checked offline. Generated instance pathfinding has not run in the game yet. Every claim carries one of four labels, defined in how to research and verify: [traced] read from the simulation's code, [data] measured on shipped tags, [live] seen in the running game, [inferred] a reading that fits the rest and has not been tested on its own.

The walkable ground of a BSP is cut into sectors: flat-ish polygons, each walkable everywhere inside. Sectors meet along links, which are shared edges. A path is a chain of sectors, crossed link by link. To know which sector an AI is in, the simulation does not search the polygons. It takes the collision surface the AI is standing on and looks that surface up in a table of refs, one per collision surface, which names the sector directly. So the pathfinding data is tied to the collision geometry surface by surface, and any tool that changes collision must rebuild it.

All of it sits in one element of the scenario's ai pathfinding data block per structure BSP (148 bytes; scenario_structure_bsp has a block of the same layout, pathfinding data, which shipped maps leave to the scenario). Indices are 16-bit and unsigned, with 0xFFFF for none [data]: A30's largest BSP has 59,826 links and link indices up to 59,356.

The tag data › Sectors and links are winged edges

A link is an edge that runs vertex 1 -> vertex 2 with its left sector on the left. forward link is the next edge around the left sector, reverse link the next around the right one. To walk a sector's ring, start at its first link and take forward wherever the sector is the link's left, else reverse, until the first link comes round again. Corners are vertex 1 when the sector is on the left, vertex 2 when it is on the right. The tag data › Sectors and links are winged edges

Rings wind counter-clockwise seen from above. Sectors are not exactly flat and not exactly convex. A tolerance of about 0.2 wu from a plane covers 99% of shipped sectors. Shipped ground is in many disconnected pieces. One connected component is not a rule the engine enforces.

Bit names from the tag definition: sector walkable (0x1), sector breakable (0x2), sector mobile (0x4), sector bsp source (0x8), floor (0x10), ceiling (0x20), wall north/south/east/west (0x40 to 0x200), crouchable (0x400), aligned (0x800), sector step (0x1000), sector interior (0x2000), sector rail (0x4000), sector user (0x8000). In shipped data [data] a plain floor is 0x11 (walkable, floor). 0x15 adds mobile: B40 BSP 8 has 149 of those plus 17 step sectors (0x1045, 0x1085, 0x1105, 0x1205: walkable, mobile, one wall bit, step), and all of them carry mobile. They are the sectors on machines and scenery (the object refs whose object id names an object) [inferred].

sector link from collision edge (0x1), sector intersection link (0x2), bsp2d creation error (0x4), topology error (0x8), chain error (0x10), threshold (0x20), wall base (0x40), ledge (0x80), leanable (0x100), leanable low (0x200), leanable high (0x400), start corner (0x800), end corner (0x1000), seam (0x2000). How shipped links use them, counted by whether the link has a sector on both sides [data] (A30 BSP 3; B40 BSP 8 has the same pattern): Flag One-sided Two-sided none 28,491 6,498 threshold 0 12,668 intersection link 955 3 wall base (always with leanable) 7,696 0 ledge 3,111 0 topology error 729 0 So threshold marks only links between two sectors, and wall base and ledge only outer edges. What threshold means to the planner, and why most outer edges carry no flag at all, is not known. Our generator writes 0 between sectors and wall base or ledge on every outer edge; that has run live on converted maps (the bots lane, bots.md) [live].
The tag data › Hints and intersection links

Sectors on separate pieces of geometry share no edge, so the data joins them with an intersection link [data, live]: each sector keeps its own outer link along the seam, flagged intersection link, with a hint; the hint (type intersection link, data (joining link, 0, 0, 0)) names one two-sided link appended after all the others. It runs along the first sector's link (same vertices, same forward link) and carries the second sector's forward link as its reverse link; a sector's hint index heads a chain (next hint index) of exactly the hints of its own links. Other hint types exist in the tag definition (jump, climb, vault, mount, hoist, wall jump, breakable floor, rail, seam, door, anticipation, takeoff). B40 BSP 8 uses only intersection link; A30 BSP 3 has two jump link hints. None of the others has been studied.
The tag data › Refs: from a collision surface to a sector

A ref is a 32-bit value: Value Meaning 0 and up a sector index -1 no sector: an AI on this surface is nowhere 0x80000000 \ n go to bsp2d nodes[n]: this surface is split between sectors A node holds a 2D plane and two children, each a ref again. The walk goes left when n . p - d > 0, else right, until it reaches a value that is not a node [traced]. There are three ref tables, one per kind of thing an AI can stand on [traced]: The BSP's shell: the top-level bsp2d refs, indexed by the shell's collision surface. No shipped campaign BSP uses it (the count is 0 in all 13 scenarios) [data]; converted maps do [live]. The scenario's structure bsps[i].flags bit 0x8, no default structure pathfinding, must be clear for it to count. Instanced geometry: instanced geometry refs[instance] names an object refs element, and that element's bsps[0].bsp2d refs is indexed by the collision surface of the instance's definition. Scenario objects (machines, scenery): the object refs element whose object id matches the object, then the bsps entry whose bsp reference matches the collision BSP that was hit.
The tag data › The instance policy gate

Each instanced geometry instances element of the structure BSP (148 bytes) has a pathfinding policy byte at +0x7c: cut-out (0), static (1), none (2). The simulation reads an instance's refs only when the policy is not none [traced]. With none it ignores the ref and casts a ray 4 wu straight down from the point to find something else to stand on. B40 BSP 8 agrees [data]: of 841 instances, 825 are none and 16 are static. Each static one has its own object ref (flags 0, one bsps entry, bsp reference 0, object id all -1) whose ref count equals its definition's surface count. The 825 none instances all carry ref index 0, which is never read. The other 14 object refs are machines and scenery. This is the trap for converted maps: a map can ship perfect sectors and still have every AI standing on nothing, because its instances say none. Pelican Warfare's 151 instances all do.

How the simulation finds a sector › The lookup, step by step

sector_of(contact): if contact has no instance and no object: refs = pathfinding.bsp2d_refs # shell frame = world else if contact is on an instance: if instance.pathfinding_policy == none: return whatever a ray 4 wu down finds object = pathfinding.instanced_geometry_refs[instance] refs = pathfinding.object_refs[object].bsps[0].bsp2d_refs frame = the instance's definition (local) else: # a scenario object entry = the object_refs element whose object id matches refs = the entry's bsps element whose bsp reference matches the hit BSP frame = the object's node that owns that BSP (local) ref = refs[contact.surface] if ref is a node: p = point taken into frame, then projected to 2D by the dominant axis of the surface's plane while ref is a node: node = pathfinding.bsp2d_nodes[ref & 0x7fffffff] ref = node.left if dot(node.n, p) - node.d > 0 else node.right return ref # a sector, or -1 For an instance the local frame is (p - position) / scale, then dotted with the instance's forward, left and up vectors. The projection is Halo's usual one: drop the axis the surface's plane normal is largest on, and order the other two by the sign of that component. Dominant normal axis Positive Negative x (y, z) (z, y) y (z, x) (x, z) z (x, y) (y, x) The table in the DLL is three rows of six 16-bit numbers, negative case first: 2 1 0 1 2 0, 0 2 1 2 0 1, 1 0 2 0 1 2.

So node planes live in the definition's local 2D frame, while vertices (what links name and paths are planned on) are world space. A generator that only ever gives a whole surface to one sector never needs a node, and never needs the local frame.
How the simulation finds a sector › What is never read

Only the two ref evaluators touch object refs, checked across every caller of the accessor and every user of the per-BSP table [traced]. They never read vertex offset or node_index. B40's vertex offset is not even its object's first vertex (object 0 uses vertices 0 to 103 and says 64) [data]. A generator can write the object's first vertex and 0.
How the simulation finds a sector › Finding these functions again after a game update

Addresses move with every build. Two anchors survive: The projection table. Search the DLL's read-only data for the 36 bytes 02 00 01 00 00 00 01 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 02 00 01 00 02 00 00 00 01 00 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 01 00 02 00. The functions that reference it include the ref evaluators. The instance element. The policy gate compares a byte at +0x7c of a 148-byte (0x94) element with 2, right after indexing a table by instance * 0x94. The function doing that is the table picker; its one caller chain leads up to the contact-to-sector function. Then confirm with data, not by eye: run pf_objects on B40 BSP 8 and check that the 16 static instances still own one object ref each.
What a writer must get right

Proved by pf_roundtrip, which empties B40 BSP 8's object refs and rebuilds all 30 of them (3,192 refs) to a file byte-identical to the original [data]: An object refs element owns a bsps block, which owns bsp2d refs. A new element needs its tag-block wrapper with those children. Writing the elements alone leaves a scenario that no longer parses: the element says one bsps entry and the block is not there. The order that works: write all elements with a donor element's wrapper (blam_tag::blockedit::element_with_wrapper), then per object replace the bsp2d refs leaf, then the bsps element. Per static instance: one object ref (flags 0, object id -1), one bsps entry (bsp reference 0), and exactly as many refs as the instance's definition has collision surfaces. Objects are per instance, not per definition: vertices are world space, so two instances of one definition need different sectors. Set the instance's policy byte to static in the structure BSP, or nothing is read. An earlier attempt at object refs crashed Blood Gulch 2 to 5 seconds after bots moved, even with every ref -1. The lookup above would have handled those values, and the writer of that attempt wrote elements without wrappers, so the missing child blocks are the likely cause [inferred].

blam_sbsp::pathfinding::Pathfinding::build turns a welded collision into sectors, one per walkable surface, with steps and crack seams (bots.md has its rules). That is enough for a converted map whose ground is a few thousand polygons in the shell. blam_sbsp::navmesh is the front end for ground that is instanced geometry: a triangle soup, unwelded and far too fine to be one sector each. Weld each instance's triangles by position. Instances stay separate objects, as in shipped data. Choose floors: not breakable, normal z at least 0.65 (about 49 degrees), accepted by the caller's filter. Merge floors that share an edge while the union stays near-convex in plan (dent), within plane_tolerance of one plane and walkable. Straighten the borders between merged floors: drop a corner that only two polygons touch when the border moves by no more than border in plan. Borders against walls and open edges only lose corners that are exactly in line. Build sectors from the result. Crack seams become intersection links between instances. Drop ground too small to matter (min_ground, in plan area, seams counted as connections) and build again. A rock's top costs links and serves nobody. Every sector is a union of whole source triangles, so every surface gets one plain ref and no nodes are written.

The generator › Sized on Pelican Warfare

Why exactly convex sectors do not fit: the terrain is an irregular triangle mesh, and a convex polygon made of whole triangles can only have a handful of corners before the mesh's edges zigzag out of it. Loosening the flatness tolerance changes almost nothing (the merge is blocked by shape about 200 times as often as by flatness). Two ways out: Accept borders that move by up to a metre or three between two walkable sectors (the dent and border settings above). An AI near a border may be told it is in the neighbouring sector. Shipped data is loose in the same way (one sector in twelve dents), but by how much the planner minds is untested. Cut triangles with bsp2d nodes, as Bungie does, so sector borders are free of the triangle mesh. The lookup side is traced (above); a node writer is not built.

Part of the engine reference. This is the method behind its articles: how a question about the simulation gets answered well enough to build on, and how the answer is written down so the next reader does not have to repeat the work.

A finding goes in an article as fact only when two different kinds of evidence agree. There are three kinds: Kind Label What it is good at How it misleads The simulation's code traced Says exactly what is read and what is not. Easy to misread a field offset or miss a second code path. Shipped tags data Shows what real, working content looks like, at scale. Shows what Bungie wrote, not what the engine requires. The running game live The only proof that something works. Slow, and a pass does not say why. A reading that only fits (one source, or none) is labelled inferred and kept out of designs until tested. The pathfinding work is the worked example (AI pathfinding). Shipped data alone suggested that each instanced-geometry definition has one pathfinding object. The code showed that the simulation ignores an instance's pathfinding unless a policy byte says static. Going back to the data with that rule explained every number: 16 static instances, 16 objects of their own, and 825 ignored instances that all point at object 0. Either source alone had led to a wrong design.

Setup. Ghidra 12 with the simulation DLL analysed, driven headless over MCP so a session can ask for decompiles and cross-references without the GUI: re/ghidra_mcp.md has the install and the commands. Start the headless server from PowerShell, not Git Bash, which rewrites the /Program path argument. Finding the code for a subsystem. The DLL has no symbols. What works: Start from data you can name. A tag block has a fixed element size, so its readers multiply an index by that size (* 0x94 for an instance element, * 0x18 for an object ref). Search for the constant near a plausible caller. Start from a script function. The HaloScript function table maps names to handlers (blam_script.md). A function such as ai_place leads straight into its subsystem. A handler that is the shared return-false stub tells you the feature is compiled out. Start from a constant table. Small lookup tables (an axis-projection table, a flag mask) are rare byte patterns and their cross-references are short lists. Follow the accessor. Most subsystems fetch their data through one small function. Once found, its callers are the whole subsystem. To prove a field is never read, check every caller, and every direct user of the table behind it. Pin the build. Record the file's size, SHA-256 and PE timestamp with any address. config/hce-build.lock.json lists them for the current build.

Leave anchors. For each function worth finding again, write down something that survives a rebuild: a byte pattern in data it references, a distinctive constant, or its position in a short caller chain. After a game update, find the function by its anchor, then re-run the data check before trusting it.

Write a small example program that reads the block through blam_tag and prints counts and distributions, and keep it in the crate (crates/blam-sbsp/examples/pf_stats.rs is the model). Three habits: Census before design. Run it over every shipped scenario, not one. Limits and rare cases only show at scale (the 16-bit link index was settled by one BSP with 59,826 links). Turn assumptions into checks. If you believe every ring closes, write the check and run it on shipped data. A check that fails on Bungie's data is your mistake, and a generator's output must pass the same checks. Round-trip before writing. Before a tool writes a block, make it read shipped data and write it back, and compare bytes (pf_roundtrip.rs). This catches container mistakes (missing child blocks, wrong wrappers) that no amount of reasoning about values will.

Use the smallest map that can show the effect, and a control: the same test with shipped data in place of ours. Read state, do not guess from behaviour: object and AI records can be read from the running game (game_state_reader.md). A crash seconds after an action usually means malformed data was read, not wrong values. Check the container before the contents. Solo first, then two or three game copies on one PC (multi_instance.md), then two PCs (two_pc_test.md). Each step finds different faults.

One article per subsystem, in the shape the engine reference describes. Facts go in the article; the session's story goes in the pull request. State behaviour in your own words, with pseudocode of your own. Decompiler output, and code or names from other people's decompilation projects, are never committed. Addresses, sizes, field offsets and measured numbers are facts and are fine. Say what is not known. Give every open question a way to settle it. Label every claim. If you later find an inferred claim was wrong, fix the article and note it in its history, so nobody builds on the old reading.

Since: CU4 (2026.08.11.1121610.2-Rel-i343-Meteorite-2607-CU4), 2026-08-18 Steam updates the game in place. The moment a patch lands, the previous build is gone, and with it any chance of asking "what did this update actually change" — CU4 nearly taught us that the hard way: the CU3 lock's hashes proved 17 container sets changed, but nobody had kept the CU3 bytes to say what changed inside them. Steam's depot history saved that run (see "Recovering an older build"), and it cannot be counted on to do so again. So every build gets kept from now on. The pipeline has three stages — snapshot, diff, publish — and ends in a blog post on mjolnircore.com/blog naming what the update changed. ---

A content-addressed archive of the install, taken after every update (and, ideally, before letting Steam patch a build you care about): python tools/game_snapshot.py --store D:/hce-snapshots snapshot \ "C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Halo Campaign Evolved" \ --lock-out config/hce-build.lock.json File bodies live under objects/ named by SHA-256; each build is a manifest of paths pointing into that pool. Unchanged files are stored once, so the first snapshot costs the full ~74 GiB and each later one only what the update touched. --lock-out stamps out the repo's build lock from the same hashing pass. The skip rules (ue4ss/, LogicMods/, .DepotDownloader/, dwmapi.dll, *_P override containers, *.log, *.dmp) are imported from build_lock.py, not duplicated — a snapshot and a lock taken from the same install must agree about what "the install" is. Other verbs: list, verify (store integrity), diff (file-level, --json for machines), and materialize, which rebuilds a build's file tree out of the pool with hardlinks: python tools/game_snapshot.py --store D:/hce-snapshots materialize CU3 D:/cu3 --only Meteorite/Content/Paks --only Meteorite/Content/Paks is the usual form — it is exactly what mjolnir --paks wants, so every existing tool runs unchanged against a dead build.

The store holds copyrighted game content. It is a private local backup of an install the user owns — it stays off the repository and off the network. What gets published is the diff: names, counts and field values, not game bytes.

Field-level comparison of two builds' shipped tags: mjolnir tagdiff --paks-a D:/cu3/Meteorite/Content/Paks \ --paks-b "C:...\Halo Campaign Evolved\Meteorite\Content\Paks" \ --label-a CU3 --label-b CU4 --json cu3-cu4.json Every tag is sorted into added, removed, changed or identical by payload bytes; changed tags are decoded on both sides and reported field by field — "jump velocity: 2.3 → 2.5", with block element counts for anything past the materialisation cap (--elements, default 256). The byte comparison is ground truth; the field list is what makes it readable. --json carries the full report for the blog post; the console shows --show differences per tag. File-level context (binaries, containers, third-party DLLs) comes from game_snapshot.py diff <old> <new>, which needs no materialisation at all. An update can add Wwise banks. Regenerate the list the hub and launcher refuse, then run pnpm sync in hub/ and ship both: cargo run -p ue-iostore --example pak_banks -- \ "C:...\Halo Campaign Evolved\Meteorite\Content\Paks" defs/hce/shipped_banks.json
3. Publish — blog/ and the update report

A game-update post is written into blog/ (see blog/README.md for the format) and ships with the next hub deploy. The repo skill game-update-report (.claude/skills/game-update-report/SKILL.md) walks an agent through the whole run — verify, snapshot, diff, re-verify the stack, draft the post — with the rule that makes the post trustworthy: every claim traces to a measurement the pipeline took this run. ---

A build that was never snapshotted is not necessarily lost: Steam's CDN keeps old depot manifests around, and tools/steam_depot_fetch.py wraps DepotDownloader to pull one into an install-shaped directory and ingest it straight into the store: python tools/steam_depot_fetch.py --list python tools/steam_depot_fetch.py 457322918737678760 --name cu3 --qr --store D:/hce-snapshots Login is interactive and stays between the user and Steam — --qr is a Steam Mobile scan, or --username makes DepotDownloader prompt for the password itself; nothing is typed into or stored by our tooling. The game is app 2806050; the content lives in depot 2806051 and the never-changed DigitalExtras in depot 4192200. Every manifest SteamDB had seen as of 2026-08-19; all three are downloaded, snapshotted and confirmed by their exe version stamps: Depot 2806051 manifest Shipped Build 5851394981381786761 2026-08-17 CU4 (2026.08.11.1121610.2) — snapshotted live 457322918737678760 2026-07-29 CU3 (2026.07.25.1112544.4) — recovered 2026-08-18, hashed identical to the CU3 lock 8153709523381701809 2026-07-23 (launch/preload) CU2 (2026.06.26.1097863.1) — recovered; no older manifest exists, so there is no Steam CU1

The build is whatever version stamp the downloaded exe carries — the snapshot reads it from there, so a wrong guess in --name mislabels the scratch directory, never the store. The .DepotDownloader state directory is excluded from hashing (see build_lock.py), so a recovered build hashes identically to the same build caught live. Two caveats. Steam grants manifest request codes per manifest, and codes for old manifests are not guaranteed forever — if DepotDownloader reports the code was denied, that build is gone through official channels, which is the whole argument for snapshotting on the day an update lands. And SteamDB's "seen" dates are its crawler's, not the release's (the ship dates above were settled from its build history on 2026-08-19), so a build-to-manifest mapping is confirmed only when the downloaded exe says so; for the three above, it did.

~~Two chunks defeat the built-in Oodle decoder (OozError)~~ — fixed 2026-08-19. D40/_Generated_/BSP_Split and E20/_Generated_/BSP_Settlement (both scenario_structure_bsp) failed identically on CU2, CU3 and CU4, so it was never an update regression. It was also not a missing codec variant: oozextract mishandles two unaligned tail reads that ooz itself performs. Both readers fetch a 32-bit word that ooz lets run past the end of the compressed region, relying on the surplus bits being masked off before they reach a value. decode_multi_array's forward varbits reader clamped the read to the bytes remaining and right-aligned the short result, which shifts the whole word down 8 bits per missing byte. On BSP_Split that turned an interval length of 65238 into 32894, leaving 32344 bytes of an entropy array unconsumed. TansDecoder::tans_forward_bits did not clamp at all and failed the decode outright as out of bounds.

Both now pad the tail with zeroes, keeping the surviving bits in position. Verified by decoding every Oodle block of every container on CU2, CU3 and CU4 with the stock and patched decoders side by side: 5 blocks per build newly decode, and every block that already decoded is byte-for-byte unchanged. The fix lives in a fork wired up through [patch.crates-io] in the workspace Cargo.toml; drop it once it lands in a published oozextract release — upstream PR. There is still no loose oo2core_*_win64.dll to fall back on — UE 5.5 links Oodle statically — but the pure decoder no longer needs one.

Does Halo Campaign Evolved run on real Blam tag data like the classic games, or are bipeds, weapons, vehicles, and levels ordinary Unreal Engine assets with Halo-themed names?

Verified: both, split by responsibility. The shipping build contains 12,328 genuine Blam tag files spanning 101 classic tag groups. Every sampled payload carries the BLAM tag-file signature and a group four-character code that matches its filename. Simulation-side definitions — bipeds, weapons, vehicles, projectiles, AI characters, squads, animation graphs, collision models, physics models, damage effects, Megalo, multiplayer variant settings — are real tags. Rendering is entirely Unreal. Zero render_model tags and zero bitmap tags ship. The classic Blam render pipeline is absent; visual representation is bound through UE5 Blueprint actors referenced from the tag packages.

Verified: reproduced by an executable check against the installed build. Observed: present in an artifact, but runtime reachability is not proven. Hypothesis: a testable interpretation that still needs a discriminating check.

Verified: all 28 IoStore containers under Meteorite/Content/Paks parse as UE 5.5 TOC version 8 (ReplaceIoChunkHashWithIoHash), Oodle-compressed, indexed, and not encrypted. The directory index lists 132,091 entries. Extension Count .uasset 89,685 .ubulk 28,151 .umap 14,240 .ushaderbytecode 15 There are no ExternalFile chunks and no loose tag or .map cache files anywhere in the install. Every tag is packaged as a normal cooked Unreal package. Verified: 24,618 index entries live under Meteorite/Content/Tags, split into 12,328 .uasset headers (8.5 MiB total) and 12,290 .ubulk payloads (5,648.6 MiB total). Each tag is one Unreal package whose bulk-data segment is the raw Blam tag file. Naming convention: the Blam path objects\characters\elite\elite.biped becomes the Unreal package /Game/Tags/objects/characters/elite/elite-biped. The group separator changed from . to - because Unreal reserves . for the object path separator.

Verified across 168 sampled payloads covering all 101 shipped groups: every .ubulk begins with a 0x4C-byte header, and header + payload_size == chunk_size holds for every sample. Offset Size Field Evidence 0x00 0x24 Zero in every sample. Verified 0x24 4 0x00000001 in every sample. Verified 0x28 4 0x00000002 in every sample. Verified 0x2C 4 0xFFFFFFFF in every sample. Verified 0x30 4 Group four-CC, little-endian (bipd, weap, vehi, sbsp, ...). Matches the filename group in 168/168 samples. Verified 0x34 4 Small integer, group-constant (bipd=3, weap=2, sbsp=5, coll=10). Observed 0x38 4 Per-tag 32-bit value, differs between tags of the same group. Observed 0x3C 4 BLAM signature, stored as the little-endian uint32 0x4D414C42. Verified 0x40 4 tag! signature, stored as 0x21676174. Verified 0x44 4 Zero in every sample. Verified 0x48 4 Payload size. Equals chunk_size - 0x4C in 168/168 samples. Verified 0x4C — Tag body begins. Verified Hypothesis: the value at 0x34 is a tag-group version number. It is constant per group and its magnitude tracks group complexity, but no discriminating check has been run.

The body opens with additional group-invariant marker dwords (blay, then 4444, CCCC, wwww in a weapon sample), followed by a per-group value and a table of record counts. Superseded 2026-07-26: the markers are fixed ASCII fill constants and the count table is a manifest for the twelve definition tables, checked against them for all 12,290 tags. See tag_body_format.md.

Verified by resolving the global ScriptObjects chunk in global.utoc (54,825 script objects) and parsing the zen package header: /Game/Tags/objects/characters/elite/elite-biped export[0] elite-biped class = /Script/BlamSynchronization/BlamBipedTagDataAsset template = /Script/BlamSynchronization/Default__BlamBipedTagDataAsset serial = 104 bytes (tag body lives in the 49,702-byte .ubulk) /Script/BlamSynchronization declares 176 Blam*TagDataAsset classes; 101 of them have shipped instances. Verified 2026-08-07: the shipped sbsp payloads carry no render geometry, only its skeleton. Walking holdouts-scenario_structure_bsp (143.1 MiB) in full shows the tag is dominated by collision data — winged-edge collision BSPs for 754 instanced-geometry definitions (~110 MiB), Havok mopp code, and kd/supernode hierarchies — while render geometry holds 755 mesh descriptors and compression-info bounds with an api resource body of zero bytes, and both resource interface pageable resources are likewise unattached (section magic third byte NUL). The same holds for per-object tags: collision_model and skeleton_model payloads are complete, but no vertex or index buffer exists anywhere in the Blam data. Mesh data ships only as Unreal SK_*/SM_* packages (593 skeletal-mesh and 22,610 static-mesh packages in the index). Reproduce with cargo run --example probe_geometry -- scenario_structure_bsp holdouts and --example probe_meshes -- elite in apps/tag-editor/src-tauri.

Verified 2026-08-08 — the game uses Nanite. Static-mesh .ubulk payloads open with the NFM fixup magic: they are Nanite cluster pages, and the "cooked out" LOD0 slots in FStaticMeshRenderData are the LODs Nanite replaced. What remains readable classically is the inline Nanite fallback mesh (correct shape and materials, reduced density). ~~Skeletal meshes do not use Nanite and keep full detail.~~ (Corrected below: the vehicles' skeletal hulls are Nanite too.) The ue-asset crate reads the whole chain — usmap reflection schemas (dumped from the running game via UE4SS DumpUSMAP, defs/ue/Meteorite-2607-CU3.usmap), zen package structure, unversioned properties, StaticMesh buffers, and MaterialInstance texture parameters — a 1,200 package soak parses 99.25%.

Verified 2026-09-06 — the Nanite pages decode. ue_asset::nanite (a Rust port of CUE4Parse's reader, Apache-2.0, credited in NOTICE) parses the FResources block that trails the LOD array — in a zen package the streamable-pages bulk header is a single i32 index into the package's bulk-data map, not the legacy inline header — and decodes every page: fixup chunk, cluster headers, strip-coded triangle indices, the low/mid/high byte streams behind positions, normals, tangents, colours and UVs, and vertex references into earlier clusters through the page dependencies. Full-leaf clusters (flag 0x4) are welded on position, normal and UV into one Lod with a section per material, which the mesh viewer, mjolnir mesh export and the glTF writer prefer over the fallback. Skeletal meshes carry the same block directly after their LOD array (no inlined-LOD bytes first), and it is where the vehicle hulls live: SK_Warthog_01 decodes to 197k triangles where its classic buffers hold the suspension alone. Weapons and the Ghost/Banshee keep a one-triangle placeholder in the pages as well as in the buffers. The gated test shipped_nanite_meshes_decode_consistently sweeps the install: 1,495 of the first 1,500 static meshes carry pages and all decode with no vertex outside its cluster's box, no unresolved reference, and a triangle count within a tenth of the builder's input;
the only meshes whose bounds differ from their fallback are biome trees and plants, whose fallbacks are wind-proxy shapes.

Verified 2026-09-06 — the World Partition cells read, and their placements land where the cook says. A mission's Unreal geometry is Levels/Halo1/Solo/<M>/<M>/_Generated_/<id>.umap, one cell per grid square (A30: 575 cells plus the persistent A30.umap; C10: 2,404). A cell's exports are its actors and their scene components; ue_asset::level::CellReader walks the components with the usmap, composes RelativeLocation/RelativeRotation/RelativeScale3D up the AttachParent chain (row-vector matrices, child × parent, Unreal's FScaleRotationTranslationMatrix), and expands instanced components from the native bytes that trail their properties: a 4-byte flag, the cached FBoxSphereBounds (seven doubles) when the flag is set, then the bulk-serialized element size 128[count × FMatrix] of doubles, found by its header and accepted only when every matrix is affine. Three things the reflection data does not say: FBox is natively serialized (six doubles and a byte, no fragment header), which the walker now knows — before that every HierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponent failed on BuiltInstanceBounds; a placed component leaves unset what equals its template, so a rock Blueprint's StaticMesh is read from StaticMeshComponent0_GEN_VARIABLE in the Blueprint package, reached through the export's template reference and the imported public export hash (zen::Package::import_target);

and the zen ImportedPackageNames batch carries an FName number per name that must be folded back (SM_Black_Locust_wdvhberja + 7 is SM_Black_Locust_wdvhberja_6), or a tenth of A30's placements name meshes that do not exist. Packed level actors (BP_ScreeAssembly_*) put their instanced components straight into the cell. The gated test shipped_cells_place_inside_their_cached_bounds reads every A30 cell — 1,825,198 placements — and checks each instance's world translation against its component's cached bounds: 71 of 59,478 fall outside, all the cook's dummy instances parked at (0, 0, -25000); every mesh a placement names resolves once /Engine/ and plugin mount points are mapped. Rendering a cell's .glb in three.js shows the rocks and ledges where the game has them.

Verified 2026-09-06 — cooked property blocks of every kind re-encode byte for byte, and an edited package loads. ue_asset::props (the lossless unversioned-block codec that already rebuilt every tag wrapper) now covers what materials, data assets and Blueprint packages use: the zero mask (a fragment flagged 0x80 carries one mask bit per value; a masked value has no bytes), floats, doubles, strings, FText (kept raw; history types None, Base and StringTableEntry), sets, enums as their underlying type, and the natively serialized structs by size — plus three layouts measured from the bytes: FMaterialOverrideNanite is eight native bytes (01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00) followed by its reflected block; FGameplayTagContainer is a raw name array; FRichCurveKey is 27 bytes. Two header rules the tag wrappers never exercised: a fragment whose skip has reached 127 may still carry values (it closes only when another absent slot follows), and a block with no value at all is one fragment skipping every slot, while trailing skip fragments after the last value are dropped. ue_asset::edit addresses a value by path (ScalarParameterValues[4].ParameterValue, RuntimeRegions{head}.Permutations{default}), sets it from text, and ZenPackage::set_export_bytes re-lays a multi-export package.

Sweep over 1,500 packages each of MI_, DA_ and BP_ (shipped_material_and_blueprint_blocks_round_trip): 22,014 exports exact, 0 mismatched, 390 refused by name (InstancedPropertyBag, NiagaraVariable, maps with removed keys); every tag wrapper still exact. In game: two vector parameters of MIP_Rifle_AssaultRifle_Default (the first-person rifle's material) set to 80,0,0,1 through mjolnir ue set, installed as pakchunk995-MJOLNIRUE2_P, read back as 80,0,0,1 from the running game's material instance by reflection. The emissive tints did not visibly recolour the rifle's lights — the display and indicator glow come from other materials — so the proof is the reflected value, not the pixels. Also found: no shipped package carries a populated RuntimeRegions map; the mesh-sync data assets hold only ModelTag, and the region-to-mesh binding is made at runtime, so a mesh swap by soft-path rewrite has nothing cooked to rewrite.

Verified 2026-08-19 — an object tag reaches its render mesh through its actor Blueprint. The tag's .uasset imports name BP_* actor packages; each Blueprint's mesh component templates (SCS SkeletalMeshComponent / StaticMeshComponent exports) carry the SK_/SM_ package as an object property, plus RelativeLocation/RelativeRotation/RelativeScale3D in actor space. The warthog resolves to SK_Warthog_01 + antenna + chaingun this way; the tag editor's Model and World views draw the chase's results (render_mesh_refs in apps/tag-editor/src-tauri/src/lib.rs). Three caveats, all verified against the install:

Characters bind placeholders. A biped's Blueprint binds an anim-dynamics helper (SK_Sacristan_AnimDynamics_PLY, 2 triangles) and picks the body at runtime. The route to the real body is the Blam*MeshSynchronizationDataAsset packages: 62 ship, each importing exactly one hlmt (ModelTag), anchoring the model tag to its asset folder — DA_Elite_MeshSynchronization → /Game/characters/Elite/Common → Mesh/SK_Elite_Common_Body (236 cm tall) + head. The editor uses these as fallbacks when no Blueprint-bound mesh is readable. The unit constant is 1 wu = 304.8 cm (the classic 10-foot world unit): the elite body's 236 cm over its 0.79 wu collision shell, and the Blam skeleton overlaying the SK bind pose exactly at that scale in the Model view. The engine negates Y between Blam and Unreal space, so a mesh drawn among tag data mirrors Y back. Some meshes stay unreadable classically. Skeletal-Nanite meshes (weapons, most Covenant vehicles) hold placeholder triangles — in their Nanite pages too, as of the 2026-09-06 decode; and vehicles like the warthog keep only the suspension in their SK's classic buffers — the hull ships as ~40 per-region rig statics (Mesh/Static/SM_Warthog_*, bone-local frames, matching Blam region names) attached at runtime, and whole in the SK's Nanite pages. ~~Assembling those rigs is open work;

affected objects fall back to their collision shells.~~ Assembled the same day; see "a vehicle's hull is rig statics" below. Verified 2026-08-19 — a vehicle's hull is rig statics on the SK's skeleton. The warthog's SK_Warthog_01 carries only the suspension geometry (one InteriorWheelsShocks material); the hull, panels, wheels and accessories ship as ~60 statics under the SK's sibling Mesh/Static/ folder, in bone-local frames, attached at runtime. No shipped data records the piece-to-bone binding (the SkeletalMeshSocket exports on SKEL_Warthog_01 are character-IK and VFX attach points, and the MeshSynchronization data assets hold only ModelTag), so the binding is by name convention, loosely spelled: SM_Warthog_Tire_Back_Left ↔ bone Wheel_Back_Left, SM_Warthog_Base_Axle_* ↔ Axle_Base_*, SM_Warthog_Hood ↔ Hood_Base. Token-set matching with a handful of synonyms places every named piece; what the rig does not name (side panels, windshield, accessories) sits in the chassis frame — attaching those to the Body bone lands them exactly inside the vehicle envelope. The assembled warthog spans 613×325×243 cm, matching its 1.92 wu posed collision shell. Implemented as rig_static_refs in apps/tag-editor/src-tauri/src/lib.rs; probe_rig_match reproduces the match table.

Verified 2026-08-19 — the material library's colour is in vector parameters, not textures. Vehicle materials (MI_Warthog_GreenHull, …) are layered: their CO/COH texture maps are channel-packed masks (decoding one as albedo paints the mesh purple), and the visible colour lives in VectorParameterValues — Color Top/Mid/Bottom is the paint gradient (the warthog's olive is Color Top = 0.397, 0.397, 0.216), BaseColor per layer index is near-black primer, Color Tint is a multiplier. The mesh viewers now carry that flat colour per material slot as the stand-in when no albedo texture resolves.
